title: Nelson Mandela
text:
Nelson Mandela was born Rolihlahla Mandela in 1918 in the village of Mvezo, South Africa, into the Thembu royal family. His father was a local chief and councillor, and Mandela received the English name “Nelson” from his teacher at a Methodist school. After his father’s death, he was placed under the guardianship of Chief Jongintaba Dalindyebo, receiving a Western-style education at Clarkebury and Healdtown, before attending the University of Fort Hare. He began studying law at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, where he encountered racial discrimination but also formed friendships with people of various ethnicities and political persuasions.

In Johannesburg, Mandela became involved in anti-colonial politics, joining the African National Congress (ANC) in 1943 and co-founding its Youth League in 1944. Fueled by a desire for Black self-determination, the Youth League advocated for more assertive action against racial segregation. He married Evelyn Mase in 1944 and began working as an articled clerk at a law firm, continuing his legal studies. With the 1948 election bringing the National Party to power and instituting the system of apartheid, Mandela and the ANC committed to dismantling racial segregation. 

Initially committed to non-violent protest, Mandela became influenced by Marxist ideas and, in 1961, co-founded the militant uMkhonto we Sizwe, which launched a sabotage campaign against the apartheid government. He was arrested in 1962 and, after the Rivonia Trial, sentenced to life imprisonment in 1964 for conspiring to overthrow the state. He spent the next 27 years in prison, serving time on Robben Island, Pollsmoor Prison, and Victor Verster Prison.

Amidst growing pressure both within South Africa and internationally, President F.W. de Klerk released Mandela in 1990. Mandela and de Klerk then collaborated to negotiate the end of apartheid, culminating in the first multiracial general election in 1994. Mandela led the ANC to victory and became South Africa's first Black head of state. As president, he focused on racial reconciliation, creating the Truth and Reconciliation Commission to address past human rights abuses. While his administration retained a liberal economic framework, he also introduced measures to address land reform, poverty, and healthcare. 

After serving one term, Mandela stepped down in 1999, dedicating himself to combating poverty and HIV/AIDS through the Nelson Mandela Foundation. Throughout his life, he was a controversial figure, facing criticism from both the right and the left, but he ultimately gained international acclaim for his activism and commitment to social justice. He received numerous honors, including the Nobel Peace Prize, and is widely revered in South Africa as “Madiba” and the “Father of the Nation”. He died in 2013, leaving behind a legacy as a global icon of democracy and equality.

title: Liam Neeson
text:
Liam Neeson, born in Northern Ireland in 1952, is a highly acclaimed actor with nominations for an Academy Award, a BAFTA Award, three Golden Globes, and two Tony Awards. Recognized as one of Ireland’s greatest film actors, he was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire in 2000. Neeson began his film career in 1978 with *Pilgrim's Progress*, followed by roles in films like *Excalibur*, *The Bounty*, *The Mission*, and *Husbands and Wives*. He achieved significant recognition for his portrayal of Oskar Schindler in Steven Spielberg’s *Schindler’s List* (1993), earning an Academy Award nomination and solidifying his status as a leading man.

Throughout the 1990s, Neeson continued to take on dramatic roles in films such as *Nell*, *Rob Roy*, *Michael Collins*, and *Les Misérables*. He also ventured into blockbuster cinema, playing Qui-Gon Jinn in *Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace*, Ra’s al Ghul in *Batman Begins*, and Aslan in *The Chronicles of Narnia* trilogy.  His filmography includes diverse projects like *Gangs of New York*, *Love Actually*, *Kinsey*, *Chloe*, *Silence*, and *A Monster Calls*. 

A turning point in his career came in 2009 when he began to be recognized as an action star with *Taken* and subsequent action thrillers like *The A-Team*, *The Grey*, *Wrath of the Titans*, *A Walk Among the Tombstones*, and *Cold Pursuit*. He developed a fruitful working relationship with director Jaume Collet-Serra, appearing in four of his films: *Unknown*, *Non-Stop*, *Run All Night*, and *The Commuter*. 

Prior to his film success, Neeson spent two years with the Lyric Players' Theatre in Belfast starting in 1976. He also had a notable stage career in New York, receiving Tony Award nominations for his performances in revivals of Eugene O'Neill's *Anna Christie* and Arthur Miller's *The Crucible*. He also portrayed Oscar Wilde in David Hare’s *The Judas Kiss*.

Born in Ballymena, County Antrim, Neeson grew up Catholic in a predominantly Protestant area, an experience he described as cautious. He attended St Patrick's College and later briefly attended Queen's University Belfast before working at Guinness Brewery.  His early interest in acting was sparked, surprisingly, by observing the theatrical presence of Ian Paisley. Before dedicating himself to acting, he even briefly pursued a career in football. 

Neeson's path to acting included a period of casual labor and teacher training before joining the Lyric Players Theatre. He gained experience in Dublin with the Project Arts Centre and the Abbey Theatre, appearing in productions like Brian Friel’s *Translations*. His breakthrough role in film came with *Excalibur*, leading to a move to London and eventual success in Hollywood.  His performance in *Schindler’s List* cemented his acclaim, and he continued to balance mainstream and independent projects, establishing himself as a versatile and respected actor.

title: Hu Qili
text:
Hu Qili, born in 1929 in Shaanxi Province, is a former high-ranking official of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) who rose to prominence as a proponent of economic reform in the 1980s. He joined the CCP in 1948 and initially focused on political studies after the founding of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, having begun his education in physics. His early career involved significant roles within the Communist Youth League, serving as secretary of its Peking University Committee and later as president of the All-China Students’ Federation. He even had an audience with Mao Zedong in 1958.

During the Cultural Revolution, Hu was sent to work at the lower levels of May Seventh Cadre Schools. Following this period, he held various leadership positions, including deputy president of Tsinghua University and party secretary and mayor of Tianjin between 1980 and 1982. He steadily climbed the ranks of the CCP, becoming a member of the Politburo and Secretariat in 1982, and a leading member of the CCP Secretariat from 1985 to 1989.  His ascent culminated in a position on the Politburo Standing Committee from 1987 to 1989, positioning him as a potential future General Secretary.

Hu’s political career was dramatically impacted by the Tiananmen Square protests of 1989.  Aligned with General Secretary Zhao Ziyang, he advocated for dialogue with the student protestors and a policy of openness and tolerance in reporting on the movement. He publicly expressed belief that the students were acting reasonably and that accurate information should be provided to them.  He and Zhao Ziyang were the only two members of the Politburo Standing Committee to oppose the implementation of martial law. This opposition led to his purge from the party following the June 1989 plenum, where he and several others were stripped of their posts.

However, Hu made a return to government in 1991, serving as vice minister of the Ministry of the Machine-Building and Electronics Industry. He later became Minister of the same ministry from 1993 to 1998. He was then elected vice chairman of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference in 1998, tasked with restoring political treatment for party and state leaders.  Finally, he became chairman of the Soong Ching-ling Foundation in 2001, a role he held until his retirement in 2016, focusing on Chinese charities and welfare projects. As of April 2024, Hu Qili is the sole surviving member of the 13th Politburo Standing Committee from the first three plenary sessions.

title: Rachel Bilson
text:
Rachel Bilson, born August 25, 1981, in Los Angeles, is an American actress who comes from a family deeply rooted in the entertainment industry. Her father, Danny Bilson, is a writer, director, and producer, and her mother, Janice Stango, is a therapist. She has an older half-brother and two younger half-sisters. Her family background includes Jewish and Catholic heritage, resulting in a “Chrismukkah” upbringing. Her great-grandfather worked in the movie trailer department for RKO Pictures, and her great-grandmother was a screenwriter.

Bilson began her acting career with appearances in commercials for brands like Subway, Raisin Bran, and Pepto-Bismol. She made her television debut in 2003 with small roles in *Buffy the Vampire Slayer* and *8 Simple Rules for Dating My Teenage Daughter*. Her breakthrough role came with the series *The O.C.*, where she was initially cast for a few episodes but became a regular due to the popularity of her character, Summer Roberts, and her romantic storyline with Seth Cohen, played by Adam Brody. During her time on *The O.C.*, she received several accolades including three awards at the 2005 Teen Choice Awards and was featured in *Maxim* and *FHM* magazines, though she previously turned down opportunities for seminude photoshoots, believing her body was private.

She transitioned to film with *The Last Kiss* in 2006 and then starred in the action film *Jumper* in 2008, where she met her future partner, Hayden Christensen. Bilson continued to appear in television, including guest spots on *Chuck* and *How I Met Your Mother*. From 2011 to 2015, she led *Hart of Dixie* as Dr. Zoe Hart, a series executive produced by *The O.C.* creator Josh Schwartz. She later joined the cast of *Nashville* in 2017 and starred in the short-lived ABC drama *Take Two* in 2018. More recently, she co-launched the podcasts *Welcome to the OC, Bitches!* with Melinda Clarke, revisiting *The O.C.*, and *Broad Ideas with Rachel Bilson* with Olivia Allen, featuring interviews with entertainment industry figures.

Beyond acting, Bilson has a strong interest in fashion. She’s described as a “fashion junkie” with a vintage style, and in 2008 launched a clothing line, Edie Rose, with DKNY Jeans, aiming for affordable fashion. She later collaborated with Steve Madden to launch the online shoe platform ShoeMint in 2011, and designed a shirt for Invisible Children in 2013. She was unfortunately the target of burglaries by the "Bling Ring" which resulted in the loss of much of her fashion collection.

Bilson dated *The O.C.* co-star Adam Brody from 2003 to 2006. She then began a relationship with Hayden Christensen in 2007 and, after a brief period where an engagement was called off, the couple reconciled and had a daughter in 2014 before separating in 2017. Both Bilson and Christensen are advocates for the No Kids Policy, protecting celebrity children from unwanted paparazzi attention.

title: Rebecca Romijn
text:
Rebecca Romijn was born in Berkeley, California, in 1972 to an English teacher mother and a Dutch furniture maker father. Her maternal grandfather was a Presbyterian minister. While she is known for her glamorous image, Romijn has spoken about feeling insecure as a teenager and even suffering from scoliosis during a growth spurt, a story she initially claimed was fabricated as a joke. She studied music at the University of California, Santa Cruz before launching a successful modeling career in 1991, appearing on covers for numerous international editions of magazines like Elle, Cosmopolitan, and Sports Illustrated, and walking runways for designers such as Giorgio Armani. She also hosted MTV’s *House of Style* from 1998 to 2000 and was frequently included on lists of the world’s most beautiful women.

Romijn transitioned into acting with her breakout role as Mystique in the *X-Men* film series, appearing in *X-Men* (2000), *X2* (2003), and *X-Men: The Last Stand* (2006). The role required extensive makeup and prosthetics. She continued to build her film career with roles in films like *Femme Fatale*, *Rollerball*, *The Punisher*, and *Godsend*. 

On television, she gained prominence for her role as Alexis Meade, a transgender character, on the ABC series *Ugly Betty* beginning in 2007, though her role later became recurring. She also appeared on shows such as *Carpoolers*, *Eastwick*, and *NTSF:SD:SUV::*. More recently, Romijn starred as Eve Baird in *The Librarians* and voiced Lois Lane in the DC Animated Movie Universe. She also played Una Chin-Riley in *Star Trek: Discovery* and subsequently in *Star Trek: Strange New Worlds*, beginning in 2022, and currently co-hosts *The Real Love Boat* with her husband. She is slated to reprise her role as Mystique in a future Marvel Cinematic Universe film. 

Romijn was married to John Stamos from 1998 to 2005. In 2007, she married actor Jerry O'Connell, and they have twin daughters born in 2008. While she uses her maiden name professionally, she revealed she never legally changed her name back from Romijn-Stamos following her first divorce. Beyond acting and modeling, Romijn has also contributed to music, providing vocals for cover songs and collaborating with RuPaul.

title: Terrence Romeo
text:
Terrence Bill Vitanzos Romeo, born March 16, 1992, is a Filipino professional basketball player currently with the Terrafirma Dyip of the Philippine Basketball Association (PBA). He is a versatile player, capable of playing both point guard and shooting guard. His professional career began after being drafted fifth overall by Barako Bull in the 2013 PBA draft, following a highly decorated amateur career.

Romeo's basketball journey started with the Letran Squires before he was recruited by Far Eastern University (FEU). He quickly made an impact, setting a UAAP Juniors basketball record by scoring 83 points in a single game, surpassing the previous record of 69. This performance earned him the UAAP Juniors' Most Valuable Player award in 2009, alongside averages of 37.1 points, 4.1 assists, and 4.0 steals per game. 

His collegiate career at FEU saw initial challenges adapting to a role secondary to UAAP MVP RR Garcia. While named Rookie of the Year, his shooting percentage was initially low at 32%, averaging 9.9 points. He steadily improved, averaging 11.4 points, 4.8 rebounds, and 3.2 assists in his sophomore year, helping FEU reach the UAAP Finals.  In his final two years, Romeo blossomed into a dominant force, earning spots on the UAAP Mythical Team and culminating in being named the 2013 UAAP Men's Basketball Most Valuable Player. He became only the third guard to win the award. During this period, he consistently scored 30+ points in multiple games, a feat only matched by a few players since 2003. He also played in the PBA D-League for the Big Chill Super Chargers while still in college.

Romeo’s PBA career began with GlobalPort Batang Pier in 2013, where he quickly showcased his scoring ability, including a 34-point performance in just his second professional game. He drew comparisons to PBA legend Mark Caguioa, who himself recognized Romeo’s potential. His sophomore year saw him lose weight to improve his agility and quickness, becoming a key component of a talented GlobalPort backcourt. He continued to develop, earning recognition at the 2015 PBA All-Star Weekend, winning the Three-Point Shootout and being named All-Star Game MVP. He was awarded the PBA Most Improved Player after leading GlobalPort to their best finish in the 2015 Governors' Cup and becoming the league's top local scorer.  He formed a potent offensive duo with Stanley Pringle, dubbed the "Slash Brothers".

He was later traded to TNT KaTropa in 2018, following disagreements with his coach, and then to San Miguel Beermen in December of the same year. With San Miguel, he contributed to their championship runs, including a significant 29-point performance in Game 2 of the 2019 Commissioner's Cup Finals. In November 2024, he was traded to Terrafirma Dyip, a move he described as difficult, but to which he committed.

Beyond the PBA, Romeo has represented the Philippines in 3x3 basketball, leading Manila West to victory at the 2014 FIBA 3x3 World Tour Manila Masters and earning individual accolades. He has also been a member of the Gilas Pilipinas national team, participating in tournaments like the William Jones Cup and the 2015 FIBA Asia Championship.  Recently, in January 2025, he began his coaching career as the head coach of the PSP Gymers in the Women's Maharlika Pilipinas Basketball League.

title: Mark Murphy (singer)
text:
Mark Murphy, a highly respected jazz singer, was born in Syracuse, New York, in 1932 and passed away in 2015. He built a career spanning over six decades, recording 51 albums under his own name and becoming known for his innovative vocal improvisations. His talent was recognized with four Down Beat magazine awards for Best Male Vocalist between 1996 and 2001, and he received five Grammy nominations for Best Vocal Jazz Performance. Beyond performing, Murphy also wrote lyrics to well-known jazz tunes, including “Stolen Moments” and “Red Clay.”

Murphy’s musical upbringing was steeped in tradition, with his parents involved in church choir direction and his grandmother and aunt serving as church organists. He began piano lessons at age seven and in his teens, joined his brother’s jazz dance band, drawing early influence from singers like Peggy Lee, Nat “King” Cole, and Ella Fitzgerald, as well as pianist Art Tatum. He studied Music and Drama at Syracuse University, graduating in 1953 after being discovered by Sammy Davis Jr. who helped connect him with opportunities in New York City.

After moving to New York, Murphy pursued both acting and singing, performing with the Gilbert and Sullivan Light Opera Company and appearing on television, while also twice placing second in amateur singing contests at the Apollo Theatre. His recording career began with Decca Records in 1956, but after modest success, he moved to Los Angeles in 1958, recording for Capitol Records and achieving a minor hit with “This Could Be the Start of Something.”  Returning to New York in the early 1960s, he recorded for Riverside Records, including the album *Rah* featuring accompaniment from jazz greats like Bill Evans and Clark Terry, and *That’s How I Love the Blues*, which became a personal favorite. His 1963 single “Fly Me to the Moon” achieved chart success and earned him a "New Star of the Year" award from *Down Beat*.

In 1963, Murphy relocated to London, establishing himself in the jazz scene at Ronnie Scott's Club and gaining regular airplay on BBC Radio. This period included recordings in London and Germany, including the acclaimed *Midnight Mood*. He also worked on Dutch radio and appeared in British film and television productions, and it was during this time he met his long-time partner, Eddie O'Sullivan. 

Returning to the United States in 1972, Murphy embarked on a prolific period with the Muse label, releasing an album per year for over fourteen years. These albums included Grammy-nominated works like *Satisfaction Guaranteed* and *Bop for Kerouac*, the latter reflecting his admiration for writer Jack Kerouac. He later explored Brazilian music, collaborating with the band Viva Brasil and incorporating the music of Antonio Carlos Jobim and Milton Nascimento into his repertoire. 

His career continued with recordings on Milestone and HighNote Records, as well as collaborations with artists in the acid jazz and hip-hop genres, including UFO. Throughout his later years, he released numerous anthologies and continued touring internationally, performing in the U.S., Europe, Australia, and Japan until shortly before his death in 2015. He was the first recipient of the Jazz Foundation of America’s “Words and Music Award” in 2009, cementing his legacy as “a major name in vocal jazz.”

title: Daniel Alexander Cameron
text:
Daniel Alexander Cameron was a Canadian politician from Nova Scotia, notable for being among the first legislators from the province to pass away while still in office in the 20th century. Born on December 10, 1870, in Sydney River, Nova Scotia, he was the son of John and Isabella (Macdonald) Cameron. His early education took place at Sydney Academy, and he later pursued legal studies at Dalhousie University, ultimately earning a Bachelor of Laws degree. 

Cameron was officially admitted to the Nova Scotia bar in October 1893, following which he established a law practice in Sydney, beginning in 1894. Beyond his legal career, he was actively involved in local government. He served as a member of the County Council for a considerable period, from 1900 to 1911. During this time, he also held the position of stipendiary magistrate for Sydney from 1905 to 1911, demonstrating a commitment to local judicial administration. In 1911, his responsibilities expanded as he was appointed treasurer and solicitor for the Municipality of Cape Breton.

Cameron’s provincial political career began in 1916 when he successfully ran for a seat in the Nova Scotia House of Assembly, representing the electoral district of Cape Breton. As a member of the Nova Scotia Liberal party, he served one term before being defeated in the 1920 election. However, his political involvement didn’t end there. From 1921 to 1923, he transitioned to the Legislative Council of Nova Scotia and was appointed as a Minister Without Portfolio in the cabinet led by George Henry Murray. He voluntarily resigned from the Legislative Council in 1923, choosing instead to contest and win a seat in the House of Assembly, this time for the electoral district of Victoria County. 

This return to the House of Assembly led to another cabinet position, serving as Provincial Secretary in the government of Ernest Howard Armstrong from 1923 to 1925. Following a period out of office, he resigned a position in 1930 and attempted a transition to federal politics, running as the Liberal candidate for the electoral district of Cape Breton South in the 1930 federal election, but was unsuccessful. He re-entered provincial politics in 1935, winning a seat in the House of Assembly for the combined district of Cape Breton North and Victoria. Unfortunately, his time in office was cut short, as he died while still serving as a Member of the Legislative Assembly in 1937, having served for just under two years of that term.

title: Andreea Marin
text:
Andreea Violeta Marin, born on December 22, 1974, is a prominent figure in Romanian television, working as a presenter and personality. Her academic background is diverse, having pursued studies in Journalism, Public Relations & Advertisement, Computer Programming, and Mathematics & Physics during her time in college. She began her career in television in 1994, initially working as an emcee at TVR Iași. 

Marin’s success in the Romanian media landscape led to recognition as the most successful female media person in the country. She gained further exposure through her involvement with the Eurovision Song Contest, presenting the Romanian votes during the finals in 2000, 2004, 2006, and 2007. A significant moment in her hosting career was when she hosted the 2006 Junior Eurovision Song Contest on December 2nd of that year.

For an extended period, beginning in 1999, Marin has been the host and director of the television program *Surprize, Surprize* ("Surprises, Surprises") which airs on TVR1. The show focuses on sharing the life stories of individuals facing various hardships, including those with disabilities, financial difficulties, or those separated from family members who have moved away.

Beyond her on-screen work, Marin also holds positions in media management. She currently serves as the communications director for Prime Time World Broadcast, a company based in Madrid. Additionally, she is the editorial director for the Romanian edition of *Business Woman Magazine*. 

Marin’s personal life has been public, marked by two marriages and subsequent divorces. In 2006, she married Romanian singer Ștefan Bănică Jr., taking the name Andreea Marin Bănică. They have one daughter together, Ana Violeta Bănică, born on December 15, 2007. This marriage ended in divorce in 2013.  She then married physician Tuncay Öztürk in 2014, but they announced the end of their relationship in October 2016, with the divorce being finalized on February 13, 2017.

title: Carrie Ann Inaba
text:
Carrie Ann Inaba, born January 5, 1968, is an American entertainer with a multifaceted career encompassing television, dance, choreography, acting, and singing. She is widely recognized as a judge on the ABC show *Dancing with the Stars*, a role she’s held since 2005, and previously co-hosted and moderated the CBS talk show *The Talk* from 2019 until 2021.

Inaba’s career began with a foray into the Japanese music scene in 1986, after winning a talent show in Hawaii. She was groomed as a pop star, releasing three singles, and hosting radio and television programs, though she eventually felt the industry prioritized image over artistry. Returning to the United States, she gained prominence as one of the “Fly Girls” on the sketch comedy show *In Living Color* from 1990 to 1992. She also performed with Prince and was a dancer in Madonna’s 1993 “Girlie Show” World Tour, famously agreeing to shave her head for the opportunity.

Throughout her career, Inaba has appeared in numerous films, often as a dancer, including *Monster Mash: The Movie*, *Austin Powers in Goldmember* where she played Fook Yu alongside Diane Mizota as Fook Mi, and *Showgirls*. She has also had smaller roles in television series like *Jack & Jill* and *Nikki*. Beyond performing, Inaba has worked extensively as a choreographer on programs such as *American Idol*, *The Swan*, and the *Miss America Pageant* for five years. She also contributed to the early seasons of *So You Think You Can Dance*.

Inaba founded EnterMediArts, Inc., a video production company, and has directed, written, and edited films including *Black Water* and documentaries about the Miss America pageant. She also served as a producer for the Broadway show *Burn the Floor* and was honored with the Visionary Award by East West Players for her contribution to the visibility of Asian Americans in entertainment.

Her television presence expanded beyond dancing and choreography with appearances on *The View* and hosting duties on the game show *1 vs. 100*. She was also a recurring guest co-host on *The Talk* before becoming a permanent co-host and moderator in 2019, leaving in 2021 after a leave of absence. 

Inaba’s personal life has included engagements to Artem Chigvintsev, Jesse Sloan (which ended in a broken engagement), and Robb Derringer. She is a passionate animal advocate, founding the Carrie Ann Animal Foundation and actively supporting organizations like the Humane Society and PETA. 

Inaba has openly discussed a number of health challenges, including severe vision impairment, spinal stenosis, Sjögren’s syndrome, lupus, chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, Tourette’s Syndrome as a child, and, most recently, acute gangrenous appendicitis requiring emergency surgery in 2023. She serves as a National Awareness Ambassador for the Sjögren Syndrome Foundation.  Despite her health struggles, she remains committed to raising awareness and funding for research into these conditions.

title: John Morris (curler)
text:
John Morris, nicknamed "Johnny Mo," is a Canadian curler born in 1978 in Canmore, Alberta, and a two-time Olympic gold medallist. He began curling at the age of five at the Navy Curling Club in Gloucester, Ontario, and his early career was marked by significant junior success. He skipped his Ottawa team to three consecutive Ontario provincial junior Men's titles from 1997 to 1999, culminating in victories at the 1998 and 1999 Canadian and World Junior Championships, where he established records for wins by a skip. 

Morris transitioned to men’s curling, initially competing out of Southwestern Ontario after attending Wilfrid Laurier University. He achieved provincial success, winning the 2002 Ontario championship and qualifying for the Brier, though he didn’t secure a national title at that time. He gained national attention at the 2001 Canadian Olympic Curling Trials, experiencing a difficult loss, and later competed in the 2003 Canada Cup, losing to Randy Ferbey. 

A pivotal move to Calgary in 2003 led to a new team with Kevin Koe, Marc Kennedy, and Paul Moffatt. While they achieved some tour success, including winning the 2004 Players’ Championship, they didn’t reach the provincial level. In 2006, Morris joined forces with Kevin Martin, embarking on a four-year plan to win Olympic gold. This partnership proved remarkably successful, with the team dominating the tour, including winning three Grand Slam events in their first season together. 

The Martin team achieved its ultimate goal at the 2010 Winter Olympics in Vancouver, winning the gold medal. They continued to excel, winning the 2008 Brier, the 2008 World Men's Curling Championship, and further provincial and Grand Slam titles. Morris was named MVP of the 2008 Brier finals. After parting ways with Martin in 2013, Morris joined Jim Cotter’s team, skipping them to a runner-up finish at the 2014 Brier. He notably became one of few curlers to represent three different provinces at the Brier, having previously played for Ontario and Alberta.

Morris then skipped a Team Canada comprised of former Kevin Koe teammates, winning the 2015 Brier and earning a bronze medal at the World Championships. He continued to switch teams and formats, eventually teaming up with Kaitlyn Lawes to win gold in mixed doubles at the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang. Following this, he continued to compete in mixed doubles and rejoined Kevin Koe’s team as second in 2020, competing at the 2020 Brier. Throughout his career, Morris has also authored a book on curling fitness, “Fit to Curl,” and is the son of Maureen and Earle Morris, the inventor of the “Stabilizer” curling broom.

title: Sila María Calderón
text:
Sila María Calderón Serra, born in San Juan, Puerto Rico in 1942, is a prominent figure in Puerto Rican politics and business, best known as the island’s first elected female governor, serving from 2001 to 2005. Her lineage includes a maternal grandfather who emigrated from Mallorca, Spain, which later granted her Spanish citizenship in 2012. She received a Bachelor of Arts degree in Government from Manhattanville College in 1964 and furthered her education at the University of Puerto Rico’s Graduate School of Public Administration.

Calderón’s career began in 1973 as an aide to the Labor Secretary, followed by a role as a special aide to Governor Rafael Hernández Colón. After a period in the private sector at Citibank, where she successfully developed new consumer products, she became president of Commonwealth Investment Company, a family-owned real estate business. She re-entered government service in 1984 as Chief of Staff to Hernández Colón, becoming the first woman to hold that position, and later served as the 12th Secretary of State of Puerto Rico in 1988. During these roles, she also participated in economic advisory councils and boards related to government development and the Fifth Centenary of the Discovery of the Americas.

Returning to the private sector in 1989, Calderón served on the boards of several major Puerto Rican corporations, including BanPonce and Banco Popular, and held leadership positions within organizations focused on economic development and public broadcasting. She re-entered political life in 1995, winning the mayoral election for San Juan in 1996, becoming only the second woman to hold that office. As mayor, she initiated extensive urban redevelopment projects across the city, focusing on revitalizing deteriorated areas and assisting impoverished communities.

In 2000, Calderón was elected Governor of Puerto Rico, leading the Popular Democratic Party to victory in a closely contested election. During her term, she prioritized aid to disadvantaged communities, establishing the Puerto Rico Office for Socioeconomic and Community Development with a significant investment of $1 billion, though the program faced criticism for incomplete projects and potential fund diversion. She chose to appoint her daughters, Sila Mari and María Elena, as joint First Ladies. She also strengthened ties with Latin American nations, receiving honors from the Dominican Republic, Panama, and Costa Rica for her efforts. 

Calderón did not seek re-election in 2004, and after leaving office, she became a partner in Inter-American Global Links, Inc., a consulting firm. She also chairs a philanthropic foundation dedicated to addressing issues like poverty, women’s rights, and urban revitalization. Throughout her career, she has received numerous awards and honorary degrees recognizing her contributions to public service and leadership. She has been married three times, first to Francisco Xavier González Goenaga, then to Adolfo Krans, and finally to Ramón Cantero Frau, all of which ended in divorce.

title: Jan Zamoyski
text:
Jan Zamoyski, born in 1542 and dying in 1605, was a pivotal figure in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, serving as a nobleman, magnate, statesman, and the first ordynat of Zamość. He rose through the ranks, holding prominent positions including Royal Secretary, Deputy Chancellor, Grand Chancellor of the Crown, and Great Hetman of the Crown, becoming a dominant force in the Commonwealth’s political landscape throughout his life. He was a key advisor to both Sigismund II Augustus and Stephen Báthory, but later became a major opponent of Sigismund III Vasa.

Zamoyski received a comprehensive education, starting in Poland and continuing abroad with studies at the Sorbonne, Collège de France, Strasbourg, and Padua, where he earned a doctorate in law in 1564. During his time abroad, he converted from Calvinism to Roman Catholicism. He became known for his active participation in university politics, even serving as rector of the law department, and authored a work on Roman government. Upon returning to Poland in 1565, he quickly gained favor with King Sigismund II, undertaking tasks like reorganizing the Chancellery archive and commanding royal forces.

He played a significant role in the royal elections following the extinction of the Jagiellon dynasty in 1572, advocating for a viritim election – allowing all nobles to vote – but his proposal for majority rule was unsuccessful, contributing to the future instability caused by the *liberum veto*. Zamoyski became a leader of the lesser nobility, championing reform and the preservation of the Commonwealth’s unique political system, earning him the nickname “the first tribune of nobility.” He supported Henry de Valois’s election, but faced embarrassment when the king abandoned Poland. He later actively opposed the Habsburgs and facilitated the marriage of Anna Jagiellon to Stephen Báthory.

Báthory rewarded Zamoyski with positions including Deputy Chancellor and, later, Grand Crown Chancellor, and he participated in quelling the Danzig rebellion. He married Krystyna Radziwiłł, strengthening his alliance with the powerful Radziwiłł family. He contributed significantly to the preparations for war against Muscovy, demonstrating a developing military aptitude. Despite personal tragedies, including the deaths of two wives and children, he continued to serve, eventually being appointed Grand Crown Hetman, a nomination considered technically illegal at the time. He participated in the prolonged Siege of Pskov, which, although unsuccessful in capturing the city, ultimately resulted in a favorable peace treaty for Poland. 

In later years, Zamoyski initially supported Sigismund III Vasa’s ascension but soon distanced himself due to the king’s pro-Habsburg policies. He clashed with Sigismund, even engaging in a heated exchange during a Sejm session. He fought against Tatar incursions, developed a plan for a buffer state in Moldavia, and successfully intervened in Moldavian and Wallachian affairs. He also led forces against Sweden in Livonia, while simultaneously opposing the war on the political front. 

Zamoyski amassed a considerable fortune from his vast estates and invested in economic development, including colonization and industry. He founded the city of Zamość, designed as a Renaissance “ideal city,” and established the Zamoyski Family Fee Tail, effectively creating a duchy. He founded the Zamojska Academy, the third university in Poland, and was a patron of the arts. While praised for his statesmanship and military leadership, Zamoyski was also noted for his pragmatic, sometimes self-serving, nature. He died in 1605, leaving a lasting legacy as one of the most significant figures in Polish history.

title: Rigoberto Torres
text:
Rigoberto Torres, born in Aguadilla, Puerto Rico in 1960, is a sculptor currently living and working in Florida. His early artistic experience involved working in a factory that produced cast religious figures, a skill that would later inform his artistic practice. He also identifies as a community-based artist, a description reflected in much of his work. Torres is particularly recognized for his collaborative sculptures with artist John Ahearn, created between 1981 and 1985. These pieces predominantly feature plaster and fiberglass depictions of the artists’ neighbors in the Bronx, New York City. 

Together, Torres and Ahearn created four significant murals: *We Are Family*, *Life on Dawson Street*, *Double Dutch*, and *Back to School*. *Double Dutch*, originally created in 1981 and restored in 2010, is now part of the collection at the Pérez Art Museum Miami. These sculptures weren’t confined to galleries; they were intentionally placed in public spaces – affixed to buildings, standing freely, and incorporated into street events as a form of performance art. Torres and Ahearn frequently moved their studio to the sidewalk to encourage neighborhood participation, with children often serving as both observers and models.

Torres’ work is characterized by a naturalistic approach to portraying people, resulting in accurate and compelling representations. His sculptures are described as demonstrating an instinctive ability to create scenes from individual figures, placing them within the tradition of humanistic naturalism. He first met Ahearn in 1980 while working at the religious statuary factory, and their partnership led to the creation of what is sometimes referred to as the “South Bronx Hall of Fame.” This body of work aimed to create monuments to everyday individuals, offering an alternative to the conventional practice of public monuments honoring only the famous or heroic.

Several of these collaborative sculptures remain installed throughout the Bronx. *Double Dutch* can be found at the intersection of Kelly Street and Intervale Avenue, while *Life on Dawson St.* is located on Longwood Avenue and Dawson Street. *We Are Family* faces 156th Street on Southern Boulevard, and additional casts are situated outside The POINT Community Development Corporation on Garrison Avenue. 

Beyond his work in the Bronx, Torres returned to his native Puerto Rico in 1990, where he created twenty-two pieces over a year, including a work titled *Ruth Fernandez* in 1991. His artistic output demonstrates a commitment to representing communities and individuals through accessible, public art.

title: Bobo Baldé
text:
Bobo Baldé, born Dianbobo Baldé in Marseille, France in 1975, was a professional footballer who primarily played as a defender. His club career began in 1995 with Marseille, but he moved to Mulhouse in 1997 seeking more playing time. A loan spell at Cannes followed, where he made 29 appearances and scored four goals, before joining Toulouse and contributing to their promotion.

The most significant period of Baldé’s career was with Celtic, where he played from 2001 to 2009. He amassed 232 appearances for the club, scoring six goals in his first season, including one in the Scottish Cup final against Rangers. He was a key player in Celtic’s successes, winning five Scottish Premier League titles, three Scottish Cups, and two Scottish League Cups. He was also part of the team that reached the 2003 UEFA Cup Final, though he was sent off during the match which they lost 3-2 to Porto. In 2003, he was voted Celtic Player of the Year by the fans, becoming the inaugural winner of the award, and also won the SPL Player of the Month for April. Later seasons saw him struggle with form and injuries, including a broken leg in 2006, and he faced criticism and a decline in his first-team opportunities. He ultimately saw out his contract with Celtic but didn’t play competitively in his final season.

After leaving Celtic, Baldé moved to Valenciennes in France in 2009 before joining Arles-Avignon in 2011. Alongside his club career, Baldé represented the Guinea national team 52 times, scoring two goals and participating in the 2002, 2004 and 2006 Africa Cup of Nations tournaments, and 2006 FIFA World Cup qualifying. 

Following his playing career, Baldé transitioned into coaching, beginning as a sports coordinator for the Guinea national team in 2013. He then took on a playing assistant manager role with his former youth club, Gombertois, in 2014, before becoming the manager of Guinea’s national U20 team in 2019. Baldé's younger half-brother, Yasser, is also a professional footballer. Throughout his career, he faced instances of racial abuse from opposing fans, which led to convictions and bans for those involved.

title: Shin Jea-hwan
text:
Shin Jea-hwan, a South Korean artistic gymnast, was born on March 3, 1998, in Seoul. He completed his education at the Korea National Sport University, graduating in 2020, and later moved to Jecheon in 2021. He considers his teammate, Yang Hak-seon, to be a significant influence.

Shin began his senior international career in 2019, competing at the Zhaoqing World Cup where he earned a silver medal on the vault and placed fourth in the floor exercise. He continued to compete on both vault and floor throughout the 2020 World Cup circuit, achieving gold medals on vault in both Melbourne and Baku. Following the 2019 World Championships, a reallocation of points placed him in a leading position to qualify for the 2020 Summer Olympics; however, the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted the remainder of the 2020 series.

To secure his Olympic qualification, Shin participated in the 2021 Doha World Cup, organized as a final qualification event by the International Gymnastics Federation. Although he finished fifth in Doha, behind Japan’s Hidenobu Yonekura, Shin ultimately won the overall World Cup series on a tiebreaker, earning him a place to compete individually at the Olympic Games in Tokyo.

At the 2020 Summer Olympics in Tokyo, Shin successfully qualified for the vault final, achieving a tie with Armenia’s Artur Davtyan with a score of 14.866. He progressed to the final based on a tiebreak, having a higher individual vault score of 15.100 compared to Davtyan’s 15.000. In the vault final itself, Shin once again faced a tie, this time with Denis Ablyazin of the ROC, both gymnasts receiving a score of 14.783. Shin won the gold medal due to his superior individual vault score of 14.833, exceeding Ablyazin’s 14.800. This victory marked South Korea’s second Olympic gold medal in the vault event, following Yang Hak-seon’s win at the 2012 London Olympics.

title: Carlos Ghosn
text:
Carlos Ghosn, born in 1954, is a businessman who rose to prominence as a leading automotive executive, holding key positions at Michelin, Renault, Nissan, and Mitsubishi Motors. He began his career at Michelin in 1978, working his way up through various leadership roles over 18 years, including a successful turnaround of the company’s struggling South American operations. This experience shaped his cross-cultural management style, emphasizing diversity.

In 1999, following Renault’s investment in Nissan, Ghosn moved to Japan to revitalize the struggling automaker. As COO and later CEO, he implemented the “Nissan Revival Plan,” a drastic restructuring that involved job cuts, plant closures, and a dismantling of the traditional Japanese *keiretsu* system. This plan successfully returned Nissan to profitability within two years, exceeding ambitious targets and establishing Ghosn’s reputation as a turnaround specialist. He simultaneously became CEO of Renault in 2005, an unprecedented position leading two Fortune Global 500 companies. His influence further expanded in 2016 with his appointment as chairman of Mitsubishi Motors after Nissan gained a controlling stake.

Ghosn’s early life was marked by a nomadic upbringing. His grandfather emigrated from Lebanon to Brazil, establishing a successful entrepreneurial legacy. Ghosn himself was born in Brazil, moved to Lebanon as a child, and later completed his education in Paris, earning degrees from École Polytechnique and École des Mines de Paris. 

Throughout his career, Ghosn was known for his bold leadership style and willingness to challenge established norms. He championed the development of electric vehicles, investing heavily in the technology and positioning the Renault–Nissan Alliance as a leader in the market. He also played a role in recovery efforts after the 2011 Japanese earthquake and tsunami. However, his career took a dramatic turn in November 2018 when he was arrested in Japan on suspicion of financial misconduct at Nissan. 

He was accused of underreporting his income and misusing company funds. Following his arrest, Ghosn was detained for an extended period and subjected to intense interrogation. He maintained his innocence, claiming the allegations were part of a corporate coup.  After being released on bail under strict conditions, Ghosn dramatically escaped from Japan in December 2019, concealing himself in a large box shipped as freight on a private jet, a move that drew international attention. The legal proceedings and the circumstances surrounding his escape remain a complex and highly publicized case.

title: Muhammad Qutb
text:
Muhammad Qutb was born in 1919, the younger brother of the prominent Egyptian revolutionary Sayyid Qutb. He pursued studies in English Literature at Cairo University, adding diplomas in psychology and education to his credentials. Following his brother’s execution by the Egyptian government in 1966, Muhammad moved to Saudi Arabia and dedicated himself to promoting and preserving Sayyid’s ideas.

In Egypt, Muhammad Qutb was arrested alongside his brother in 1965, accused of plotting against the government and prominent figures. While Sayyid was executed, Muhammad found refuge in Saudi Arabia, where he became a significant figure in Islamic scholarship. He spent years editing and publishing his brother’s works, ensuring their continued circulation. He also taught Islamic Studies at universities in Mecca and Jeddah, with figures like Osama bin Laden and Ayman al-Zawahiri reportedly among his students. Bin Laden specifically recommended one of Qutb’s books in a 2004 video.

Within the Saudi context, Muhammad Qutb worked to bridge ideological gaps between more radical followers of his brother and the more conservative Muslim community, particularly those within the Muslim Brotherhood. He offered a less stringent interpretation of Sayyid Qutb’s assertion that the modern Muslim world had reverted to a state of *jahiliyya* (pre-Islamic ignorance), specifically denying that Saudi Arabia itself fell into this category. He also publicly opposed *takfir*, the practice of declaring Muslims as non-believers, and sought to reconcile the Brotherhood’s doctrines with prevailing Salafism. He supervised several dissertations, including one by Safar Al-Hawali, whose work contributed to the “sahwa” – an Islamist awakening blending radical Wahhabism and Sayyid Qutb’s ideas.

Qutb’s writings often criticized the state of the Muslim world, attributing its weakness to the failings of Muslims themselves and to external enemies, specifically Christians and Jews. He employed terms like “Crusaders” and “Zionists” to invoke historical conflicts, and believed Jews exerted significant control over Western society and actively sought to undermine Islam through cultural imperialism, perceiving this as a more insidious threat than military invasion. He expressed concern over the influence of Western education and the changing role of women, seeing both as corrupting influences on Islamic values. His arguments frequently drew on anti-Semitic conspiracy theories, including references to *The Protocols of the Elders of Zion*. Interestingly, he also defended traditional Islamic slavery, arguing it was preferable to Western forms of exploitation.

Muhammad Qutb was a prolific author, publishing 36 books on varying subjects, including religion, psychology, and literary criticism. His work, notably *Jahiliyya of the Twentieth Century* and *Islam: The Misunderstood Religion*, had a wide reach within the Arab world and played a significant role in shaping 20th-century Muslim thought. He died in Mecca in 2014 at the age of 94, leaving behind a legacy of scholarship and influence within Islamist circles. He also held editorial control over his brother’s publications, allowing him to shape their dissemination.

title: F. Gwynplaine MacIntyre
text:
Fergus Gwynplaine MacIntyre, born Paul Grant Jeffery in 1956 and known to many as Froggy, was a New York City-based writer and artist who died in 2010. He worked across multiple genres, publishing science fiction, fantasy, horror, and mystery stories in magazines like *Weird Tales*, *Analog*, and *Asimov’s Science Fiction*, as well as contributing to various anthologies. He authored the novel *The Woman Between the Worlds* and a collection of humorous pieces titled *MacIntyre’s Improbable Bestiary*. Beyond his published work, MacIntyre also wrote as a ghostwriter, including a novel in the Tom Swift IV series, *The DNA Disaster*, credited to Victor Appleton, though acknowledged by MacIntyre himself.

MacIntyre’s personal history was notably complex and largely fabricated. Born to Grant Turner Peter Jeffery and Mathilde Barbara Mantano, he created elaborate stories about his origins, claiming to be orphaned and raised in Australia, including time in a labour camp. He adopted different aliases throughout his life, including Timothy C. Allen and Oleg V. Bredikhine. However, acquaintances remembered him speaking with a New York accent even in his twenties, and his brother later confirmed after his death that many of the stories he told about his past were untrue, though the reasons remained undisclosed. He derived the “Gwynplaine” portion of his name from the protagonist of Victor Hugo’s *The Man Who Laughs*, identifying with the character’s permanently fixed smile.

Professionally, MacIntyre’s career had unusual turns. In the 1970s, he worked for a publisher of pornographic novels, tasked with writing entire books in a single week. He was known for his linguistic creativity, coining new words and reviving obscure ones, and even gained the acknowledgement of William Safire for a neologism he created. He also contributed illustrations to *Analog* and wrote numerous book reviews for *The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction*. He claimed to have contributed significantly to a documentary about Theda Bara, but was only credited with “Special Thanks.”

MacIntyre’s life was also marked by legal trouble and mental health struggles. In 2000, he was arrested and pleaded guilty to misdemeanor assault after a violent attack on a neighbor. Prior to his death, he experienced increasing depression, referencing a troubled childhood and suicidal thoughts in mass emails to friends. He also faced financial hardship and health issues. 

He died in a fire in his Brooklyn apartment in June 2010, after setting it ablaze. The fire required sixty firefighters to extinguish. He had posted a final review on the Internet Movie Database the day before, framing it as his last. MacIntyre was also known for writing over 1,600 often-fabricated reviews on IMDb, sometimes openly admitting to making them up for films he hadn’t seen. His brother’s revelation about the fabricated nature of his life story came after his death, adding a final layer of mystery to a life already filled with invention and complexity.

title: Daniil Medvedev
text:
Daniil Sergeyevich Medvedev, born in Moscow in 1996, is a Russian professional tennis player who has reached the world No. 1 ranking. He currently holds 20 ATP Tour-level singles titles, most notably the 2021 US Open and the 2020 ATP Finals. He began his professional career with a debut in the 2015 Kremlin Cup and first competed in a Grand Slam tournament at Wimbledon in 2017. His breakthrough year was 2019, marked by reaching the top 10 and a string of six consecutive tournament finals, including a run to the US Open final. 

Medvedev’s most significant achievement to date was winning the 2021 US Open, defeating Novak Djokovic and preventing him from completing a calendar-year Grand Slam. He followed this with a period of fluctuating form, briefly dropping out of the top 10 before returning to the top 5 in early 2023, reaching two further major finals. In 2022, he became the first player since Andy Murray, outside of the “Big Three” (Federer, Nadal, Djokovic), to achieve the world No. 1 ranking, joining fellow Russians Yevgeny Kafelnikov and Marat Safin in this accomplishment. 

Growing up in Moscow, Medvedev's father, a computer engineer, ran a building materials business. He has two older sisters. His introduction to tennis came at age six, prompted by an advertisement and encouraged by his father. His first coach was Ekaterina Kryuchkova, who had previously worked with Vera Zvonareva. He pursued both musical interests, studying the harpsichord and guitar, alongside his athletic training. He initially studied physics and math, then economics at Moscow State Institute of International Relations, but later switched to physical education to focus on tennis, eventually training at an academy in Antibes, France, where his parents now reside as retirees.

Medvedev is fluent in Russian, French, and English, having spent much of his career living and training abroad. He married Daria Chernyshkova in 2018, and they have two daughters, Alisa born in 2022 and Vika born in 2025. He credits his marriage with improving his tennis results, noting a significant ranking increase after proposing. He is also a supporter of FC Bayern Munich. 

As a junior player, Medvedev achieved a career-high ranking of No. 13 and reached the third round of the Junior Australian Open and US Open in 2013 and 2014 respectively. His professional career began with doubles play at the 2015 Kremlin Cup, followed by his first ATP singles main draw appearance in 2016. He faced controversy early in his career, being disqualified from a Challenger event for comments perceived as racially insensitive. He steadily climbed the rankings, achieving his first ATP title in Sydney in 2018 and subsequently winning titles in Winston-Salem and Tokyo that same year. He continued his success in 2019 with Masters 1000 titles in Cincinnati and Shanghai, and a runner-up finish at the US Open. He capped off 2020 by winning the ATP Finals, defeating the top three ranked players en route to the championship. He began 2021 strongly, winning the ATP Cup and reaching the Australian Open final before securing his first Grand Slam title at the US Open.

title: Date Narikuni
text:
Date Narikuni was a samurai who lived during the late Edo period in Japan. Born on November 6, 1817, he became the 12th daimyō, or feudal lord, of the Sendai Domain located in the Tōhoku region of northern Japan, and was the 28th head of the prominent Date clan. His lineage was somewhat indirect; he was the son of Date Munemitsu, belonging to the Tome-Date clan, a branch family of the main Date line, and consequently the grandson of Date Yoshimura, a previous daimyō of Sendai. Throughout his childhood, he was known by several names—first Kōgorō, then Tosaburō, and finally Sojirō.

Narikuni’s rise to power was directly linked to a succession crisis within the Sendai Domain in 1828. The previous daimyō, Date Nariyoshi, died leaving behind a two-year-old son, Date Yoshikuni, as his heir. The Tokugawa shogunate, while having previously intervened to secure the Date line's continuation, was growing impatient with the repeated succession issues within the domain and considered the possibility of stripping the Date clan of their lands. 

An initial proposal involved marrying Nariyoshi’s young daughter, Masahime, to a son of the shōgun Tokugawa Ienari, but this plan failed to materialize. Instead, Masahime was wed to Narikuni, who was from a cadet branch of the Date family. Crucially, Narikuni then formally adopted the infant Date Yoshikuni as his heir, ensuring the continuation of the main Date line and appeasing the shogunate. 

Following this arrangement, in 1828, Narikuni was granted the Court rank of Junior Fourth, Lower Grade, and received the title of Mutsu-no-kami. His status was further elevated in 1831 with promotions to Junior Fourth, Upper Grade, and Sakonoe-chūshō. 

Despite his political maneuvering, Narikuni was known primarily for his intellectual pursuits. He possessed a scholarly disposition and was well-versed in literature. However, his time as daimyō was cut short. He became ill during a mandatory trip to Edo in 1840, a practice known as *sankin-kōtai*, and ultimately died in Edo on September 9, 1841, at the relatively young age of 25. Narikuni’s father was Date Munemitsu, who lived from 1787 to 1843, and his mother was Tsuneko-hime. He was married to Masahime, who outlived him, passing away in 1861.

title: Ilhan Omar
text:
Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, born in Mogadishu, Somalia in 1982, is currently serving as the U.S. Representative for Minnesota's 5th congressional district since 2019. A member of the Democratic Party, she previously served in the Minnesota House of Representatives from 2017 to 2019. She is a prominent figure, being the first Somali American, and the first woman of color to represent Minnesota in Congress, as well as one of the first two Muslim women to serve in the U.S. Congress.

Omar’s early life was marked by the Somali Civil War, leading her family to spend four years in a Kenyan refugee camp before arriving in the U.S. in 1995. The family eventually settled in Minneapolis, where her father worked as a taxi driver and later for the post office. She became a U.S. citizen in 2000.  Her upbringing emphasized the importance of democracy, and she recalls experiencing bullying in school due to her appearance and religious attire. She earned a bachelor's degree in political science and international studies from North Dakota State University in 2011.

Before entering politics, Omar worked as a community nutrition educator and held positions managing campaigns and serving as a policy aide for Minneapolis city council members. In 2016, she was elected to the Minnesota House of Representatives, becoming the first Somali-American legislator in the United States. She then successfully ran for the U.S. House of Representatives in 2018, winning with a significant margin and being sworn in on a copy of the Quran. She has since been re-elected in 2020, 2022, and 2024.

In Congress, Omar is the deputy chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and advocates for policies such as a $15 minimum wage, universal healthcare, student loan debt forgiveness, and the protection of DACA recipients. She also supports abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). She is a vocal critic of Israel, supporting the BDS movement and opposing Israeli settlement policies.  Her views on Israel have attracted controversy and accusations of antisemitism, culminating in a vote by the Republican-controlled House in 2023 to remove her from the Foreign Affairs Committee. 

Omar is a member of "The Squad," a group of progressive female members of Congress advocating for policies like the Green New Deal and Medicare for All. She introduced a resolution supporting the right to boycott as a form of political expression and has introduced articles of impeachment against former President Trump. One of her sponsored bills, designating a Minneapolis post office, became law in 2022.  She has faced scrutiny regarding campaign finance practices, resulting in a requirement to reimburse funds spent on out-of-state travel and a fine, as well as questions regarding joint tax filings.

title: Joji (musician)
text:
George Kusunoki Miller, known professionally as Joji, was born in Osaka, Japan in 1993 to an Australian father and a Japanese mother. He attended Canadian Academy in Kobe, Japan, graduating in 2012 before moving to the United States to study at the New York Institute of Technology, earning a Bachelor of Fine Arts degree in 2016. Before his music career, Miller gained prominence on YouTube, beginning with a channel in 2006 showing him breakdancing. He later created the channels DizastaMusic, TVFilthyFrank, and TooDamnFilthy, achieving viral success with his character Filthy Frank and related comedy, including the persona Pink Guy. This comedy incorporated shock humor, hip-hop, challenges, and ukulele performances. He even played a role in popularizing the “Harlem Shake” internet meme.

Miller released two studio albums and an extended play as Pink Guy between 2014 and 2017 – *Pink Guy*, *Pink Season*, and *Pink Season: The Prophecy*. However, in late 2017, he ceased production of all Filthy Frank-related content, including Pink Guy, due to health concerns and a desire to focus on a more serious musical path. He had initially intended to pursue music alongside his YouTube work, even stating he started his channel to promote his music, but the comedy content overshadowed his musical aspirations.

Transitioning to the name Joji, derived from the Japanese pronunciation of his first name, Miller signed with 88Rising and 12Tone Music Group. He released his debut EP, *In Tongues*, in 2017 and followed with the studio albums *Ballads 1* (2018) and *Nectar* (2020). Both *Ballads 1* and *Nectar* reached number three on the Billboard 200 chart, featuring singles like "Slow Dancing in the Dark" and "Sanctuary". His 2022 single, "Glimpse of Us," became his most successful track, reaching number eight on the Billboard Hot 100 and topping the ARIA Charts, preceding his album *Smithereens*.

Joji’s musical style is a blend of R&B, lo-fi, and trip-hop, with influences ranging from James Blake and Radiohead to boom bap instrumentals. He describes his work as “dark love songs.” Throughout his career, he’s embarked on several tours, including the *Ballads 1 Tour*, *Nectar: The Finale*, *Smithereens Tour* and the ongoing *Pandemonium* tour. His early web-show contributed significantly to internet culture, notably kickstarting the Harlem Shake meme. He also released an unreleased album titled *Chloe Burbank: Volume 1*.

title: Diosdado Cabello
text:
Diosdado Cabello Rondón, born in 1963, is a prominent Venezuelan politician and current Minister of Interior, Justice and Peace, with a long and controversial career deeply intertwined with the country’s political landscape. He began his involvement in politics through his close relationship with Hugo Chávez, assisting in Chávez’s return to power after the 2002 coup attempt and becoming a key figure in the Movimiento V República (MVR), later the United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV). 

Cabello’s career has included roles in the military, where he holds the rank of captain, and numerous high-level political positions. He served as Governor of Miranda state from 2004 to 2008, losing the election to Henrique Capriles Radonski, after which he became Public Works & Housing Minister. He later simultaneously headed the National Commission of Telecommunications in 2009, a position traditionally independent of his ministerial role.  He was elected to the National Assembly in 2010 and became its President in 2012, holding the position until 2016, and later served as president of the 2017 National Constituent Assembly.

During a brief period in April 2002, following a coup attempt against Chávez, Cabello briefly held the office of President of Venezuela, for only a few hours, making his presidency one of the shortest in history. He also served as Vice President earlier that year. Throughout his career, he has risen to become a highly influential figure, described in 2013 as the second most powerful man in Venezuela, possessing considerable sway within the military and among lawmakers.

However, Cabello’s career has been plagued by numerous accusations. He has been repeatedly linked to the “Cartel of the Suns,” an alleged drug trafficking organization, and accused of using his power for personal enrichment through corruption, nepotism benefiting family members, and directing illicit payments to pro-government groups.  Formal corruption allegations were lodged against him in Venezuela as early as 2013. In 2020, the U.S. Department of State offered a $10 million reward for information leading to his arrest or conviction on charges of drug trafficking and narco-terrorism.

Beyond corruption allegations, Cabello hosts a weekly television program, *Con el Mazo Dando*, where he discusses political issues and often makes accusations against the opposition, raising concerns about intimidation from organizations like the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and Amnesty International. He has also been the subject of security concerns, with reports in 2017 alleging a possible assassination plot targeting U.S. Senator Marco Rubio. 

Internationally, Cabello has been sanctioned by the United States, Canada, the European Union, Switzerland, Panama, and Argentina, with asset freezes and travel bans imposed due to his alleged human rights violations, involvement in corruption, and undermining of democratic processes. He is also banned from entering Colombia.  A recent development saw a federal court in Argentina issue an arrest warrant against him and other Venezuelan officials for crimes against humanity in September 2024.

title: Benjamin Lawrence Reid
text:
Benjamin Lawrence Reid was born in Louisville, Kentucky, on May 3, 1918, and spent some of his childhood in Texas. He was a dedicated athlete in his youth, initially playing baseball and later transitioning to basketball during his teenage years. Reid pursued higher education, beginning with a Bachelor of Arts degree from the University of Louisville in the 1940s. He continued his studies, earning a Master of Arts from Columbia University and a Doctor of Philosophy from the University of Virginia, both in the 1950s.

Reid’s career as an English professor spanned from the 1940s to the 1980s. He began teaching in 1946 at Iowa State College as an English lecturer for two years, followed by a position at Smith College from 1948 to 1951. He then moved to Sweet Briar College, starting as an instructor in 1951 and eventually becoming an assistant English professor there until 1957. The majority of his academic life, however, was spent at Mount Holyoke College. He joined Mount Holyoke in 1957 as an assistant professor and steadily rose through the ranks, becoming an associate professor in 1959, a professor in 1963, and finally an English professor in 1970. He remained at Mount Holyoke until his retirement in 1983.

Beyond his teaching responsibilities, Reid was a prolific writer. He began publishing books in the late 1950s and early 1960s, drawing upon the material from his university theses focusing on the works of Gertrude Stein and William Butler Yeats. He then turned his attention to biographical writing, publishing a biography of New York lawyer John Quinn in 1968 and another on Irish politician Roger Casement in 1976. In the later years of his life, between 1988 and 1990, Reid dedicated himself to writing his autobiographies.

Reid received significant recognition for his writing. He was awarded the 1969 Pulitzer Prize for Biography or Autobiography for his work, *The Man from New York: John Quinn and His Friends*.  He was also a finalist for the National Book Award for Biography and Autobiography in 1977 for *The Lives of Roger Casement*.  His research was also supported by prestigious grants; he received a Fulbright Program research grant in 1963 to study at the University of London and a fellowship from the National Endowment for the Humanities in 1971 to support his work on Bertrand Russell.

Benjamin Lawrence Reid died on November 30, 1990, in South Hadley, Massachusetts, as a result of a heart attack and multiple strokes. Prior to his academic career, during World War II, he served as a conscientious objector, working as both a bridge constructor and a psychiatric hospital orderly.

title: Lennie Hayton
text:
Lennie Hayton, born Leonard George Hayton in New York City in 1908, was a versatile American musician known for his work as a composer, conductor, and arranger. He was instantly recognizable for his signature captain’s hat, worn at a distinctive angle. Growing up in a Jewish family where his parents appreciated classical music, Hayton developed an early interest in the piano, learning from player piano rolls. Though his parents initially discouraged jazz, he discovered it at age sixteen and soon left school to play piano with the Broadway Hotel Orchestra.

His career gained momentum when Paul Whiteman hired him in 1928 as a pianist and arranger. During his time with Whiteman, he collaborated with prominent musicians like Frankie Trumbauer and Bing Crosby. Following a reduction in the Whiteman orchestra due to economic conditions in 1930, Hayton joined the Charles Previn Orchestra before reuniting with Bing Crosby in 1932. He became Crosby’s musical director, leading orchestras for recordings and radio broadcasts, including the hit song “Brother, Can You Spare a Dime?” in 1932. He continued as Crosby’s musical director for radio and film, notably for *Going Hollywood* in 1933, marking the start of his Hollywood career.

Hayton eventually became a musical director at Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer in 1940, a position he held until 1953, overseeing the studio’s prolific output of movie musicals. He received four Academy Award nominations for his work on *The Harvey Girls* and *The Pirate*, and won an Oscar for *On the Town* in 1950, alongside Roger Edens. He also arranged the music for *Singin’ in the Rain* and received further nominations for *Star!* and *Hello, Dolly!*. Later in his career, he arranged Frank Sinatra’s initial recording of “Something” by George Harrison. He also composed pieces like “Apple Blossoms” with several contemporaries, and co-arranged Hoagy Carmichael’s “Stardust” with Artie Shaw.

Hayton’s personal life included two marriages. His first wife, Helen Maude Gifford, died in 1943. He married Lena Horne in 1947, also acting as her musical director. Their marriage, though initially strategic for Horne’s career advancement, developed into genuine affection but was strained by the challenges of an interracial relationship and eventually led to separation. A lifelong smoker and drinker, Hayton died of a heart attack in Palm Springs, California, in 1971 and is buried in Hollywood Forever Cemetery.

title: Pallavi Joshi
text:
Born in Mumbai on April 4, 1969, Pallavi Joshi is an Indian actress, writer, and film producer working primarily in Hindi cinema and television. Her career began at the remarkably young age of four with a small role in the 1973 film *Naag Mere Sathi*, and continued with appearances in films like *Badla* (1976) and *Aadmi Sadak Ka* (1977). She gained recognition for playing a blind child who positively influences a gangster in *Dada* (1979).

Joshi’s career took a significant turn with her involvement in the parallel cinema movement of the 1980s and early 1990s. She starred in critically acclaimed films such as *Bhujangayyana Dashavathara*, *Rihaee*, *Rukmavati Ki Haveli*, and *Woh Chokri*, earning a National Film Award – Special Jury Award for her performance in the latter. She also appeared in several mainstream commercial films including *Insaaf Ki Awaaz*, *Andha Yudh* – for which she received a Filmfare Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress – *Mujrim*, and *Saudagar*. 

Beyond Hindi films, Joshi has also worked in regional cinema, playing the central character of Shantha in the Malayalam film *Ilayum Mullum* and appearing in a significant role in the Kannada film *Bhujangayyana Dashavathara*. She also took on a lead role in the Marathi film *Rita*. 

In television, Joshi found success with popular Doordarshan shows including *Talaash*, *Aarohan*, *Alpviram*, and *Justujoo*. She also hosted the music show *Zee Antakshari* for five years and the singing competition *Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Marathi Li'l Champs*. More recently, she has frequently collaborated with her husband, director Vivek Agnihotri, producing and acting in *The Tashkent Files* (2019) and *The Kashmir Files* (2022), winning two National Film Awards for Best Supporting Actress for these roles.

Joshi has received further recognition for her work, including the Excellence In Cinema Award at the Global Film Festival, Noida. She was initially nominated to the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII) society but declined the position in solidarity with student protests. She is currently serving as the Vice-President of FTII, Pune, alongside President Ranganathan Madhavan. Her upcoming project is *The Delhi Files*. She is also a producer of Marathi serials, including *Asambhav* and *Anubandh*. She married Vivek Agnihotri in 1997 and they have two children, and she is the sister of former child actor Master Alankar Joshi.

title: Billy Conigliaro
text:
William “Billy” Conigliaro was a professional baseball outfielder who played in Major League Baseball for five seasons between 1969 and 1973, appearing for the Boston Red Sox, Milwaukee Brewers, and Oakland Athletics. Born in Revere, Massachusetts in 1947, he followed in the footsteps of his older brother, Tony Conigliaro, also a major league player, with whom he briefly played as teammates on the Red Sox. Their parents, Sal and Teresa, encouraged both sons to pursue baseball.

Billy Conigliaro was a three-sport athlete at Swampscott High School, where he pitched a no-hitter in 1964 shortly after his brother debuted in the majors. He was drafted by the Red Sox in the first round of the inaugural MLB draft in 1965 and spent the next four years honing his skills in the minor leagues. He made his MLB debut in April 1969, stealing a base as a pinch runner, and quickly demonstrated offensive potential with two home runs in his first start a few days later. He finished his rookie year with a .288 batting average in 32 games.

His most productive season came in 1970, where he recorded career highs in several categories, including 108 hits, 59 runs scored, 18 home runs, and 58 RBIs across 114 games. That year, the Red Sox even shifted Carl Yastrzemski to first base to accommodate Conigliaro in the lineup. He was notably upset when his brother Tony was traded to the California Angels at the end of the season. In 1971, he hit 11 home runs and finished eighth in the American League in doubles with 26.

In October 1971, Conigliaro was traded to the Milwaukee Brewers in a ten-player deal. However, he became dissatisfied and retired mid-season in 1972. He sought reinstatement and was sold to the Oakland Athletics in 1973, appearing in both the American League Championship Series and the World Series, though he did not achieve any hits in seven at-bats. Following knee surgery, he was waived by the Athletics in 1974 and briefly attempted a comeback in 1977, ultimately declining a minor league assignment. Throughout his career, he maintained a .256 batting average with 40 home runs and 128 RBIs in 347 games. 

Beyond baseball, Conigliaro studied Shotokan karate under Kazumi Tabata, who acknowledged him in one of his books. He married Keisha in 2002 and passed away on February 10, 2021, from a heart attack at his home in Beverly, Massachusetts.

title: Felician of Foligno
text:
Felician of Foligno was a Christian figure who lived approximately from 160 to 250 AD and is recognized as the patron saint of Foligno, Italy. He was born in Forum Flaminii, now known as San Giovanni Profiamma, located along the Via Flaminia, and came from a Christian family. His early religious education was guided by Pope Eleuterus, and he dedicated his life to spreading the Christian faith throughout the region. He actively evangelized in several cities including Foligno, Spello, Bevagna, Assisi, Perugia, Norcia, Plestia, Trevi, and Spoleto.

Around the year 204 AD, Felician was consecrated as the first Bishop of Foligno by Pope Victor I. Importantly, he was the first bishop to be granted the pallium, a vestment signifying his authority and office. During his more than fifty-year episcopate, he ordained Valentine of Terni as a priest, establishing a further link in the early Christian leadership of the area. He is considered to be among the earliest Christian bishops in northern Italy. 

Later in his life, at the advanced age of 94, Felician faced persecution under the Roman Emperor Decius for his refusal to participate in sacrifices to the Roman gods. He was arrested as a result of his unwavering faith. While imprisoned, he received a visit from one of his devoted followers, Messalina of Foligno. He endured torture and scourging as a consequence of his beliefs. Ultimately, Felician died while being transported from Foligno to Rome for his scheduled execution.

Following his death, a church was constructed over his burial site in Foligno, marking the beginning of his veneration as a saint. Over the centuries, his relics were dispersed. In 970 AD, a significant portion of his remains were moved to Metz, France. Several years earlier, in 965, some relics had been taken to Minden, Germany, mistakenly leading to the belief that Felician had been a bishop of that city and the establishment of a separate feast day for him on October 20th – an error that was even recorded in the Roman Martyrology.  However, some of his relics were eventually returned to Foligno in 1673 and 1674. 

Today, Foligno Cathedral houses a statue depicting Saint Felician, crafted from silver and bronze by the sculptor Giovanni Battista Maini, serving as a visual testament to his enduring importance to the city and its people.

title: Sam Michael
text:
Samuel David Michael, born in Western Australia in 1971 and raised in Canberra, is an Australian motorsports engineer and designer with a significant career spanning Formula One and Australian Supercars. His early involvement in motorsport began with work on Neal Bates’ rally car, a Toyota Celica GT-Four, before he pursued mechanical engineering at the University of New South Wales, focusing his thesis on data acquisition systems for racing cars.
