title: Sayaka Ando
text:
Sayaka Ando is a Japanese model and gravure idol who was born on May 24, 1981, in Takasaki, Gunma, but spent her formative years growing up in Sendai, Japan. She began her career in the entertainment industry with her debut in 2004, specifically through a release titled *Eternal*. 

Ando’s professional background includes a university education; she is a graduate of Miyagi Gakuin Women's University. Her work has primarily centered around the gravure industry, a popular genre in Japan featuring photographic and video releases focused on models. This is evidenced by the extensive list of DVDs she has released throughout her career.

Starting in December 2004 with *Eternal*, Ando consistently released DVDs over the following years. *Lesson 2* followed in March 2005, then *Healing Venus* in June of the same year. She continued this pattern with *Aqua* in October 2005, and a compilation release, *Ando Sayaka Collection Box* in December 2005. Releases continued in 2006 with *Fascino* in April and *Toi Kimi no Kioku* in August. 

In 2007, she released *Duet* in February, followed by *Day* and *Night* in October and December respectively. Her DVD releases concluded, as listed, with *Poison* in March 2008. Alongside her DVD work, Ando has also been involved in photobook production, having released *Mitsu no A* in April 2005, though the specific day within April is not stated. 

Outside of her professional life, the article notes information regarding her personal life. Sayaka Ando became a mother, giving birth to her first child in September 2012 and her second child in November 2014. 

Information regarding Ando can be found at the Japanese Idol Directory, and a fan website is also noted. The article also includes a link to her official website, and a reference to a broader “List of Race Queens,” suggesting a possible connection to promotional work in motorsports, though the nature of this connection isn’t detailed within the provided text.

title: Enamul Haque (engineer)
text:
Enamul Haque was born on October 21, 1969, and is a politician affiliated with the Bangladesh Awami League. He served as a member of the Jatiya Sangsad, representing the Rajshahi-4 constituency for three consecutive terms, beginning in 2008 and concluding in 2024. His educational background includes an undergraduate degree in engineering, as well as the completion of an MBA program. 

Haque initially won his seat in the Jatiya Sangsad in the 2008 election as a candidate for the Bangladesh Awami League, and successfully defended that seat in the election held on January 5, 2014, again running under the Awami League banner. However, his political career has been marked by several controversies and accusations.

In September 2014, the Bangladesh Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) suggested that formal corruption charges be filed against him, relating to activities involving his company, Ena Enterprise. This recommendation signaled the beginning of scrutiny regarding his business dealings and potential financial misconduct. Later, in January 2017, Haque publicly criticized Iqbal Sobhan Chowdhury, the editor of *The Daily Observer*, following the publication of a newspaper report that alleged his involvement in the drug trade. He took issue with the report’s claims and responded with a public rebuke of the editor.

Internal party disputes also surfaced in September 2017 when local leaders of the Awami League in the Rajshahi region accused Haque of contributing to divisions within the party and instigating internal conflicts. These accusations suggest that his actions were perceived as disruptive to party unity.

A more serious and personal accusation arose in June 2020, when Ayesha Akter Liza, a woman estimated to be between 35 and 36 years old, accused Haque of deception and of having compelled her to undergo an abortion. Liza claimed that they had entered into a marriage on April 30, 2013, which was officially registered on May 11, 2018.  Haque acknowledged the marriage but stated that it had ended in divorce on April 23, 2020, presenting a differing account of the relationship’s status. 

Most recently, in September 2024, the ACC announced it would launch a full investigation into new allegations of corruption against Haque. These latest accusations center around claims of money laundering, irregularities in the implementation of development projects, and the illegal accumulation of wealth. This renewed investigation indicates that concerns regarding his financial conduct continue to persist, even after his term in the Jatiya Sangsad concluded.

title: Diego Suarez (garden designer)
text:
Diego Suarez was born in Bogotá, Colombia in 1888 and died in New York City in 1974. He was a garden designer most recognized for his work on the gardens of James Deering’s Villa Vizcaya in Miami, Florida. His background was steeped in diplomacy and art; his father, Roberto Suarez, was a Colombian diplomat and historian, and his mother, Maria Costa, was Italian. After his father’s death, Suarez and his siblings were raised in Italy. 

He received training in architectural design at the Accademia delle Belle Arti in Florence, where he came under the influence of Arthur Acton. Acton, while restoring the gardens of his Villa La Pietra, imparted Renaissance garden ideals to Suarez, reviving styles favored by designers like Achille Duchêne. Through Acton’s connections, Suarez began designing gardens for wealthy Anglo-Americans in Florence, including projects at Villa Schifanoia for Lewis Einstein and for Charles Loeser, an early collector of Cézanne’s work.

Suarez’s most significant commission came about through a chance encounter. While visiting La Pietra with James Deering and Paul Chalfin, Acton arranged for Suarez to show them various villas. Later, stranded in New York due to the outbreak of war, Suarez reconnected with Deering and Chalfin and was subsequently commissioned to design the gardens at Villa Vizcaya.

The gardens at Vizcaya are designed around the villa’s boat basin, featuring a boat-shaped island, and a south-facing expanse leading to a casino. A key element was a fountain purchased by Deering and Chalfin, which Suarez deliberately placed off the main axis to create a sense of discovery. His design incorporated French baroque-style parterres, contrasts of light and shadow, and subtle changes in elevation to add interest to the flat landscape.

Later in his career, in 1952, Suarez collaborated with architect Frederic Rhinelander King to build a neoclassical house with gardens in Brookville, New York. In 1937, he married Evelyn Marshall Field, the daughter of Charles Henry Marshall and former wife of Marshall Field III, becoming stepfather to Barbara, Bettine, and Marshall Field IV. Diego Suarez is buried at Woodlawn Cemetery in The Bronx, New York City.

title: Celâl Bayar
text:
Mahmut Celâl Bayar was born in 1883 in Bursa, Ottoman Empire, to a family of religious scholars who had migrated from Bulgaria. His early career involved work in various administrative and banking roles, including positions at the Gemlik Régie Company, Ziraat Bank, and Deutsche Orientbank. He received education at the Collège Français de l'Assomption and in silk production. Bayar became involved in the Committee of Union and Progress (CUP) in 1907, establishing branches in Bursa and İzmir, and participating in the 1913 coup. During this period, he was involved in organizing the deportation of Ottoman Greeks and contributed to the foundation of several schools and a sports club in İzmir.

Following World War I and the Armistice of Mudros, Bayar was initially tried as a war criminal but acquitted. He then actively participated in the Turkish War of Independence, forming associations to resist Allied occupation of İzmir and fighting alongside nationalist forces. He was elected to the Ottoman Parliament in 1919 and later joined Mustafa Kemal (Atatürk) in Ankara, becoming a deputy in the newly established Grand National Assembly of Turkey. He served as Minister of Economy between 1921 and 1937, playing a key role in the development of Turkey’s early financial institutions, including the founding of İş Bankası. 

Bayar served as Prime Minister from 1937 to 1939, appointed by Atatürk to liberalize the economy. After Atatürk’s death and a change in leadership, he resigned due to disagreements with İsmet İnönü.  Remaining within the Republican People’s Party (CHP) until 1946, he then co-founded the Democrat Party (DP) alongside Adnan Menderes and others, marking a crucial shift towards multi-party politics in Turkey. The DP won the 1950 elections, and Bayar was subsequently elected as Turkey’s third president, a position he held for ten years, being re-elected in 1954 and 1957. 

During his presidency, Turkey aligned more closely with the West, joining NATO in 1952, and experienced significant social and economic changes. However, the latter part of the DP’s rule saw a drift towards authoritarianism.  In 1960, Bayar was overthrown in a military coup and imprisoned. He was initially sentenced to death, but his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment due to his age and health.  He was released in 1964 due to ill health, but faced periods of re-arrest and house arrest before finally being fully released. He spent his later years advocating for the restoration of rights for former DP politicians. 

Celâl Bayar was noted for his longevity, being the longest-lived former head of state for many years, and died in 1986 at the age of 103. His career represents a significant period in Turkish political history, from the final years of the Ottoman Empire through the establishment of the Republic and the introduction of a multi-party system.

title: Karyn Pugliese
text:
Karyn Pugliese, also known by her Anishinaabemowin name Pabàmàdiz, is an accomplished investigative journalist with a significant impact on Canadian journalism and press freedom. A citizen of the Algonquins of Pikwàkanagàn First Nation and a status Indian, she notably became the first Indigenous person to be elected President of the Canadian Association of Journalists, serving from 2018 to 2020 and remaining on the board until 2024. She has intervened in over three cases before the Supreme Court of Canada.

Pugliese was raised in Ottawa, Ontario, with frequent visits to Pikwàkanagàn, though most of her family lived off-reserve. She began her career with short-term contracts at CBC Radio Ottawa and CTV, later working as a technical writer for the federal government while completing a Master's degree in history at Carleton University. Her thesis focused on the history of Ottawa-Gatineau’s urban Indigenous communities. She holds a combined honours degree in Journalism and History from Carleton University (1998) and a Master’s degree in History (2006), and was selected as the twenty-fifth Martin Wise Goodman Canadian Nieman Fellow at Harvard University, graduating in 2020.

Throughout her career, Pugliese has held several key positions. She first joined the Aboriginal Peoples Television Network (APTN) in 2000 as their first Parliamentary Correspondent, a role she held until 2006, winning three Native American Journalism Awards during her tenure. She briefly worked at Vision TV’s 360 Vision and then the Assembly of First Nations, rising to Communications Director before leaving in 2010. She then returned to journalism, hosting and producing programs for ichannel, including the innovative #FAQMP, which allowed viewers to select MPs for interview and submit questions via social media. 

Pugliese later returned to APTN in 2012 as Executive Director of News and Current Affairs, launching new programs like *Nation to Nation* and *InFocus*. Under her leadership, APTN National News secured interviews with national party leaders during the 2015 federal election. From 2021, she served as Managing Editor Investigative at the CBC, overseeing *The Fifth Estate* and *Marketplace*. She also held the position of Executive Editor at Canada’s National Observer, a climate change focused online news service.

Pugliese’s dedication to journalism and press freedom has been widely recognized. She has received two Charles Bury Awards from the Canadian Association of Journalists (2016 and 2023), the Gordon Sinclair Award from the Academy of Canadian Cinema and Television (2018), the Hyman Solomon Award for Public Policy Journalism (2019), and the Elias Boudinot Free Press Award from the Native American Journalists Association (2019), shared with Justin Brake. She also won a National Newspaper Award in 2021.  She is an ambassador for Journalist for Human Rights and has provided journalism training internationally, including in South Sudan, and is a board member of Canadian Journalists for Free Expression. She is a single mother; her son, Zackery Liberty, is a musician.

title: Heinrich Himmler
text:
Heinrich Himmler was a leading figure in Nazi Germany, rising to become the 4th Reichsführer of the Schutzstaffel (SS) and a key architect of the Holocaust. Born in Munich in 1900 to a conservative middle-class family, he served in a reserve battalion during World War I but didn’t see combat. He joined the Nazi Party in 1923 and the SS in 1925, steadily climbing the ranks to become Reichsführer-SS by 1929. Under his leadership, the SS expanded from a small unit to a powerful institution within the Nazi regime, known for its organizational skills and competent leadership, exemplified by figures like Reinhard Heydrich.

Throughout his career, Himmler accumulated significant power. From 1943, he headed both the Kriminalpolizei (Criminal Police) and served as Minister of the Interior, granting him control over all internal and external security forces, including the Gestapo. He also commanded the Waffen-SS, a combat branch of the SS that fought alongside the regular German army during World War II.  His role as the principal enforcer of Nazi racial policies led to the operation of concentration and extermination camps and the formation of the Einsatzgruppen death squads. He was centrally responsible for the genocide of approximately 5.5–6 million Jews, as well as the deaths of millions of others during the Holocaust.  He commissioned and oversaw the implementation of Generalplan Ost, a plan for the ethnic cleansing of Eastern Europe, resulting in an estimated 14 million deaths.

Early in his life, Himmler was a studious, though somewhat awkward, youth who struggled with his health. He kept a diary from age ten documenting his interests in current events and religion. He attempted a military career, but his efforts were thwarted by the war’s end before he could become an officer. He later studied agriculture but was drawn to nationalist and antisemitic ideologies.  He initially joined Ernst Röhm’s group and became increasingly focused on “the Jewish question”, reading antisemitic literature and participating in demonstrations. 

His involvement in the failed Beer Hall Putsch led to job loss and hardship, fueling his political radicalization. He abandoned Catholicism, embracing Germanic mythology and occult beliefs.  He joined the SS in 1925 and steadily gained influence, leveraging the party’s disarray after Hitler’s arrest to solidify his position. He developed a bureaucratic system focused on control and racial purity.  He persuaded Hitler to establish the SS as an independent organization, and under his leadership, it grew rapidly, enforcing strict racial requirements for membership. 

As the Nazi Party rose to power, Himmler’s influence expanded. He was elected to the Reichstag in 1930 and used his positions to consolidate SS control over the police and implement racial policies. He established departments like the RuSHA, dedicated to enforcing racial “purity” within the SS, and appointed key subordinates like Heydrich to build the SS’s intelligence and security apparatus. In the final years of the war, Hitler appointed Himmler to oversee the Replacement Army and the administration of the Third Reich, though he was later relieved of these commands after failing to achieve his objectives. Ultimately, he attempted to negotiate a separate peace with the Western Allies against Hitler’s wishes, leading to his dismissal, arrest, and eventual suicide while in British custody in 1945.

title: Ingo Titze
text:
Ingo R. Titze is a prominent voice scientist currently serving as Executive Director of the National Center for Voice and Speech and an Adjunct Professor in the Department of Otolaryngology/Head and Neck Surgery at the University of Utah. He also holds a position as a Distinguished Professor at the University of Iowa’s Department of Communication Sciences and Disorders and teaches at the Summer Vocology Institute, both at the University of Utah.

Titze’s academic background began with a Bachelor of Science in electrical engineering from the University of Utah, followed by a Master of Science in the same field with a minor in physics, also from the University of Utah. He then earned a Ph.D. in physics from Brigham Young University in 1972. His career launched with engineering roles at Argonne National Laboratory, the National Reactor Test Station, and North American Aviation before moving to Boeing in 1968-1969. He later transitioned into academic research, beginning at Gallaudet University in 1976 where he received his first National Institutes of Health grant.

Over the years, Titze has held numerous academic positions, including roles at King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals in Saudi Arabia, the University of Maryland, and the University of Iowa – beginning at Iowa in 1990 and jointly with the University of Utah starting in 2009. He also served as Director of Research and later Chief Scientist and Executive Director for the National Center for Voice and Speech, initially located at the Denver Center for the Performing Arts. He was an adjunct professor at Westminster Choir College in Princeton, New Jersey from 1989-1994.

A key contribution to the field is the development of ‘vocology,’ a discipline he conceived as parallel to audiology, born from his university courses on voice production, acoustics, and related subjects developed starting in 1979. His extensive research on voice health and disorders has been supported by multiple grants from the National Institutes of Health, resulting in over 160 research articles listed with the NIH. 

Titze’s work has garnered significant recognition, including numerous awards from organizations such as the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association, the Acoustical Society of America, and the German Ear, Nose, Throat Association. He has also been featured in various media outlets, including BBC Radio 3, Reuters, and CNN, as well as documentaries produced by NDR in Germany and the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. 

He is a prolific author, having written and edited several books on the human voice, including “Fascinations with the Human Voice,” “Vocology: The Science and Practice of Voice Habilitation,” and “The Myoelastic-Aerodynamic Theory of Phonation," many of which have been translated into multiple languages.

title: Ivan Toms
text:
Ivan Toms was a South African physician renowned for his activism against apartheid and his dedication to public health. Born in Johannesburg in 1952, he received his medical degree from the University of Cape Town in 1976, following an early experience with police brutality during a demonstration against the Bantu Education system. After completing his internship, he also obtained a BA in theology.

In 1978, Toms was drafted into the South African Defence Force as a non-combatant doctor, serving in what was then South West Africa (Namibia). However, witnessing the violence inflicted on the Crossroads squatter settlement near Cape Town in 1983, where he was the sole physician for approximately 60,000 residents, solidified his opposition to the regime. This experience led him to co-found the End Conscription Campaign (ECC) in 1983, alongside activists like Nan Cross, and to refuse further service in the SADF. 

Toms actively protested government policies, notably undertaking a three-week hunger strike in 1985 to oppose the planned demolition of the Crossroads settlement. He publicly stated his moral objection to the SADF, citing his Christian beliefs. His defiance resulted in a 21-month prison sentence in 1988, though he ultimately served nine months. 

Beyond his anti-apartheid work, Toms was a pioneer in gay rights activism, becoming a founding member of Lesbians and Gays Against Oppression (LAGO) in 1987, and facing homophobic attacks as a result.  

Following the end of apartheid in 1991, Toms dedicated himself to public health initiatives. He became the national co-ordinator of the National Progressive Primary Healthcare Network, focusing on programs to combat the emerging AIDS epidemic and advocating for the use of antiretroviral drugs. He later directed the Students' Health and Welfare Centres Organisation, running mobile clinics in impoverished areas. In 1996, he assumed the role of Health Director for the City of Cape Town, later becoming the executive director of the health department in 2002.

His contributions were recognized with the bronze Order of the Baobab in 2006, awarded by President Thabo Mbeki. Ivan Toms died unexpectedly in 2008 at the age of 55 from meningococcal meningitis, and was remembered as a selfless and dedicated public servant by prominent figures such as Archbishop Desmond Tutu and the Mayor of Cape Town, Helen Zille. A centre for men's health in Greenpoint, Cape Town, bears his name, continuing his work in addressing public health challenges.

title: León Dujovne
text:
León Dujovne was an Argentine writer, philosopher, essayist, and journalist who lived from November 15, 1898, to January 16, 1984. His origins lie in Eastern Europe; he was born in the village of Kurilovich, located near Mohyliv-Podilskyi in the Russian Empire, a region bordering Bessarabia, which is now part of Moldova. Dujovne’s family was Jewish, and they emigrated to Argentina when he was just one year old. 

The family chose to settle in Basavilbaso, a town within the province of Entre Ríos, Argentina. This location was significant as it was one of the Jewish agricultural colonies established by Baron Maurice de Hirsch. These colonies were created to provide opportunities for Jewish people facing persecution and limited prospects in Eastern Europe. 

Throughout his career, Dujovne produced a number of notable written works. One of his most substantial projects was a four-volume exploration of the philosopher Baruch Spinoza, titled *Spinoza. Su vida, su época, su obra, su influencia*. This work, published between 1941 and 1945 by the Faculty of Philosophy and Letters of the University of Buenos Aires, thoroughly examined Spinoza’s life, the historical context in which he lived, his philosophical work, and the lasting impact of his ideas.

Later in his life, Dujovne published *El judaísmo como cultura* in 1980, through Ediciones Nueva Presencia. This book focused on exploring Judaism as a cultural phenomenon, likely delving into its traditions, history, and societal impact.

Dujovne also contributed to the accessibility of important philosophical texts through his translations. He undertook the translation of Maimonides' *The Guide for the Perplexed*, a significant work of medieval Jewish philosophy. His translation, titled *Guía de los perplejos*, was published in three volumes in 1955. Importantly, his translation was based on the French version created by Salomon Munk. A revised edition of Dujovne’s translation, enhanced with an introduction and notes by Angelina Muñiz-Huberman, was later published in Mexico City by Conaculta in 2001, demonstrating the continued relevance and scholarly interest in his work.

title: Rachel Weisz
text:
Rachel Weisz is an English actress born in London in 1970, known for her work in both independent and mainstream films. She’s received numerous accolades throughout her career, including an Academy Award, a BAFTA Award, a Golden Globe, and a Laurence Olivier Award.

Weisz began her acting career in the early 1990s with stage and television roles, making her film debut in 1994 with *Death Machine*. A breakthrough came with her performance in the 1994 revival of Noël Coward’s *Design for Living*, for which she won a Critics' Circle Theatre Award. Her film career gained momentum with the blockbuster *The Mummy* (1999) and its sequel, *The Mummy Returns* (2001). Throughout the 2000s, she appeared in a diverse range of films including *Enemy at the Gates*, *About a Boy*, *The Constant Gardener*, and *The Fountain*. 

Her performance as an activist in *The Constant Gardener* (2005) earned her the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress. She continued to balance independent projects with larger productions, appearing in films like *The Bourne Legacy* and *Oz the Great and Powerful* in the 2010s. Critical acclaim followed for roles in *The Deep Blue Sea*, *Denial*, and particularly *The Favourite* (2018), for which she won the BAFTA Award for Best Actress in a Supporting Role and received another Academy Award nomination. More recently, she portrayed Melina Vostokoff in the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s *Black Widow* (2021) and starred in the thriller miniseries *Dead Ringers* (2023).

Weisz’s parents were Jewish immigrants to the United Kingdom, fleeing Nazi Germany before World War II. Her father was a mechanical engineer and her mother a teacher-turned-psychotherapist. She has a younger sister, Minnie, who is a visual artist. Her upbringing emphasized independent thought and appreciation for the arts. She attended several schools, including Benenden School, and ultimately graduated from Trinity Hall, Cambridge with an upper second-class honours degree in English. While at Cambridge, she was involved in student theatre, co-founding a drama group and winning an award at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe for an improvised piece she wrote.

Before becoming a professional actress, Weisz did some modelling, famously turning down a role in *King David* with Richard Gere at the age of 14.  She trained at École Philippe Gaulier, studying under master clown Philippe Gaulier. Her early television work included roles in *Advocates II*, *Inspector Morse*, and *Scarlet and Black*. She’s maintained a consistent stage presence throughout her career, winning a Laurence Olivier Award for her portrayal of Blanche DuBois in a 2009 revival of *A Streetcar Named Desire*.



Weisz was in a long-term relationship with director Darren Aronofsky, with whom she has a son, before marrying actor Daniel Craig in 2011. They have a daughter together. She has worked with major fashion houses and remains a prominent figure in the entertainment industry. She became a naturalised American citizen in 2011, while retaining her British citizenship.

title: Will Voigt
text:
William Voigt, born August 18, 1976, is an American basketball coach currently an assistant coach for Brigham Young University’s men’s basketball team. His career has spanned multiple levels of basketball, from professional leagues to international competition, and includes a diverse range of coaching positions.

Voigt’s basketball journey began in Cabot, Vermont, where he played both basketball and soccer at Cabot High School. He then attended Pomona College in California, participating in soccer while earning a degree in political science. While in college, he gained initial experience with an internship with the Los Angeles Clippers. After graduating, he joined the San Antonio Spurs as a video coordinator, transitioning into college coaching a year later as an assistant under Rick Barnes at the University of Texas. He continued his college assistant work at Metro State under Mike Dunlap.

His first head coaching opportunity came with Ulriken Elite in Norway, a position he held from 2003 to 2006. A unique fan-vote selection process led to him becoming the head coach of the Vermont Frost Heaves in the American Basketball Association. He successfully led the team to consecutive ABA championships during its first two seasons. 

In 2009, another fan vote secured him the head coaching position for the Bakersfield Jam of the NBA Development League, now known as the G League. He guided the Jam to three playoff appearances over five seasons before departing in 2014. Voigt then took his coaching skills internationally, serving as an assistant coach for the Shanxi Brave Dragons in the Chinese Basketball Association. 

A significant achievement came in 2015 when he was chosen to coach the Nigerian national team at AfroBasket. Under his leadership, Nigeria won its first AfroBasket title, earning automatic qualification for the 2016 Summer Olympics. He later signed a three-year contract in November 2017 to coach the Angola national basketball team, and also served as a consultant for a team in the Philippine Basketball Association that same year. 

Voigt’s international coaching continued with Telekom Baskets Bonn of the German Bundesliga, initially in February 2020, and then again from January 2021, before parting ways after the 2020-21 season. In 2022, he accepted a one-year deal to coach Zamalek in the Egyptian Basketball Super League and the Basketball Africa League, leading them to a third-place finish in the BAL Playoffs and the semi-finals of the Super League. Most recently, prior to his appointment at BYU, he was head coach of the Austin Spurs of the NBA G League, a position he held since June 2023.

Voigt’s mother is Ellen Bryant Voigt, a former Vermont Poet Laureate. His career demonstrates a breadth of experience and success across various basketball landscapes.

title: Rohit Sharma
text:
Rohit Sharma, born on April 30, 1987, is an Indian international cricketer renowned as one of the greatest opening batters of all time. He currently captains the India national team in One Day Internationals (ODIs) and has previously led the team in Test matches and Twenty20 Internationals (T20Is), retiring from the latter format after the 2024 Men's T20 World Cup victory. He represents Mumbai Indians in the Indian Premier League (IPL) and Mumbai in domestic cricket.

Sharma holds numerous batting records, including the most runs in T20 Internationals, the most sixes in international cricket, and the most double centuries in ODI cricket – a remarkable three. He also boasts the most centuries in Cricket World Cups (seven) and is tied for the most hundreds in Twenty20 Internationals (five). He holds the world record for the highest individual score in an ODI, with 264, and scored a record-breaking five centuries in a single Cricket World Cup, earning him the ICC Men's ODI Cricketer of the Year award in 2019. Notably, he is the first captain to lead a team to the final of all ICC tournaments. 

As captain of the Mumbai Indians, Sharma led the team to five IPL titles in 2013, 2015, 2017, 2019, and 2020, sharing the record for most successful IPL captain with MS Dhoni. He is one of only two players to have participated in every edition of the T20 World Cup, from its inception in 2007 to 2024, and the only Indian player to win the tournament twice. He became the second Indian captain to secure a T20 World Cup title. He has been recognized with the Arjuna Award in 2015 and the Khel Ratna Award in 2020 by the Government of India. Under his leadership, India also won the 2018 and 2023 Asia Cups, and the 2018 Nidahas Trophy.

Sharma's early life was marked by modest beginnings in Nagpur, Maharashtra. Raised largely by his grandparents and uncles due to his father’s financial circumstances, he joined a cricket camp in 1999 with his uncle’s financial support. His coach, Dinesh Lad, facilitated a scholarship to Swami Vivekanand International School to improve his access to cricket facilities, recognizing his batting potential after initially identifying him as an off-spinner.

His personal life includes marriage to Ritika Sajdeh in 2015, and they have two children. He follows the Sahaj Marg meditation technique and maintains an eggetarian diet. He has numerous commercial endorsements with brands like CEAT, Hublot, Maggi, and Adidas.

Sharma’s domestic career began with List A debut for West Zone in 2005 and First-Class debut for India A in 2006. He quickly established himself with impressive scores, including a 309 not out in the Ranji Trophy in 2009, and was appointed captain of Mumbai in 2013. 

His international career began with an ODI debut against Ireland in 2007. Despite facing periods of inconsistent form, he eventually solidified his place in the team, becoming a key player in India’s victories in the 2013 Champions Trophy and subsequent World Cups. He was appointed Test captain in February 2022, succeeding Virat Kohli, but retired from Test cricket in May 2025 after a period of poor form and team performance. He was also appointed captain for the 2023 Cricket World Cup, becoming the oldest player to captain India in the tournament and surpassing Sachin Tendulkar’s record for most centuries in World Cup history.

title: Joseph Jaquet
text:
Joseph Jaquet, a Belgian sculptor born in Antwerp on January 30, 1822, and who died in Schaerbeek on June 9, 1898, achieved recognition for his work throughout his lifetime. Born to a baker, Jaquet received his artistic training at the Brussels Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts under the guidance of Guillaume Geefs. He formed a close friendship with Peter Ludwig Kühnen, a landscape painter from Aachen. 

Throughout his career, Jaquet was consistently supported by his brother Jacques, who moved from Antwerp to Brussels to assist him. Jacques also pursued his own artistic endeavors, exhibiting his sculptures at Brussels art salons in 1843, 1854, 1860, 1866, 1872, and 1873. Joseph Jaquet first gained attention in 1842 at the Brussels Art Salon, showcasing a collection of work including a marble bust, three plaster busts, a depiction of ‘Moses Saved from the Waters’, and ‘Meditating Saint Paul’. 

He further developed his reputation with a model for a bronze statue of Froissart intended for Chimay, presented at the 1845 Salon, but it was ‘The Golden Age’ in 1854 that truly cemented his notoriety. Jaquet resided on Goffard street before later moving to Charles Quint street. His talent led to commissions beyond Belgium, beginning in 1864 with ‘The Victory’ for the Paleis voor Volksvlijt in Amsterdam, followed by work decorating the national monument in The Hague’s Willemspark. 

In 1868, he completed a significant work, the equestrian statue of Baldwin I of Constantinople, which was installed in Mons. Two years later, in 1872, he contributed the pediment and lion sculptures to the Brussels Stock Exchange.  One of his later notable pieces was a statue of Louise of Orléans, the first Queen of the Belgians, created in 1879. This statue was initially placed on the Place d'Armes in Philippeville before being relocated to the old École moyenne on Namur street.

Jaquet was also dedicated to education, serving as a professor at the Brussels Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts, where he mentored Charles Samuel.  His contributions to the arts were formally recognized with several honours during his life, including being appointed an Officer of the Order of Leopold and an Officer of the Order of the Oak Crown. He was also elected as a Member of the Royal Academy of Science, Letters and Fine Arts of Belgium, signifying the high esteem in which his peers held his artistic achievements.

title: Dana Awartani
text:
Dana Awartani is a Saudi visual artist born in 1987, with Palestinian heritage. She currently lives and works in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and is known for her diverse artistic practice encompassing painting, video art, and sand mosaic. A defining characteristic of her work is the integration of traditional methods found within Islamic art into a contemporary context.

Awartani’s education began with a Foundation Degree in Art and Design from the Byam Shaw School of Art in 2006. She continued her studies at Central Saint Martins in London, graduating with a bachelor’s degree in fine art in 2009. Furthering her specialization, she earned a master’s degree in traditional arts from The Prince’s School of Traditional Arts in London in 2011. Her time at The Prince’s School provided her with training in techniques like stained glass, miniature painting, and gilding, drawing from a broad range of global artistic traditions. Recognizing a gap in the curriculum regarding the illumination of texts, she sought out a private instructor in Turkey to specifically learn and master this discipline. 

Awartani’s art is distinguished by its meticulous detail and prominent use of geometric patterning, drawing heavily from the aesthetics of Islamic art. She explores the connection between geometry and the natural world, and believes geometric principles can convey deeper truths and function as a symbolic visual language. This approach stems from a tradition, developed over a millennium ago, which utilized geometry as a means of artistic expression in place of depicting divine figures. While this practice is becoming less common, Awartani continues to refine and employ these specialized techniques.

She believes that appreciation for Islamic art is often overlooked within Arab culture, despite its pervasive presence in everyday environments like mosques.  She describes finding a personal connection to these forms, recognizing the intentionality and storytelling embedded within each structured piece. Awartani views her work not merely as artistic creation, but as a spiritual practice, a form of worship and remembrance of God, requiring complete focus and a positive mindset. 

Awartani’s work has gained international recognition, including her inclusion in the Rhizoma project at the 55th Venice Biennale in 2013. Her pieces are now part of the permanent collections of prominent institutions such as the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in Washington D.C., and the British Museum in London.

title: Prince Carl Philip, Duke of Värmland
text:
Prince Carl Philip, Duke of Värmland, born on May 13, 1979, is the only son and second of three children of King Carl XVI Gustaf and Queen Silvia of Sweden. He is currently fourth in the line of succession to the Swedish throne, following his sister Crown Princess Victoria, niece Princess Estelle, and nephew Prince Oscar. He resides in Villa Solbacken, Stockholm, with his wife Princess Sofia and their four children.

For a brief period, Prince Carl Philip was the heir apparent to the Swedish throne after his birth, holding the title of Crown Prince. However, a constitutional change in 1980, shifting to absolute primogeniture, changed the succession, making his sister Victoria the heir. He received his early education at Västerled parish preschool and then attended Smedslättsskolan and Ålstensskolan in Bromma, before completing his senior studies at Enskilda Gymnasiet in Stockholm. He was confirmed in 1994 and later studied at Kent School and Lundsbergs upper secondary school, graduating in 1999. Further studies included a year at the Rhode Island School of Design focusing on graphic design and completion of an Agricultural and Rural Management degree at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences in 2011. Like his father and sister, Prince Carl Philip has dyslexia. 

The Prince has a variety of interests, including scouting and outdoor activities. He actively participates in sports such as football, swimming, sailing, and skiing, and notably completed the Vasaloppet, a challenging cross-country ski race. He shares a passion for car racing with his great-uncle, Prince Bertil, and competes in the Porsche Carrera Cup Scandinavia and the Scandinavian Touring Car Championship. He also completed his military service with the Amphibious Battalion and progressed through the ranks to Major by 2014.  He continues to pursue his interest in design, co-founding the company Bernadotte & Kylberg in 2012.

Prince Carl Philip is involved in numerous charitable and public activities. He and Princess Sofia established a foundation dedicated to combating bullying. He also founded the Prince Carl Philip Racing Cup to support young karting talents and frequently visits companies with the Royal Swedish Academy of Engineering Sciences. He serves as a patron for several organizations, including The Swedish National Dyslexia Association and The International Union for Conservation of Nature.

He was in a long-term relationship with Emma Pernald from 1999 to 2009 before becoming linked to Sofia Hellqvist in 2010. They married in 2015 and have four children: Prince Alexander, Prince Gabriel, Prince Julian, and Princess Ines.  In 2019, his father rescinded the royal status of his two eldest sons to allow them greater freedom in their future choices, though they remain princes and in the line of succession. 

Prince Carl Philip holds a number of national and foreign honours, including being a Knight and Commander of the Royal Order of the Seraphim, and has received numerous commemorative medals.  His coat of arms incorporates elements of the Swedish greater coat of arms, the House of Bjälbo, and the arms of Värmland, reflecting his ducal title.

title: Carol Chell
text:
Carol Chell was born in July 1941 and is a British television personality known for her work presenting children’s programmes and later, as a television executive. Her initial career path led her to qualify as a teacher, and she began working in education before transitioning to television production in the 1960s, focusing on educational content. She became a familiar face to British children through her long-standing roles on two popular programmes: *Play School* and *Play Away*. 

Chell’s presenting career took off in 1966 when she joined the cast of *Play School*, remaining with the show until 1988. Simultaneously, from 1971 to 1980, she also presented *Play Away*, solidifying her position as a prominent figure in children’s television. Before achieving this widespread recognition, Chell received her education at Nottingham Girls’ High School, a direct grant grammar school, where she lived on Tudor Road in West Bridgford. She furthered her training at the Royal Central School of Speech and Drama.

Prior to her television work, Chell gained experience as a teacher at Pierrepont Secondary Modern School for Girls in Nottingham. Interestingly, a fellow teacher at the school during that time was Brian Clark, who later became a television writer, known for his work on *Telford's Change*. While best known for presenting, Chell also made guest appearances as herself in other programmes. In 1981, she participated in an episode of the BBC quiz show *The Adventure Game*, appearing as one of a group of ‘time-travellers’ attempting to solve puzzles. She also contributed to the ATV schools series *Starting Out* in 1982.

Beyond presenting, Chell moved into television management, taking on the role of head of pre-school programming at The Children's Channel, a satellite television station. She held this position until the channel ceased operations in 1998. Later in her career, she revisited her on-screen presence with an appearance on a celebrity edition of the BBC One game show *Pointless* in 2014, alongside fellow children’s television presenter Johnny Ball.

Chell married Ian Price on October 9, 1965, at St Peter's Church in Tollerton, Nottinghamshire; she was 23 years old at the time. The couple resided in Blackheath, London, while her parents lived in Christchurch, Dorset. Chell and Price have two daughters, Emily and Sophie, and together they have six grandchildren.

title: Michael Coulson (barrister)
text:
James Michael Coulson, born in 1927 and passing away in 2002, was a British barrister and judge who also spent five years as a Member of Parliament. He came from a prosperous background in the East Riding of Yorkshire, his father being a wool merchant. Coulson was educated at Fulneck School in Leeds and Merton College, Oxford, and completed his national service with the East Riding Yeomanry.

He was called to the Bar at the Middle Temple in 1951, practicing on the North Eastern Circuit while also taking on cases in London. Simultaneously, he became involved in Conservative politics, actively reorganizing the Young Conservatives in the north of England and even drafting their constitution. He also continued his military service, achieving the rank of Major in the Queen’s Own Yorkshire Yeomanry.

In 1955, Coulson married Dilys Adair Jones, gaining a 400-acre farm near Tadcaster as part of the marriage. He enjoyed farming, even training at the Royal Agricultural College, though a turkey farming venture proved disastrous, requiring him to house the birds in an airing cupboard and ultimately ending in their mass poisoning. He was also a keen equestrian and huntsman, serving as secretary for local point-to-point races.

Coulson’s political career took off when he was selected as the Conservative candidate for Kingston upon Hull North in 1958. He won the seat in the 1959 general election, increasing the previous slim majority, and delivered a well-received and witty maiden speech. As an MP, he was a supporter of the Conservative leaders of the time and successfully introduced a Private Member’s Bill to abolish the farthing as legal tender. He also served as Parliamentary Private Secretary to the Solicitor General and was involved with the Conservative Commonwealth Council.

Losing his parliamentary seat in 1964, Coulson focused on his legal career. He became an Assistant Recorder of Sheffield in 1965, followed by roles as Deputy Chairman of the Northern Agricultural Land Tribunal and Regional Chairman of Industrial Tribunals. Personal difficulties led him to relocate to the East Midlands in the 1970s to become a full-time chairman of Industrial Tribunals. He remarried in 1977 to Barbara Chambers, a hunting acquaintance significantly younger than himself. 

He progressed through the judiciary, becoming a Recorder of the Crown Court in 1981 and a Circuit Judge on the Midland and Oxford Circuit in 1983, earning the nickname "the hunting Judge" in his village. In 1990, he was appointed a Deputy Circuit Judge. A significant judgment in 1994 saw him award damages to Trevor McAuley for unfair dismissal based on racial discrimination, establishing a precedent for enhanced damages in such cases. Coulson retired in 1998 at the age of 70.

title: Ramli Sarip
text:
Ramli Sarip, born on October 15, 1952, is a Singaporean musician widely recognized as a pioneer of the nation’s rock scene and known affectionately as “Papa Rock.” He is a multifaceted artist, functioning as a singer, songwriter, arranger, and record producer. His musical career began in 1964 with the formation of the Malay rock band Sweet Charity, where he served as the frontman and lead vocalist for over two decades, remaining with the group until 1986. Sweet Charity achieved significant success throughout the 1970s and 1980s, reportedly sparking a widespread “rock explosion” across both Singapore and Malaysia.

Following his departure from Sweet Charity, Ramli embarked on a solo career, eventually signing with Warner Music. He distinguished himself as the first Malay rock singer to perform two solo concerts at the prestigious Istana Budaya in Kuala Lumpur. His contributions to the arts were acknowledged with the COMPASS Artistic Excellence Award in 1998. To support his solo work, Ramli formed the band Sangkakala, which functioned as his backing group.

Beyond music performance, Ramli has ventured into other creative areas. He hosted a Malaysian Hari Raya Puasa television special, *Bersama Ramli Sarip*, broadcast in 1990. However, his career faced a setback in 1993 when Radio Televisyen Malaysia imposed a seven-year ban on his appearances due to his long hair, which violated the broadcaster’s performance standards at the time. He contributed vocals to the 2011 remake of the song "Home" and, as of that year, had released a total of twelve solo albums. He also showcased his acting skills in the 2002 Singaporean satirical film, *Talking Cock the Movie*.

In 2019, Ramli Sarip performed a rendition of Singapore’s national anthem, "Majulah Singapura," at the National Day Parade. This performance drew considerable criticism, including a strong rebuke from Dr. Rohana Zubir, the daughter of the anthem’s original composer, Zubir Said, who publicly stated the rendition lacked the necessary quality and respect for the original composition. 

In 2013, Ramli Sarip was bestowed with the title of ‘Datuk’ by the Yang di-Pertua Negeri of the State of Malacca, in recognition of his contributions. He holds the Companion Class II of the Exalted Order of Malacca (DPSM), granting him the honorific Datuk.

title: Aert van der Neer
text:
Aert van der Neer was a Dutch Golden Age landscape painter born around 1603 in Gorinchem and who died in poverty in Amsterdam on November 9, 1677. He is known for his specialized depictions of small night scenes, illuminated by moonlight or fires, and winter landscapes, often featuring canals or rivers. A contemporary of artists like Aelbert Cuyp and Meindert Hobbema, he shared a similar fate of relative obscurity during his lifetime.

Early in his life, van der Neer worked as a steward for the lords of Arkel, which explains the lack of known artwork from his youth. He later married Lysbeth Camphuysen in 1629, sister to the painters Rafael and Joachim Govertsz Camphuysen, and together they had six children. Despite being an artist, van der Neer struggled financially, barely managing to support his family through the sale of his paintings. He briefly attempted to supplement his income by running a wine tavern in 1659, but was unsuccessful and declared bankruptcy two years later. Upon his death, his paintings were valued at a mere five shillings each, highlighting his lack of recognition at the time. His son Eglon followed in his footsteps and became a portrait painter.

Van der Neer's earliest dated works, from 1639 and 1642, are considered immature and of poor quality. However, his skills developed quickly, as evidenced by pieces from 1643 and 1644. He depicted real locations throughout the Netherlands, including areas around Haarlem, Leiden, and along the Meuse and Rhine rivers. He was particularly drawn to Dordrecht, the home of Aelbert Cuyp, and the two artists developed a friendship and even collaborated on paintings, sometimes contributing different elements to the same canvas. 

Cuyp was the more prominent artist, often enhancing van der Neer’s work with figures and cattle.  Their collaboration is evident in landscapes where Cuyp painted foreground details, such as figures and animals, within van der Neer’s settings. Van der Neer excelled at capturing atmospheric effects, particularly translucence in darkness, using warm browns and steel greys to reveal distant objects. He was also skilled at portraying frozen water, creating lively winter scenes with figures skating, sleighing, and fishing, yet avoiding a harsh, frosty impression. 

While his paintings are not as highly valued as those of Cuyp or Hobbema, they are appreciated for their unique charm and are sought after by collectors. Approximately 150 of his works are publicly accessible, with a significant collection housed in the Hermitage Museum in Saint Petersburg, and others found in the National Gallery and Wallace Collection in England.

title: Leo Kokubo
text:
Leo Kokubo, born on January 23, 2001, is a professional footballer who currently plays as a goalkeeper for Sint-Truiden, a Belgian team. He is of mixed heritage, with a Nigerian father and a Japanese mother, and was born in Japan. Kokubo has represented Japan at various youth levels, including the U16, U18, and U23 national teams.

His involvement with the Japan U23 squad culminated in a significant achievement in April 2024 when he was selected for the 2024 AFC U-23 Asian Cup. During the final match of this tournament against Uzbekistan, Kokubo played a crucial role in securing a 1–0 victory for Japan. Late in the game, during stoppage time, he successfully saved a penalty kick taken by Umarali Rakhmonaliev. This pivotal save directly contributed to Japan winning the AFC U-23 Asian Cup for the second time in the nation’s history. 

As a direct result of his outstanding performance in the final, Kokubo was awarded the “Man of the match” honor. This recognition highlighted his key contribution to the team's success and his individual skill as a goalkeeper.

Beyond his national team achievements, Kokubo has also experienced club-level success. He was part of the Benfica team that won the Supertaça Cândido de Oliveira in 2023, a Portuguese Super Cup competition. As of February 15, 2025, his career statistics are recorded, though specific details of those statistics are not provided in the available information. 

In summary, Leo Kokubo has established himself as a promising goalkeeper, demonstrating his abilities both at the youth international level for Japan and with his club, Benfica. His performance in the 2024 AFC U-23 Asian Cup final, marked by a crucial penalty save and a “Man of the match” award, stands as a highlight of his career thus far.

title: Abdulqawi Yusuf
text:
Abdulqawi Ahmed Yusuf is a Somali lawyer and judge currently serving on the International Court of Justice (ICJ), having been appointed in 2009. He notably served as the President of the ICJ from 2018 to 2021, becoming the third African to hold the position, following judges from Nigeria and Algeria. He has announced his resignation, effective September 30, 2025, before the conclusion of his term in February 2027, prompting a future election to fill the remainder.

Born in Eyl, Puntland, Somalia, Yusuf pursued higher education in law, earning a Juris Doctor from the Somali National University and a PhD in international law from the Graduate Institute of International Studies of Geneva. He supplemented his education with post-graduate studies in international law at the University of Florence in Italy. He is proficient in five languages: Somali, Arabic, English, French, and Italian.

Prior to his role at the ICJ, Yusuf held a distinguished career in international organizations. He was the Legal Adviser and Director of the Office of International Standards and Legal Affairs for UNESCO from 2001 to 2009. Before that, he served with the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) in Vienna as Legal Advisor and later as Assistant Director General for African Affairs. Earlier positions include Representative and Head of the New York office of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), and Chief of the Legal Policies Service of UNCTAD. He also lectured in law at both the Somali National University and the University of Geneva and was a delegate for Somalia at the Third United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea.

Beyond his positions within international bodies, Yusuf is a respected scholar in the field of international law. He was elected to the Institut de droit international in 1999 and remains a member. He founded and continues to serve as the General Editor of the *African Yearbook of International Law* and is a founder and chairperson of the executive committee of the African Foundation for International Law. He has authored and edited numerous publications on international law, including books focusing on Pan-Africanism, intellectual property, and trade. He also contributes articles to newspapers concerning current affairs in Northeast Africa and Somalia. He is involved with several editorial boards and institutes dedicated to international law and relations. He previously served as a judge *ad hoc* at the ICJ.

title: Jashubhai Dhanabhai Barad
text:
Jashubhai Dhanabhai Barad was an Indian politician from the state of Gujarat who served prominently in both state and national politics until his death in 2016. Born on September 15, 1955, Barad represented the Junagadh constituency in the 14th Lok Sabha, the lower house of India’s Parliament, and held a ministerial position within the Gujarat state government. He was widely known and respected, earning the nicknames “lion of Saurashtra” and “lion of Sorath.”

Barad’s political career spanned several decades and included multiple terms as a Member of the Legislative Assembly. He first entered the Gujarat Legislative Assembly in 1990, winning election from the Somnath constituency. He was re-elected from Somnath in 1995, and during this period, he served as a Cabinet Minister responsible for Water Resources and Irrigation. His work as minister involved significant contributions to the development of major water projects within Gujarat, specifically the Narmada and Ukai Dam Projects. 

He later shifted his focus to the Talala Gir constituency, successfully contesting and winning elections there in both 1998 and 2012.  He was actively serving his fourth term as a Member of the Legislative Assembly representing Talala Gir at the time of his passing. In 2004, Barad expanded his political reach to the national level, being elected to the Lok Sabha – the Parliament of India – representing Junagadh. 

Jashubhai Barad’s life was cut short on January 25, 2016, when he died in Ahmedabad due to a brain tumour. His death prompted a by-election in the Talala Gir constituency, which was won by his brother, Bhagvanjibhai Barad. Bhagvanjibhai secured his victory with a substantial margin of 31,000 votes over his opponent, Govindbhai Parmar of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). 

Barad came from the Yadav, also known as Ahir, community and his family originated from Badalpara village, located near Veraval. Throughout his career, he established himself as a significant figure in Gujarat’s political landscape, leaving a legacy through his involvement in crucial infrastructure projects and his continued representation of his constituents.

title: Kathleen A. McGrath
text:
Kathleen Anne McGrath, born June 4, 1952, in Columbus, Ohio, was a pioneering figure in the United States Navy, most notably becoming the first woman to command a US Navy warship. She was the daughter of Colonel James H. McGrath and Martha McGrath. Prior to her naval career, McGrath worked for the United States Forestry Service until 1980. She received a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science from California State University, Sacramento in 1975, and later earned a Master of Arts degree in Educational Management from Stanford University in 1987. She completed Officer Candidate School in Rhode Island as part of her training.

McGrath’s naval career included deployments to the Western Pacific, the Persian Gulf, and the Mediterranean and Caribbean seas. In 1993 and 1994, she commanded the rescue and salvage ship USS Recovery. While Lieutenant Commander Darlene Iskra had commanded a similar ship, the USS Opportune, in 1990, McGrath’s command of the frigate USS Jarrett in December 1998 marked a significant milestone, as the Jarrett was a combatant ship – a vessel with the capacity to engage in warfare – making her the first woman to achieve this distinction. She was selected as one of five women, alongside Michelle J. Howard, Maureen Farren, Ann O'Connor, and Grace Mehl, to break barriers as the first female combatant commanders in the Navy.

In March of 2000, McGrath led the USS Jarrett on a deployment from San Diego, California, to the Persian Gulf. The mission focused on intercepting vessels suspected of illegally smuggling Iraqi oil, in violation of United Nations sanctions. This deployment occurred only six years after Congress lifted restrictions preventing women from serving on combat ships and aircraft. McGrath was promoted to the rank of Captain in May 2002. Following her command of the Jarrett, she served at the Joint Advanced Warfighting Unit in Alexandria, Virginia.

Throughout her career, Captain McGrath received numerous accolades, including the Legion of Merit, the Meritorious Service Medal with three gold stars (representing four awards), the Navy Commendation Medal with two gold stars, the Navy Achievement Medal, the Joint Meritorious Unit Award, the Meritorious Unit Citation, the Navy E Ribbon, the National Defense Service Medal with a star, the Armed Forces Expeditionary Medal, the Southwest Asia Service Medal with a star, the Sea Service Deployment Ribbon, the Navy Overseas Service Ribbon, and the Kuwait Liberation Medal. 

Kathleen McGrath passed away on September 26, 2002, at the age of 50, succumbing to lung cancer at the National Naval Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland. She was married to Gregory H. Brandon and had two children. She is interred at Arlington National Cemetery, a testament to her dedicated service to the nation.

title: Clancy Brown
text:
Clancy Brown, born Clarence James Brown III on January 5, 1959, is a highly prolific American actor known for portraying villains and authoritative figures in a career spanning since the 1980s. He has built a substantial body of work in both live-action and voice-over roles across film and television.

Brown’s early life was shaped by his family’s involvement in the newspaper business; his father, Clarence J. “Bud” Brown Jr., was a newspaper publisher and later a congressman, continuing a legacy begun by Clancy’s grandfather. He graduated from St. Albans School and Northwestern University, with a performance in *The Crucible* at the former. He began his film career with a role in *Bad Boys* (1983) and quickly gained recognition for roles like Rawhide in *The Adventures of Buckaroo Banzai Across the 8th Dimension* (1984), Frankenstein’s monster in *The Bride* (1985), and the Kurgan in *Highlander* (1986). He continued to appear in numerous films including *The Shawshank Redemption* (1994) as Captain Hadley, *Starship Troopers* (1997) as Sgt. Zim, and more recently *Promising Young Woman* (2020) and *John Wick: Chapter 4* (2023). 

Alongside his film work, Brown has maintained a successful television career. Notable roles include Brother Justin Crowe in *Carnivàle* (2003-2005), Waylon "Jock" Jeffcoat in *Billions* (2018-2019, 2023), Kurt Caldwell in *Dexter: New Blood* (2021-2022), and Sal Maroni in *The Penguin* (2024). He frequently appears in guest roles on shows like *ER*, *Lost*, and *The Flash*.

However, Brown is arguably just as renowned for his voice work. Since 1996, he has been the voice of Lex Luthor in numerous DC Comics animated projects, surpassing all other actors in the length of time portraying the character. He is also the iconic voice of Mr. Krabs on *SpongeBob SquarePants* since 1999, and has contributed to the *Avatar: The Last Airbender* franchise, *Star Wars: The Clone Wars* as Savage Opress, and *Thor: Ragnarok* as Surtur. His voice acting extends into video games, including roles in the *Crash Bandicoot* series, *Detroit: Become Human*, and many others. 

Brown has been married to Jeanne Johnson since 1993 and they have two children. His career demonstrates remarkable versatility, allowing him to excel in both on-screen and voice-over performances, often embodying characters that leave a lasting impression.

title: Rangi Te Kanawa
text:
Rangituatahi Te Kanawa, also known as Warnes after marriage, is a New Zealand textile conservator and weaver dedicated to the preservation of Māori textiles. Her career began with a scholarship from the Department of Internal Affairs, driven by a desire within the Aotearoa Moananui a Kiwa Weavers for Māori involvement in conserving Māori artefacts held in institutions. Her initial training took place in Canberra, followed by a year at the National Museum of New Zealand’s conservation unit in Wellington. To qualify for a three-year degree in Conservation in Cultural Materials at Canberra University, she successfully completed sixth-form chemistry studies through a Wellington secondary school.

Further practical experience was gained through a six-month internship at the Textile Conservation Centre at Hampton Court Palace and time spent at the British Museum. Currently, Te Kanawa works at Te Papa Tongarewa, the Museum of New Zealand, where she specializes in the conservation of Māori textiles and conducts related research. A significant project she’s involved in is ‘Whakapapa of Paru’, a collaboration with a forensic scientist from GNS, focused on determining the origins of cloaks within Te Papa’s collection. 

Te Kanawa’s own weaving practice is also recognized, with examples of her work being collected by Te Papa itself. She is an active member of the New Zealand conservators of cultural materials association. In 2023, her contributions to Māori art and heritage preservation were formally acknowledged with her appointment as a Member of the New Zealand Order of Merit in the King's Birthday and Coronation Honours.

Te Kanawa comes from a strong lineage of artistic and cultural practitioners. She is the daughter of Diggeress Te Kanawa and the granddaughter of the renowned Dame Rangimarie Hetet. She is affiliated with the Ngāti Maniapoto iwi, highlighting her deep connection to Māori heritage.

Beyond her practical work, Te Kanawa is also a published researcher. She co-authored an article titled “The Conservation of Māori Textiles in Aotearoa New Zealand” in the *Surface Design Journal* in 2020. She was also involved in a scientific study published in *Molecular Biology and Evolution* in 2011, which used ancient DNA to trace the origins of Māori feather cloaks. In 2021, she completed a PhD thesis entitled *Mana Taonga Kākahu: Exploring Approaches to Reconnecting Taonga Kākahu to Tangatawhenua* at Victoria University of Wellington, which is accessible through their Open Access Repository. Additional resources detailing her work, including a film about conserving cloaks and an interview discussing the challenges of Māori textile preservation, are publicly available.

title: Asafa Powell
text:
Asafa Powell, born in 1982 in Jamaica, is a retired sprinter renowned for his dominance in the 100 metres. He twice held the world record for the event, first with a time of 9.77 seconds in 2005, then 9.74 seconds in 2007. His personal best of 9.72 seconds ranks fourth all-time, and as of 2016, he had broken the 10-second barrier a record 97 times. Beyond the 100m, Powell also holds the world record for the 100-yard dash with a time of 9.09 seconds, set in 2010. He achieved Olympic gold in the 4x100m relay in 2016.

Powell’s Olympic journey included participation in the 100m at the 2004, 2008 and 2012 games, achieving fifth place finishes in the first two. He suffered a groin injury during the 2012 race, finishing eighth. He secured a bronze medal in the 100m and a silver in the 4x100m relay at the 2007 World Championships. He also experienced success at the Commonwealth Games, winning two golds and a silver medal. In 2009, he earned a bronze in the 100m at the World Championships, followed by a gold in the relay. Throughout his career, Powell won the IAAF World Athletics Final five times and was, for a period, the official 100m world record holder.

A challenging period arose in 2013 when Powell tested positive for the stimulant oxilofrine, alongside teammate Sherone Simpson. Both athletes maintained their innocence, claiming they unknowingly consumed a contaminated supplement. Initially facing an 18-month suspension, their bans were ultimately lifted in 2014 by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which determined the positive tests were due to the undisclosed presence of oxilofrine in the supplement.

Born into a family of runners – his father clocked 10.2s, his mother 11.4s, and his brothers 9.5s for 100 yards – Powell initially aspired to be a mechanic. He began training seriously while studying in Kingston, and in 2001 joined the MVP Track & Field Club, coached by Stephen Francis. Francis utilized an unusual training method, incorporating a 10% sloped stretch of road to improve starts. 

Powell’s early career saw limited success at the ISSA High School Championships, but he quickly improved under Francis’ guidance. He quickly climbed the ranks, achieving a personal best of 10.26s at the 2002 Commonwealth Games and winning the Jamaican 100m National Championship in 2003. He experienced a controversial moment at the 2003 World Championships, being disqualified for a false start alongside Jon Drummond. His breakthrough came in 2004 with his first sub-10 second run (9.99s) and a fifth-place finish at the Athens Olympics. He continued to break records in 2005, culminating in a new world record of 9.77 seconds, beating the previous mark held by Tim Montgomery. He continued his success into 2006 and 2007, winning multiple Grand Prix events and achieving a second world record of 9.74 seconds in 2007. Despite consistent success, injuries plagued his 2008 and 2009 seasons, including groin and pectoral muscle injuries, ultimately impacting his individual performances at the 2008 Beijing Olympics.

title: Idris Elba
text:
Idrissa Akuna Elba, known professionally as Idris Elba, is a highly successful English actor and musician born in London in 1972. He has achieved significant recognition for his work, including a Golden Globe Award and numerous nominations for BAFTA and Emmy Awards. In 2016, *Time* magazine included him on its list of the 100 Most Influential People in the World. His films have collectively grossed over $9.8 billion worldwide, placing him among the top 20 highest-grossing actors of all time.

Elba’s acting journey began with studies at the National Youth Music Theatre and early roles in television productions like *Crimewatch* and *The Boot Street Band*. He gained prominence playing Stringer Bell in the acclaimed HBO series *The Wire* (2002-2004) and later as DCI John Luther in the BBC One series *Luther* (2010-2019), a role which earned him a Golden Globe. He’s also appeared in notable television shows like *The Office* and *The Big C*, and more recently in the Apple TV+ thriller *Hijack*. 

His film career is extensive, including roles in *American Gangster*, *Prometheus*, *Star Trek Beyond*, and *The Suicide Squad*. He portrayed Nelson Mandela in *Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom*, earning another Golden Globe nomination. Notably, he received a Screen Actors Guild Award for his performance in the Netflix drama *Beasts of No Nation*. Elba has also lent his voice to animated films such as *Zootopia*, *The Jungle Book*, *Finding Dory*, and the *Sonic the Hedgehog* franchise, voicing Knuckles the Echidna. He made his directorial debut with the film *Yardie* in 2018.

Elba’s early life was spent in Hackney and East Ham, London, where he shortened his name from Idrissa to Idris while at school. He comes from a Sierra Leonean and Ghanaian heritage, with his parents having immigrated to London from Sierra Leone. He supported himself through various jobs while pursuing acting, including DJing, tyre-fitting, and working at the Ford Dagenham plant. He began DJing professionally in his teens under the name DJ Big Driis.

Beyond acting, Elba is a successful DJ and R&B singer, performing under the monikers DJ Big Driis and Idris. He is also a co-owner of the Formula E racing team, Kiro Race Co. He has established his own production company, Green Door Pictures, with Apple, and more recently 22Summers, focusing on developing original content. He is currently involved in projects including an Afrofuturist animated series and a film studio in Zanzibar, as well as a documentary on knife crime in the UK.

title: Michael H. Schneider Sr.
text:
Michael H. Schneider Sr., born in 1943, dedicated his career to the legal system in Texas and at the federal level, culminating in his service as a United States District Judge. His educational background began with an Associate of Arts degree from Lon Morris College in 1963, followed by a Bachelor of Science from Stephen F. Austin State University in 1965. He completed his legal training at the University of Houston Law Center, earning a Juris Doctor in 1970.

Schneider’s early career involved public service as an assistant district attorney in Harris County, Texas, a position he held from 1971 to 1975. He then transitioned into private practice for a year before becoming a general attorney for Dresser Industries from 1976 to 1980. During this period, he also served part-time as a municipal judge for the City of West University Place, Texas, for twelve years, from 1978 to 1990. He continued his work as a general attorney, first with Bawden Drilling, Inc. from 1980 to 1986, and later as a general solicitor for the Union Pacific Railroad Company from 1986 to 1989, before briefly returning to private practice in 1989 and 1990.

Schneider's career then shifted toward judicial roles within the Texas state court system. He served as the presiding judge of the 157th District Court in Harris County from 1990 to 1996. He was subsequently appointed as chief justice of the First Court of Appeals of Texas in Houston, a position he held from 1996 to 2002. While serving on the Court of Appeals, he pursued further education, earning a Master of Laws degree from the University of Virginia Law School in 2001. In 2002, he reached the highest level of the Texas state judiciary, becoming a justice on the Supreme Court of Texas, a role he fulfilled until 2004.

In 2004, President George W. Bush nominated Schneider to the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas, filling the vacancy left by John H. Hannah Jr. The Senate confirmed his appointment on September 7, 2004, and he received his commission a few days later, on September 10, 2004. He served as a district judge for over eleven years, assuming senior status on January 7, 2016, before ultimately retiring from the bench on October 1, 2016.

title: Jonathan Roy
text:
Jonathan Piuze-Roy, born on March 15, 1989, is a Canadian singer and songwriter who notably comes from a family steeped in hockey history as the son of Hockey Hall of Fame goaltender Patrick Roy. While initially following in his father’s footsteps and pursuing a career in junior hockey, Roy transitioned to music in 2007 with his father’s encouragement. He has since released six studio albums throughout his career.

Roy’s upbringing was marked by a move to Colorado at age six due to his father’s trade, but he also found early artistic influence through his mother’s piano playing. He began writing poetry as a teenager, around ages 13 or 14, and soon started composing music to accompany his verses around age 16. He did play competitive hockey, even joining the Quebec Remparts at 17 while his father was the team’s coach, but simultaneously harbored musical ambitions, drawing inspiration from artists like the Backstreet Boys, John Mayer, and Ray LaMontagne. At 18, a conversation with his father solidified his decision to pursue music, rather than continue with hockey and formal education.

His early musical efforts resulted in the release of *What I’ve Become* in 2009, followed by *Found My Way* in 2010. In 2011, he released his first French-language album, *La route*, which featured a duet with Natasha St-Pier on the title track, garnering the most attention of his earlier work. Beyond music recording, Roy also took on an acting role in the 2012 revival of the musical *Don Juan*, receiving critical praise.

A pivotal moment in his career came in 2012 when his father facilitated a meeting with Corey Hart, the 1980s pop singer and head of Siena Records, an affiliate of Warner Music. Impressed by Roy’s performance of a Teddy Thompson song, Hart signed him to the label. This partnership led to a successful holiday collaboration in 2016, a duet with Hart on the Chris Rea song "Driving Home for Christmas." 

Roy's major-label debut, *Mr. Optimist Blues*, arrived in 2017 on Siena Records, with Hart serving as executive producer and contributing to the songwriting. The album was described as a blend of contemporary pop, reggae, and influences from artists like Ed Sheeran, Paolo Nutini, and Bob Marley. He frequently collaborates with Kim Richardson, utilizing her talents as a duet partner or backing vocalist. More recently, in 2023, Roy contributed to a charity single, joining an all-star lineup for Serena Ryder’s “What I Wouldn’t Do,” benefiting youth mental health initiatives. He is currently based in Toronto.

title: Diafra Sakho
text:
Diafra Sakho, born in Senegal in 1989, was a professional footballer who primarily played as a striker. He began his career in the French football system, starting with Génération Foot, a feeder club for FC Metz, before joining Metz directly in 2007. After initially playing for Metz’s reserve team where he scored 17 goals in 22 games, he earned a place in the first team in 2010, scoring his first goal against Nantes. A loan spell at Boulogne followed in 2012, but he returned to Metz and played a key role in their promotion back to Ligue 2, scoring 19 goals in 33 appearances. He then led Metz to the Ligue 2 title with another impressive goal-scoring season, netting 20 goals in 36 games, earning him the Ligue 2 Player of the Year award for the 2013–14 season.

In August 2014, Sakho moved to West Ham United in England, fulfilling a long-held dream. He quickly made an impact, scoring his first goal for the club against Sheffield United in the League Cup. He then became known for a remarkable run of scoring in his first six Premier League starts, matching a record previously held by Micky Quinn, and was awarded the Premier League Player of the Month for October 2014. However, his first season was disrupted by injury, sustained in a match against West Bromwich Albion, which also led to a dispute with the Senegal national team who wanted him to participate in the 2015 Africa Cup of Nations. FIFA ultimately fined West Ham for playing him in an FA Cup match during the tournament.

Sakho continued with West Ham for several more seasons, although injuries continued to hamper his progress. He scored in both the Europa League and Premier League in the 2015-16 season, and after a transfer request and a failed medical at West Bromwich Albion, he remained with the club. The 2016–17 season saw limited appearances due to injury, and in January 2018, he moved to French side Rennes. He then had a loan spell with Turkish club Bursaspor before joining Swiss side Neuchâtel Xamax in 2020, where he failed to score in eight appearances. He later signed for Nancy in 2022, eventually retiring from playing in July 2023.

Sakho also represented the Senegal national team, making his debut in 2014 and scoring his first international goal against Kosovo. He played a part in Senegal's qualification for the 2018 FIFA World Cup, their first appearance in the tournament since 2002. Throughout his career, he achieved honors including a Ligue 2 title with Metz and individual accolades such as the Ligue 2 Player of the Year award. He also had a period of legal trouble in 2015, being arrested on suspicion of assault, but was later cleared of any wrongdoing.

title: Andreas Ivanschitz
text:
Andreas Ivanschitz, born on October 15, 1983, is a retired Austrian footballer who played as an attacking midfielder throughout an 18-year career. He represented Austria internationally and played for a variety of clubs including Rapid Wien, Red Bull Salzburg, Panathinaikos, 1.FSV Mainz 05, Levante, Seattle Sounders FC, and Viktoria Plzen.

Ivanschitz began his youth career with ASK Baumgarten in Eisenstadt, spending nine years with the local team before being scouted by Rapid Wien in 1998.
