Bogue’s influence extended to the training of some of the earliest Protestant missionaries to China, notably Robert Morrison and William Milne, whom he instructed in 1804-1805 and 1809-1812 respectively. He himself had intended to travel to India as a missionary in 1796, but was prevented from doing so due to opposition from the East India Company. Later in his life, in 1824, he prepared Samuel Dyer for missionary work before Dyer departed for Penang. 

Beyond his work in education and the ministry, Bogue was actively involved in the founding of both the British and Foreign Bible Society and the Religious Tract Society. He collaborated with James Bennett, the minister of Romsey, to produce a notable three-volume *History of Dissenters*, published in 1809. He also authored *An Essay on the Divine Authority of the New Testament*. In 1815, Yale University recognized his contributions by awarding him a Doctor of Divinity degree. David Bogue died on October 25, 1825, in Brighton while accompanying the London Missionary Society on their annual tour. He left behind a legacy as a pivotal figure in the development of missionary work and nonconformist religious thought.

title: Don DeLillo
text:
Donald DeLillo, born November 20, 1936, is a highly regarded American author known for his novels, short stories, plays, screenplays, and essays. His work frequently explores themes of consumerism, nuclear anxieties, language, art, television, the digital age, mathematics, politics, economics, and sports. While respected within literary circles for some time, he achieved widespread recognition with the 1985 publication of *White Noise*, which won the National Book Award. He followed this success with *Libra* (1988), a novel focusing on the assassination of John F. Kennedy, and later received the PEN/Faulkner Award for *Mao II* and the William Dean Howells Medal for *Underworld*. Further accolades include the Jerusalem Prize (1999), the PEN/Saul Bellow Award (2010), and the Library of Congress Prize for American Fiction (2013). DeLillo views his writing as a form of opposition, believing writers should challenge power structures – corporations, the state, and the prevailing culture of consumption.

Born and raised in the Bronx, New York City, DeLillo grew up in an Italian-American Catholic family with roots in Molise, Italy. He recalls a childhood filled with imaginative play, particularly pretending to be a baseball announcer, and a multilingual household where English and Italian were frequently mixed. His serious engagement with reading began during a summer job as a parking attendant, a period he describes as a “golden age.” Influenced by modernist writers like James Joyce, William Faulkner, Flannery O’Connor, and Ernest Hemingway, he also found inspiration in jazz music – artists like Ornette Coleman and Miles Davis – and European and Asian cinema, particularly the works of Antonioni, Godard, and Truffaut. He credits his parents’ support for allowing him to pursue a literary career.

DeLillo graduated from Fordham University in 1958 with a degree in communication arts and initially worked as a copywriter at Ogilvy & Mather, writing advertisements for companies like Sears Roebuck. He published his first short story in 1960 and began working on his first novel in 1966, but only truly committed to writing after leaving advertising in 1964. He described his initial foray into novels as a slow process, acknowledging a lack of ambition and a developing sense of what constituted serious writing. William Gaddis’s *The Recognitions* proved a particularly formative influence.

The 1970s were DeLillo’s most prolific period, with six novels published between 1971 and 1978. These included *Americana*, *End Zone*, *Great Jones Street*, *Ratner's Star*, *Players*, and *Running Dog*.  He supported his writing through a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1978, which allowed him to travel and write in Greece. DeLillo later reflected that while he doesn't regret the work of the 70s, he might have benefited from a slower, more deliberate pace. He also published *Amazons* under a pseudonym, later requesting it be removed from his bibliographies.  The 1980s brought further success with *The Names* (1982) and the breakthrough novel *White Noise* (1985), solidifying his reputation as a major contemporary novelist. *Libra* followed in 1988, sparking both acclaim and controversy for its depiction of Lee Harvey Oswald and the Kennedy assassination.

title: Andy Middleton
text:
Andy Middleton, born May 22, 1962, is an American jazz saxophonist proficient in both tenor and soprano saxophone. He has collaborated with numerous prominent musicians throughout his career, including Ralph Towner, Dave Holland, Kenny Wheeler, and Renee Rosnes. His musical journey began in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, where he started playing the alto saxophone at the age of nine, nurtured by a musical family.

Middleton’s formal education included studies at the University of Rochester (1980-1982) and the University of Miami (1982-1987). A pivotal experience was his attendance at the Banff Centre in Alberta, Canada in 1985 and 1986, where he connected with influential figures like Steve Coleman, John Abercrombie, Richie Beirach, and David Liebman. In 1987, he relocated to the New York City area and became involved with several big bands, including those led by Bob Mintzer and Lionel Hampton – the latter of which recorded a composition he co-wrote with his brother, Rob Middleton, titled “Two Brothers.” He also performed with the Maria Schneider Jazz Orchestra. 

Throughout his career, Middleton led his own quartet, which featured a rotating roster of musicians including Ben Monder, John Hollenbeck, Scott Colley, Henry Hey, and others. He released his debut album, *Acid Rain*, in 1991 on Owl Records. *Terra Infirma* followed in 1995, produced by David Liebman and released by EMI France. He also co-led the group The Fensters, recording two albums, *Jazz Music, Vol. 1* (1992) and *Jazz Music, Vol. X* (1996). Later albums as a leader included *Nomad’s Notebook* (1999) with Ralph Towner and Dave Holland, and *Reinventing the World* (2003) featuring Kenny Wheeler and Nils Wogram.

Middleton has also contributed as a sideman to recordings by artists such as Lionel Hampton, Maria Schneider, and Stefan ‘Pista’ Bartus. In 2006, he moved to Vienna, Austria, to take a teaching position at the Music and Arts University of the City of Vienna.

Throughout his career, Middleton has received several accolades, including an Outstanding Jazz Soloist award from *DownBeat* magazine in 1987, and first prize awards for both best soloist and best arranger at the 13th Europ’ Jazz Contest in Belgium in 1991. He has also been a recipient of grants from organizations like the National Endowment for the Arts, the Brooklyn Arts Council, and Chamber Music America, supporting his work and performances.

title: Gubby Allen
text:
Sir George Oswald Browning “Gubby” Allen was a prominent cricketer and influential administrator, born in Australia in 1902 but raised in England from the age of six. He captained England in eleven Test matches and was known as a fast bowler and hard-hitting lower-order batsman, primarily playing first-class cricket for Middlesex and Cambridge University. His early life included education at Eton College, where he developed his cricketing talent despite battling rib injuries that plagued his career. He was accepted to Trinity College, Cambridge, and continued to excel, facing some early accusations of illegal bowling that were later dismissed. 

Allen's first-class career began with appearances for Middlesex in 1921, alongside his university matches. His time at Cambridge was marked by success, including a nine-wicket haul against Winchester and a crucial performance against Oxford in the University Match, earning him a blue. However, academic shortcomings led to a period of rustication, and he returned to Middlesex. He found balancing cricket with a full-time job in the City of London challenging, initially working for the Royal Exchange Assurance Corporation and later for Debenhams, which impacted his availability for matches. He spent time working in France, where he demonstrated financial acumen by identifying and warning against a risky business venture.

Despite the difficulties of balancing work and cricket, Allen continued to impress, showcasing his all-round abilities with both bat and ball. He gained recognition with the Gentlemen's team and was frequently mentioned as a potential England player, though selection was often delayed. He finally debuted for England in 1930, filling in for an injured Harold Larwood, but faced criticism in the press regarding his Australian birth. Allen’s bowling was often described as erratic but capable of devastating spells, and he frequently delivered crucial runs when his team was under pressure. A particularly memorable performance came in 1929 when he took all ten wickets for Middlesex against Lancashire at Lord’s.

Allen became England captain in 1936, leading the team on the 1936–37 tour of Australia, which England narrowly lost 3-2 after initially winning the first two matches. He continued to play intermittently for Middlesex following World War II, in which he served in military intelligence, and made a final Test appearance as captain in the West Indies in 1947-48. His career was often hampered by his work commitments and the recurring rib injury. 

As his playing career wound down, Allen transitioned into cricket administration, becoming a highly influential figure within the Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC). He played a key role in developing an MCC coaching manual and worked to eliminate illegal bowling actions. He served as chairman of the England selectors from 1955 to 1961, overseeing a period of success in English cricket alongside captain Peter May. He later became MCC president in 1963 and treasurer the following year, where he became embroiled in the controversial D’Oliveira affair. He was knighted in 1986 and lived near Lord’s until his death in 1989 at the age of 87.

title: Namita Gokhale
text:
Namita Gokhale, born in Lucknow in 1956, is a prominent Indian author, editor, festival director, and publisher. She spent her formative years in Nainital, raised by her aunts and grandmother, and studied English Literature at Delhi University. Her life took several turns early on; she married and had two daughters while still a student, and later faced both cancer survival and the loss of her husband by the age of forty. 

Gokhale’s career began unusually with editing the film magazine *Super* at age seventeen, a role she held for seven years. She then transitioned to writing, publishing her debut novel, *Paro: Dreams of Passion*, in 1984. This novel, a satirical portrayal of Delhi’s social scene, gained both controversy and acclaim, becoming a cult classic and later re-released alongside its sequel, *Priya: In Incredible Indyaa*. While *Priya* received a more mixed reception, Gokhale continued to explore themes of societal dynamics and personal narratives in subsequent works like *Gods, Graves, and Grandmother*, which was adapted into a musical play, and *A Himalayan Love Story*. She’s also written nonfiction, including *Mountain Echoes – Reminiscences of Kumaoni Women*, which focuses on the lives of women in her ancestral region, and a version of the *Mahabharata* for children. More recently, her novel *Things to Leave Behind*, set in the Kumaon hills, has earned significant recognition, winning the 2021 Sahitya Akademi Award and appearing on the longlist for the International Dublin Literary Award.

Beyond her writing, Gokhale is deeply involved in the literary world as a facilitator and organizer. She conceptualized and hosted *Kitaabnama: Books and Beyond*, a Doordarshan show highlighting Indian literature in multiple languages. She is a founder and co-director of the renowned Jaipur Literature Festival, alongside William Dalrymple and Sanjoy K Roy, and also advises other festivals like 'Mountain Echoes' in Bhutan and The Himalayan Echo Kumaon Festival. She co-founded Yatra Books in 2005, a publishing house specializing in creative writing and translations. Earlier, she was involved with a government initiative to translate Indian literature into UNESCO languages, though funding issues led her to refocus on the Jaipur Literature Festival’s publishing imprint, Jaipur Bookmark.

Gokhale’s writing is influenced by a diverse range of authors, from Tolstoy and Dostoyevsky to Muriel Spark and Kalidasa, as well as *The Tale of Genji*. Her Kumaoni Brahmin upbringing and connection to the Himalayas are also central to her work, often exploring themes of identity and mythology. Critics have noted her “sparkling” style and acerbic wit. Throughout her career, she has received several awards, including the Centenary National Award for Literature and the Sushila Devi Literature Award, culminating in the prestigious Sahitya Akademi Award for *Things to Leave Behind*.

title: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo
text:
Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, known as “El Jefe de Jefes” or “The Boss of Bosses,” was a key figure in the establishment of the Guadalajara Cartel, which dominated Mexican drug trafficking in the 1980s. Born in 1946 in Sinaloa, he initially worked as a police officer and leveraged political connections – including being the godfather to a governor’s son – to build his criminal organization. He rose to prominence by brokering corruption and taking control of trafficking routes after the death of a previous trafficker.

The Guadalajara Cartel’s success stemmed from a deal with Colombian cartels, who began using Mexico as a transit point for cocaine due to increased interdiction efforts in Florida. Rather than accepting cash, Félix Gallardo’s cartel took a 50% cut of the cocaine they transported, generating an estimated $5 billion annually. By the end of the 1980s, the Guadalajara Cartel, which would later splinter into the Sinaloa, Tijuana, Juárez, and Pacifico Sur cartels, had a near monopoly on the Mexican drug trade.

Félix Gallardo’s operations came under intense scrutiny following the 1985 kidnapping and murder of DEA agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena. Camarena had been investigating the cartel’s marijuana plantations and uncovering connections between drug traffickers, Mexican law enforcement, and government officials within the ruling PRI party. Félix Gallardo allegedly ordered Camarena’s abduction, which led to a brutal torture and murder. This sparked “Operation Leyenda,” a massive DEA investigation that ultimately implicated Félix Gallardo and his associates.

Arrested in 1989, Félix Gallardo was charged with Camarena’s murder, racketeering, and drug smuggling. Though initially protected by political influence, he was eventually convicted and sentenced to 40 years in prison, later increased to 77 years after a 2017 trial. Even while incarcerated, he maintained influence within the drug world, communicating via mobile phone. 

Critically, Félix Gallardo orchestrated the division of his organization before his ultimate loss of control. In 1989, he brought together the country’s top drug lords and designated territories to them, effectively creating the foundations for the modern cartels. This included assigning routes to his nephews, the Arellano Félix brothers (forming the Tijuana Cartel), the Carrillo Fuentes family (Juárez), Miguel Caro Quintero (Sonora), and Joaquín Guzmán Loera and Ismael Zambada García (Pacific coast, forming the Sinaloa Cartel). 

His story has been dramatized in several television series, including *Narcos: Mexico* and *El Cartel*, and he penned memoirs while in prison, detailing his life and experiences. His arrest is widely considered a turning point, exposing widespread corruption in Mexico and ultimately contributing to the escalating Mexican Drug War. He was granted house arrest in September 2022, citing declining health, a decision applauded by Mexican President Andrés Manuel López Obrador.

title: Shigeru Fukudome
text:
Shigeru Fukudome was a Japanese admiral who served as Chief of Staff of the Imperial Japanese Navy during World War II. Born in 1891, he graduated from the Imperial Japanese Naval Academy in 1912, placing eighth in his class of 144. His early naval career involved service aboard various ships including cruisers like the Soya, Izumo, and Kashima, and battleships such as Satsuma and Hizen. He progressed through the ranks, attending torpedo and naval artillery schools, and serving as a navigator on destroyers and cruisers. 

He continued to climb the ranks, becoming a lieutenant commander after graduating from the Naval War College in 1924 and a commander in 1929. Fukudome held numerous staff positions throughout the 1930s, eventually becoming captain of the battleship Nagato from 1938 to 1939. He was promoted to rear admiral in November 1939 and later to vice admiral in 1942. 

During the early stages of the Pacific War, Fukudome served with the Combined Fleet, participating in aerial torpedo exercises with Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto in 1940 as part of the planning for the attack on Pearl Harbor. He later became Chief of Staff under Admiral Mineichi Koga from May 1943 to March 1944. In a remarkable and historically significant event, Fukudome was captured by Filipino guerrillas led by Lieutenant Colonel James M. Cushing in March 1944 after his plane crashed while en route to deliver the “Z plan,” Japan’s defense strategy for the Marianas Islands. This made him the first Japanese flag officer to be captured by the enemy. He was released to prevent further civilian reprisals, but the battle plans fell into American hands.

Following Koga’s death on the same night as his capture, Fukudome was appointed commander-in-chief of the 1st Combined Base Air Force and 2nd Air Fleet, operating in the Kyūshū-Okinawa-Formosa area. He later commanded forces in the Philippines and, eventually, Singapore, where he oversaw the IJN 10th Area Fleet, consisting largely of training aircraft and a few operational ships. He was largely sidelined in Singapore due to American air and sea dominance.

After the war, Fukudome was interrogated by the U.S. Navy and tasked with assisting in the repatriation of Japanese nationals from Singapore. He was later arrested and tried for war crimes relating to the execution of American airmen while in command in Singapore, and was found guilty of negligence.  He was released in 1950 and contributed to the formation of the Japanese Self-Defense Force before his death in 1971. He is buried at Tama Cemetery in Tokyo, and was portrayed in the 1970 film *Tora! Tora! Tora!* by Koji Kawamura.

title: Takuma Asano
text:
Takuma Asano, born November 10, 1994, is a Japanese professional footballer currently playing as a forward for La Liga club Mallorca. His younger brother, Yuya Asano, is also a professional footballer with Nagoya Grampus in the J1 League. Asano began his career with Sanfrecce Hiroshima in January 2013, winning the J1 League title in his debut season with a single appearance. He further contributed to the team’s success by winning the Japanese Super Cup in 2014 and a second J1 League title in 2015, during which he scored nine goals in 34 appearances, earning him the J1 League Rookie of the Year award.

In July 2016, Asano signed with Arsenal, but was unable to secure a work permit to play in the Premier League. He was subsequently loaned to VfB Stuttgart until the end of the season, with an option to extend. He played a key role in Stuttgart’s promotion to the Bundesliga, scoring a brace against Karlsruher SC and helping them win the 2. Bundesliga. The loan was extended for another season, before he moved to Hannover 96 on a season-long loan in May 2018.

Asano then transitioned to Serbian club Partizan in August 2019, signing a three-year contract and becoming the first Japanese player in the club’s history. He scored on his debut in the Europa League qualifying rounds and contributed to Partizan’s group stage qualification, playing in all their European matches and scoring against AZ Alkmaar and Astana. While Partizan finished second in the Serbian SuperLiga, and reached the Serbian Cup final, they were unsuccessful in winning either competition. After a period where Partizan didn’t qualify for the Europa League group stage, Asano scored 18 league goals in the 2020/21 season before rescinding his contract in May 2021.

He then joined VfL Bochum in June 2021, making his Bundesliga debut in August. He became a consistent performer for Bochum, contributing crucial goals to help the team avoid relegation, including a brace against Hoffenheim and a goal and assist against Bayer Leverkusen in the final match of the 2022-23 season. He continued with Bochum into the 2023-24 season, scoring multiple goals in draws against Augsburg and Darmstadt 98, and even scoring against Bayern Munich before departing at the end of the season. In July 2024, Asano signed a two-year contract with Spanish side Mallorca, making his debut in August against Real Madrid.

On the international stage, Asano won a gold medal with the Japan U-23 team at the 2016 AFC U-23 Championship, scoring twice in the final. He also represented Japan at the 2016 Summer Olympics. He made his senior debut for Japan in 2015 and scored his first goal in 2016. He was initially overlooked for the 2018 World Cup squad due to a lack of playing time, but famously scored the winning goal against Germany in the 2022 World Cup. Asano has been recognized for his performances, earning the J.League Rookie of the Year award in 2015 and a spot in the Japan Pro-Footballers Association Best XI in 2022. He has won the J1 League twice with Sanfrecce Hiroshima, the 2. Bundesliga with VfB Stuttgart and the AFC U-23 Championship with Japan U23.

title: Ziaur Rahman
text:
Ziaur Rahman was born in 1936 in Bogra, East Bengal, to a Bengali Muslim family. His father was a chemist, and he received his early education in Calcutta and later Karachi after the partition of India in 1947. He joined the Pakistan Military Academy, graduating in 1955 and eventually serving as a company commander in the 1965 Indo-Pakistani War, earning the Hilal-e-Jurrat for his bravery. He served in East Pakistan, becoming increasingly aware of the disparities and Bengali grievances within Pakistan.

During the 1971 Liberation War, Ziaur Rahman played a pivotal role, famously broadcasting the declaration of independence from Chittagong on March 27th, earning him the title “Announcer of the Liberation”. He commanded sectors within the Bangladesh Forces, ultimately leading ‘Z Force’, a conventional brigade. After independence, he rose through the ranks of the Bangladesh Army, becoming Chief of Army Staff in 1975. Following the assassination of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman in August 1975, a period of political instability ensued, marked by coups and counter-coups. Ziaur Rahman was briefly removed from his position but regained power through the November 1975 Sipahi–Janata Revolution led by Abu Taher, becoming the de facto head of government under Justice Sayem. He consolidated his power, suppressing dissent and executing those involved in previous coups. He officially became President in 1977, retiring from the army as a Lieutenant General in 1978.

As President, Ziaur Rahman founded the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) in 1978, ushering in a return to multi-party politics and civil liberties, including freedom of the press and speech. He focused on economic development, initiating programs to boost irrigation and food production. He also pursued improved relations with Western countries and China, shifting away from the close alignment with India favored by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. He worked to establish regional cooperation, laying the groundwork for the creation of SAARC. However, his rule was marked by numerous coup attempts, leading to the establishment of military tribunals and the execution of at least 200 soldiers and air force personnel, giving him a reputation for strictness.

Ziaur Rahman was assassinated in 1981 in Chittagong during an attempted coup. His death sparked a divided legacy in Bangladeshi politics. He is credited with restoring order after the turbulent years following independence and establishing a democratic framework by abolishing the one-party BAKSAL system. However, he is also criticized for suppressing opposition. His economic reforms are seen as contributing to the rebuilding of the nation's economy and his adoption of certain Islamic policies garnered popular support. The BNP, founded by him, remains a significant political force in Bangladesh, with his widow, Khaleda Zia, later becoming a three-time Prime Minister.

title: Rory Burns
text:
Rory Burns, born in 1990 in Epsom, Surrey, is an English cricketer who currently captains Surrey in first-class and List A cricket, while also having represented England in Test matches. A left-handed opening batsman, he began his domestic career with Surrey, making his first-class debut in 2011 after playing Second XI cricket for both Surrey and Hampshire. He initially filled various roles, including wicket-keeping, before establishing himself as a consistent opening batsman, reaching 1000 runs in a season for the first time in 2014. 

A significant incident in his domestic career occurred in 2015 during a T20 Blast game where he collided with teammate Moisés Henriques, both sustaining injuries that led to the match being abandoned. Burns’s leadership qualities were recognized when he was appointed Surrey captain in 2018, leading the team to County Championship titles in 2018, 2022, 2023 and 2024. He consistently performed well with the bat, scoring over 1000 runs in five consecutive seasons up to 2018, and being the leading run-scorer in Division One that year with 1359 runs. His availability for Surrey was sometimes limited due to his international commitments.

Burns earned his England Test debut in 2018, stepping in to replace Alastair Cook for the tour of Sri Lanka. He continued to feature in the Test side, touring the West Indies and eventually securing his place as an opener. A breakthrough moment came during the 2019 Ashes series, where he scored his maiden Test century at Edgbaston, contributing significantly to England’s campaign and becoming the third-highest run scorer in the series. 

His form continued into the 2019-20 winter with a second Test century against New Zealand, but an ankle injury sustained while playing football ruled him out of the remainder of the South Africa series. He returned for series against the West Indies and Pakistan in 2020, with mixed results, and was later dropped after a disappointing showing in India in 2021. However, he regained his place and was named England’s player of the series against New Zealand in 2021, showcasing strong form. The following series against India proved less successful, and he endured a particularly difficult start to the 2021-22 Ashes, becoming the first batsman since 1936 to be dismissed with the first ball of an Ashes series. He was subsequently dropped from the Test team after the series.

Outside of cricket, Burns is close friends with fellow cricketer Jason Roy, with whom he attended school and who served as his best man at his wedding, and vice versa. He missed the 2021 tour of Sri Lanka due to the birth of his daughter.

title: Christian Almeida
text:
Christian Almeida, born on December 25, 1989, is a Uruguayan professional footballer who currently plays as a left-back for River Plate. He began his senior career with Liverpool in Uruguay, playing for the club for six years. His first appearance for Liverpool came on August 13, 2011, in a match against Racing Club (M), and he went on to make four appearances during the 2011–12 Uruguayan Primera División season. 

Almeida remained with Liverpool for several years, accumulating a total of fifty-four appearances before finally scoring his first goal for the club in March 2015. This goal came in a 5–2 victory over Cerrito, but it was during a period where Liverpool was competing in the Uruguayan Segunda División, having been relegated from the Primera División in the 2013–14 season. Despite this relegation, Liverpool achieved success in the following season, winning the Segunda División championship in 2014–15 and securing immediate promotion back to the Primera División. Almeida also experienced continental competition with Liverpool, making his debut in the Copa Sudamericana in 2017 against Fluminense.

In January 2018, Almeida moved to Argentina to join Defensa y Justicia, a team in the Argentine Primera División. During his time there, he played in sixteen matches and scored two goals – one against Racing Club (A) and another against Mitre in a cup game. He left Defensa y Justicia in January 2019, signing with Belgrano. However, his time at Belgrano was marked by the team’s relegation to Primera B Nacional, and he departed after twelve months, in January 2020, to join Godoy Cruz.

Almeida then experienced a return to his former club, Liverpool, in October 2020, though this stint was brief, ending at the close of the year. He subsequently signed with Nacional on April 9, 2021. 

Throughout his career with Liverpool, Almeida achieved success, notably contributing to their championship win in the Segunda División during the 2014–15 season, earning the club promotion. As of July 6, 2020, detailed career statistics are available, though the article does not specify these numbers.

title: Andry Rajoelina
text:
Andry Rajoelina, born in 1974 in Antsirabe, Madagascar, is a politician and businessman who has twice served as President of Madagascar, first in a transitional role from 2009 to 2014 and again since 2019. Before entering politics, Rajoelina developed a career in the private sector, founding a printing and advertising company, Injet, in 1999 and later acquiring the Viva radio and television networks in 2007. He entered politics by forming the political association Tanora malaGasy Vonona (TGV) and was elected Mayor of Antananarivo in 2007, capitalizing on a desire for younger leaders.

His mayoral term was marked by conflict with then-President Marc Ravalomanana, stemming from issues like advertising regulations and escalating with controversies surrounding large-scale land leases and the purchase of a presidential jet. Rajoelina led an opposition movement, and in 2009, following a series of protests and a military intervention after violence resulting in multiple deaths, he was installed as President of the High Transitional Authority (HTA) by the military, a move widely condemned internationally as a coup d'état. As President of the HTA, he dissolved the Senate and National Assembly and implemented governance through decrees and new structures.

During his transitional leadership, Rajoelina faced international isolation, including frozen aid and sanctions. He oversaw a constitutional referendum in 2010, which established the Fourth Republic and altered presidential eligibility requirements. Following elections in 2013 – in which neither he nor Ravalomanana were permitted to run – he stepped down in 2014. He subsequently won the 2018 presidential election and was inaugurated in January 2019. 

His more recent presidency has included navigating the COVID-19 pandemic, during which he promoted unproven treatments, and responding to a food security crisis and Cyclone Batsirai. He was re-elected in the 2023 presidential election. Throughout his career, Rajoelina has faced accusations of authoritarian tendencies, including dissolving legislative bodies and pursuing legal action against political opponents. His family background includes a father who served in the French army, and he married Mialy Razakandisa in 2000, with whom he has three children. His rise to power represents a trend toward younger leadership in Madagascar, though it has been consistently accompanied by political turmoil and international scrutiny.

title: William G. Angel
text:
William Gardner Angel was born in Rhode Island in 1790 and spent much of his life in New York, becoming a lawyer, politician, and judge. His family moved to a farm in Richfield, New York, in 1792, where he received a basic education while helping with farm work, and later attended Dr. Buckingham’s Grammar School. He briefly pursued the study of medicine before turning to law.

Angel began his legal career in an unconventional way. He impressed a lawyer, William Dowse, while serving as a witness in a trial and was subsequently hired as a handyman. During this time, he read law and worked as a clerk in Dowse’s office. Following Dowse’s death, Angel continued his legal studies with Farrand Stranahan, and eventually entered into a partnership with Luther Elderkin in 1817. This partnership was short-lived, however, as Elderkin absconded with client funds, leaving Angel responsible for reimbursing them. He then established his own practice in Burlington, New York, where he practiced law until 1833. Prior to his congressional service, he served as the Surrogate of Otsego County from 1821 to 1824.

Angel served three terms in the U.S. House of Representatives, representing New York’s 13th congressional district from 1825 to 1827 and again from 1829 to 1833 as a Jacksonian Democrat. After leaving Congress, he relocated to Hammondsport and re-entered the practice of law, first in partnership with Morris Brown. He later mentored and partnered with Martin Grover, and then with his son, Wilkes Angel, practicing in Angelica, New York, from 1835 to 1843 and 1843 to 1847 respectively. He was also a delegate to the New York State Constitutional Convention in 1846. 

In 1847, Angel was appointed as the First Judge and Surrogate of the Allegany County Court, a position he held until 1851. He was married twice, first to Emily P. English in 1812 with whom he had several children including William P. and Wilkes Angel, and later to Clarissa English, with whom he had ten children, including James R. Angel and Texas Angel, who himself became a lawyer and political figure in Idaho. William G. Angel died in Angelica, New York, in August of 1858 and is buried in the Until the Day Dawn Cemetery.

title: Chacho Gaytán
text:
Gonzalo “Chacho” Gaytán is a multifaceted Mexican musician with a career spanning composition, production, arrangement, direction, and conducting. He is perhaps most widely recognized as the co-founder and keyboardist of the popular Mexican pop band Sentidos Opuestos, a group he formed alongside Alessandra Rosaldo. Beyond his work with the band, Gaytán enjoys a significant family connection to the entertainment industry, being the brother of actress and singer Bibi Gaytán and brother-in-law to actor and singer Eduardo Capetillo.

Gaytán’s talents extend beyond performance and band leadership into the realm of music production. He received a Latin Grammy Award nomination in 2000, recognized in the category of Best Latin Children's Album for his work on *Ellas Cantan a Cri-Cri*. His skills as a musical director have been showcased in large-scale productions, most notably his direction of *West Side Story*. He is also highly regarded for his orchestral work within Mexico, encompassing musical arrangement, orchestration, and conducting. 

He has demonstrated his conducting abilities by presenting work with the National Philharmonic Orchestra at the prestigious Palace of Fine Arts in Mexico City. This showcases his capacity to work with and elevate established and respected musical institutions. Further demonstrating his versatility, Gaytán collaborated with Fernando de la Mora in a concert setting, accompanied by the Campeche Philharmonic Orchestra.

In addition to his work with established productions and artists, Gaytán founded the Mexican jazz band, Manzana Jazz Band, indicating a personal passion for and involvement in the jazz genre. Currently, he holds the position of director at Azteca Music, a television network in Mexico, signifying a move into music administration and broadcasting. 

Furthermore, Gaytán is a co-founder of MYST, where he continues to contribute as both musical producer and director. His solo discography includes the album *Un día después*, released in 2007, showcasing his individual artistic output. Throughout his career, Chacho Gaytán has established himself as a prominent figure in Mexican music, displaying a broad range of skills and a dedication to various musical forms.

title: Jose Canseco
text:
José Canseco was a Cuban-American professional baseball player who enjoyed a 17-season Major League Baseball (MLB) career, primarily known for his powerful hitting. Born in Havana, Cuba in 1964, he and his twin brother Ozzie were brought to Miami as young children after their family left Cuba following Fidel Castro’s rise to power. Canseco excelled in high school baseball, though he didn’t make the varsity team until his senior year. He was drafted by the Oakland Athletics in 1982 and spent several years in the minor leagues before debuting with the A’s in 1985.

Canseco quickly became a star with the Athletics, winning the American League Rookie of the Year award in 1986. He was a six-time All-Star and won the Most Valuable Player award in 1988, a year he achieved the unprecedented feat of hitting 40 home runs and stealing 40 bases – the first player in MLB history to do so. He secured World Series championships with the Athletics in 1989 and the New York Yankees in 2000. Alongside teammate Mark McGwire, he formed the formidable “Bash Brothers” duo, known for their combined power hitting. 

Throughout his career, Canseco played for seven different teams, accumulating impressive statistics. He ranks fourth in Athletics history with 254 home runs and is one of only 14 players in MLB history to achieve 400 home runs and 200 stolen bases. Despite battling injuries, he averaged a remarkable 40 home runs, 120 RBIs, and 102 runs scored per 162 games over his 17 seasons. He finished his career with 462 home runs, the 12th-highest total in the American League and the second most for a player with fewer than 2,000 games played. He also won four Silver Slugger Awards.

Later in life, Canseco admitted to using performance-enhancing drugs during his career and detailed widespread steroid use in MLB in his controversial 2005 book, *Juiced*. After retiring from baseball, he briefly pursued careers in boxing and mixed martial arts. His early life was marked by his family’s emigration from Cuba, and he quickly established himself as a dominant force in baseball, known for his exceptional power and speed.

title: Maxime Masson
text:
Maxime Masson, born on October 15, 1867, in Saint-Justin, Quebec, was a Roman Catholic priest who profoundly shaped the religious landscape of Sainte-Thècle, a town in the Mauricie region of Quebec. He served as the parish priest of Sainte-Thècle for an impressive 52 years, beginning on February 6, 1903, and leaving a lasting legacy through his extensive building projects and pastoral work. 

Before arriving in Sainte-Thècle, Masson completed his studies in classics at Séminaire Saint-Joseph de Trois-Rivières and theology at the Grand Seminary Trois-Rivières, culminating in his ordination on July 8, 1894, by Bishop L.F. Lafleche. He initially served as a vicar in several parishes – Saint-Justin (1894–1899), Saint-Léon-le-Grand (1902), and Saint-Timothée of Hérouxville (1902–1903) – before taking on the role of pastor in Sainte-Thècle.

As pastor, Masson spearheaded the construction of numerous important buildings. He was the primary coordinator for the building of the Sainte-Thècle church between 1903 and 1905, and also oversaw the construction of the rectory and other buildings belonging to the Fabrique de Sainte-Thècle. He was also key to the establishment of the local monastery in 1912, built for the Daughters of Jesus, and the first college run by the Brothers of St. Gabriel in 1939.

Beyond large-scale construction, Masson possessed significant artistic and crafting skills. He designed and built the calvary in the cemetery in 1935, a cement lion placed outside the church in 1939, and painted the ceiling of the sacristy. He also personally carved the Stations of the Cross from stone imported from France and created decorative elements like cement flowerpots, balls, steps, and a fountain for the church and rectory grounds. He crafted a carved wood clock, mirroring the church’s tower design, and the high altar itself. 

During his time as pastor, Masson administered 2497 baptisms, recorded between February 7, 1903, and April 30, 1955. He was also a relatively early adopter of automobile technology, owning a Ford Model T in 1911, one of the first cars in Sainte-Thècle. A significant challenge during his tenure was the collapse of the church’s two towers during the hurricane of August 3, 1938. 

Masson also contributed to the community as the first president of the Sainte-Thècle School board, serving from July 19, 1915, to April 14, 1947. He concluded his service in Sainte-Thècle on July 1, 1955, and passed away on October 2, 1960, being buried in the local cemetery. His contribution to the town was recognized through the naming of School Masson and Masson Street in his honor. He was also a chaplain for Catholic Action and other pious associations.

title: David Oyite-Ojok
text:
David Oyite Ojok was a Ugandan military officer born in Lira District in 1940, who played a pivotal role in Ugandan history, particularly during and after the regime of Idi Amin. He joined the Uganda Army in 1963, progressing through the ranks and becoming a key figure within the military during Milton Obote’s first presidency. He was considered a trusted advisor to Obote, serving as Assistant Military Secretary and undergoing training in Great Britain.

When Idi Amin seized power in 1971, Oyite Ojok was forced into exile in Tanzania, where he joined Obote’s guerrilla forces. He gained a reputation for daring raids into Uganda, even becoming the subject of a bounty placed on his head by Amin. He commanded Obote’s naval forces on Lake Victoria, supporting the rebel effort through smuggling operations. During the Uganda–Tanzania War, beginning in 1978, Oyite Ojok emerged as a crucial leader in the coalition that overthrew Amin, initially commanding Obote’s private army, Kikosi Maalum, and later becoming head of a battalion within the Uganda National Liberation Army (UNLA). His tactical abilities were widely recognized, with some crediting him with key victories like those at Lukaya and the fall of Kampala.

Following Amin’s removal, Oyite Ojok became a member of the powerful Military Commission that governed Uganda. He amassed considerable wealth, particularly through coffee exports, and remained a staunch supporter of Obote’s return to power. He actively worked to consolidate power for Obote and the Uganda Peoples Congress, ensuring the UNLA was dominated by Northerners, particularly from his own Lango ethnic group. This created tensions with Southern groups, especially the Buganda, who opposed Obote’s return. He was instrumental in the removal of President Yusuf Lule and, later, Godfrey Binaisa, consolidating the Military Commission's control. 

Oyite Ojok’s influence peaked in 1980 when he helped pave the way for Obote’s second presidency through a contested election. As Army Chief of Staff, he led the brutal suppression of guerrilla movements led by Yoweri Museveni and Andrew Kayiira, employing harsh tactics that resulted in significant civilian casualties, particularly in the Luwero Triangle, and widespread fear in Kampala through practices like “Panda Gari”. 

Despite initial successes against the guerrillas, tensions arose within the army, particularly between the Lango and Acholi ethnic groups, and between Oyite Ojok and Obote himself over corruption.  Oyite Ojok died in a helicopter crash in December 1983. While the NRA claimed responsibility, the government attributed the crash to technical failure, sparking conspiracy theories about Obote’s involvement. His death and the subsequent appointment of a Lango officer over a more senior Acholi officer contributed to the conditions that led to Obote's overthrow in 1985. Despite his controversial role, Oyite Ojok has since been recognized as a national hero by the government of Yoweri Museveni.

title: Cleopatra
text:
Cleopatra VII, the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt, reigned from 51 to 30 BC. Descended from Ptolemy I Soter, a companion of Alexander the Great, she was uniquely among her dynasty in learning the Egyptian language alongside Koine Greek and several others, including Latin, Hebrew, and Arabic. Her reign marked the end of the Hellenistic period, initiated by Alexander, as Egypt subsequently became a Roman province.

Born in Alexandria around 70/69 BC, Cleopatra inherited the throne alongside her brother Ptolemy XIII following their father Ptolemy XII Auletes’ death in 51 BC. A power struggle quickly erupted between them, leading to civil war. This conflict was dramatically impacted by the Roman civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey. Pompey, having been defeated by Caesar at Pharsalus in 48 BC, fled to Egypt seeking refuge, but was betrayed and murdered by Ptolemy XIII’s forces. 

Caesar arrived in Alexandria and attempted to reconcile Cleopatra and Ptolemy XIII, but she was besieged in the palace by her brother’s troops.  After reinforcements arrived, Ptolemy XIII was defeated and killed in battle. Caesar then installed Cleopatra and her younger brother Ptolemy XIV as joint rulers, beginning a personal affair with Cleopatra that resulted in a son, Caesarion. Cleopatra visited Rome in 46 and 44 BC, residing in Caesar’s villa. Following Caesar’s assassination and the subsequent death of Ptolemy XIV – potentially orchestrated by Cleopatra – she named Caesarion as her co-ruler, Ptolemy XV.

During the ensuing power struggles in Rome, Cleopatra aligned herself with the Second Triumvirate consisting of Octavian, Mark Antony, and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus. A romantic relationship with Antony blossomed after their meeting in Tarsos in 41 BC, producing three children. Antony increasingly depended on Cleopatra for financial and military support in his campaigns, and he granted territories under his control to Cleopatra and their children in the Donations of Alexandria. 

Octavian used this as propaganda, accusing Antony of treason and declaring war on Cleopatra in 32 BC.  The conflict culminated in the Battle of Actium in 31 BC, where Octavian’s forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra’s fleet.  Octavian invaded Egypt in 30 BC, leading to Antony’s suicide.  Shortly after, Cleopatra reportedly took her own life, likely through poisoning, to avoid being paraded as a prisoner in Octavian’s Roman triumph.

Cleopatra’s legacy endures through art and literature, though early Roman accounts often portrayed her negatively.  She has been a subject of artistic representation throughout history, from Roman busts and coins to Renaissance paintings and modern films, becoming a prominent symbol of Egyptomania and enduring fascination. Her name, meaning “glory of her father,” was a common one in the Ptolemaic dynasty and Greek mythology.

title: Vance Joy
text:
Vance Joy, born James Gabriel Keogh on December 1st, 1987, is an Australian singer-songwriter and musician who rose to prominence with his 2013 hit single “Riptide.” He initially signed a five-album deal with Atlantic Records that same year and quickly followed it with his debut EP, *God Loves You When You're Dancing*. His musical journey began after a period playing Australian rules football; he played as a key defender for the Coburg Football Club in 2008 and 2009, but ultimately felt his potential in the sport was limited and pursued music instead.

Joy’s breakthrough came with “Riptide,” which topped the 2013 Triple J Hottest 100 and achieved significant commercial success both in Australia and the United States, becoming the longest-charting song in ARIA Charts history and earning 5x platinum certification in the US. The song’s inspiration stemmed from childhood family holidays and a motel called “Riptide.” His debut studio album, *Dream Your Life Away*, released in September 2014, earned him the ARIA Award for Best Male Artist in 2015, along with six further nominations. This album included singles like “Mess Is Mine,” “First Time,” “Georgia,” and “Fire and the Flood.”

Beyond his own tours, Joy supported Taylor Swift on her 1989 World Tour across North America, the UK, and Australia, and was featured on NBC’s *Today* show. He also performed a duet of “Riptide” with Quentin Alexander on *American Idol*. In 2018, he released his second studio album, *Nation of Two*, which debuted at number one in Australia and won the ARIA Award for Best Adult Contemporary Album. Singles from this album included “Lay It on Me,” “Like Gold,” “We’re Going Home,” and “Saturday Sun.” He also released a live album, *Live at Red Rocks Amphitheatre*, capturing a performance from his world tour.

His third studio album, *In Our Own Sweet Time*, was released in June 2022. Prior to this, he collaborated with Benny Blanco and Marshmello on the single “You” in 2021 and released “Missing Piece,” which achieved platinum status in Australia and won an ARIA Award for Best Video. More recently, in 2023, he collaborated with Noah Cyrus on the single "Everybody Needs Someone."

Joy’s personal life includes his marriage to Selen Us, whom he engaged to in November 2022 and married in June 2023. They welcomed their daughter, Gigi, in early 2024. He revealed that his song "Missing Piece" was inspired by his wife. Throughout his career, he has consistently toured, both headlining his own shows and as an opening act for major artists like Taylor Swift and P!nk.

title: Thierry Henry
text:
Thierry Henry, born in 1977, is a French football icon considered one of the greatest players of all time, and particularly celebrated as the best in Premier League history. Renowned for his finishing, dribbling, speed, and ability to create chances, he twice came close to winning the Ballon d'Or and FIFA World Player of the Year awards in 2003 and 2004. He achieved numerous individual accolades, including a record three FWA Footballer of the Year awards and being named to the PFA Team of the Year six consecutive times. He was also recognized by Pelé in the FIFA 100 list of the world’s greatest living players in 2004.

Henry began his professional career with Monaco in 1994 before a relatively short and unfulfilling stint with Juventus, where limited playing time and disagreements with management prompted a move to Arsenal in 1999. Under the guidance of Arsène Wenger, he flourished, becoming Arsenal’s all-time leading scorer with 228 goals. He led the team to three FA Cups and two Premier League titles, famously being a key member of the ‘Invincibles’ team that went undefeated throughout the 2003-04 Premier League season. He served as club captain in his final two seasons, reaching the 2006 Champions League final before transferring to Barcelona in 2007. At Barcelona, he was instrumental in a historic treble win in the 2008-09 season, securing La Liga, Copa del Rey, and Champions League titles. He later played for the New York Red Bulls in Major League Soccer, with a loan spell back at Arsenal in 2012 before retiring in 2014.

Henry also enjoyed significant success with the French national team, winning the 1998 FIFA World Cup, UEFA Euro 2000, and the 2003 FIFA Confederations Cup. He was a five-time French Player of the Year and held the record for most international goals for France from 2007 until 2022. He retired from international football after the 2010 FIFA World Cup, having made 123 appearances and scored 51 goals.

Following his retirement as a player, Henry transitioned into coaching. He began by coaching Arsenal’s youth teams while also working as a pundit. He then served as an assistant coach for Belgium before taking on the head coach role at Monaco in 2018, followed by a managerial position at Montréal Impact. He subsequently returned to Belgium as an assistant coach and, more recently, managed the France national under-21 and Olympic teams, leading them to a silver medal at the 2024 Summer Games.

Born and raised in Les Ulis, a suburb of Paris, Henry’s talent was evident early on, initially encouraged by his father despite his initial lack of enthusiasm for the sport. He progressed through youth academies, eventually joining Monaco after impressing a scout with a six-goal performance in a single match. While at Monaco, he was initially deployed as a winger before being developed into a prolific striker, a position where he would ultimately achieve global recognition. His early career was marked by a desire to prove himself and reach the highest levels of the game.

title: Deyverson
text:
Deyverson Brum Silva, known simply as Deyverson, is a Brazilian professional footballer currently playing as a forward for Fortaleza, having joined the club in March 2025. Born in Rio de Janeiro in 1991, he began his career with Grêmio Mangaratibense in 2011, where he quickly established himself as a prolific scorer, netting 18 goals in 31 appearances over two seasons and becoming the team’s top scorer in the Carioca Série C twice.

In 2012, Deyverson moved to Benfica in Portugal, initially joining the reserve side. He made a quick impact, scoring eight league goals in his first season, despite starting only 12 matches. He then spent a year with Belenenses, where he scored a notable goal against Alvalade, before a six-month loan spell with 1. FC Köln in Germany in 2015, where he scored against Eintracht Frankfurt. 

Deyverson then moved to Spain, signing a four-year deal with Levante in 2015. He scored his first goal in La Liga against Eibar and later contributed a brace against Sporting de Gijón. Following Levante’s relegation, he joined Deportivo Alavés on loan in 2016, famously scoring the winning goal against Barcelona at Camp Nou.

He returned to Brazil in 2017, joining Palmeiras on a five-year contract. During his time with Palmeiras, he was a key contributor to their success, scoring seven goals in his first season and nine goals in 2018, helping them win the Campeonato Brasileiro Série A.  He later had loan spells back in Spain with Getafe and Alavés, though he didn’t find consistent success.

A highlight of his career came in 2021 when, playing for Palmeiras, he scored the winning goal in the Copa Libertadores Final in extra time against Flamengo, earning him the Man of the Match award. He also played a part in Palmeiras winning the Recopa Sudamericana in 2022 and the Campeonato Paulista in the same year.

After leaving Palmeiras, Deyverson joined Cuiabá in 2022, where he scored six goals and had a run of three goals in three consecutive matches. He then moved to Atlético Mineiro in 2024, where he quickly made an impact, earning Man of the Match awards for performances in the Copa Libertadores against Fluminense and River Plate, scoring multiple goals in both ties. He also helped Atlético Mineiro win the Campeonato Mineiro in 2025.



Deyverson’s honours include the Campeonato Brasileiro Série A, Copa Libertadores, Recopa Sudamericana, Campeonato Paulista with Palmeiras, and the Campeonato Mato-Grossense with Cuiabá, and Campeonato Mineiro with Atlético Mineiro.

title: Braulio Lara
text:
Braulio Armando Lara Peguero was a Dominican professional baseball pitcher born on December 20, 1988, and tragically died in a car accident in his home country on April 20, 2019. His professional career began in 2008 when he signed as an international free agent with the Tampa Bay Rays, spending his initial two seasons in the Dominican Summer League where he compiled a 7-5 record and a 3.73 ERA. After a brief release and re-signing, he progressed through the Rays’ minor league system, pitching for the Princeton Rays, Bowling Green Hot Rods, and Charlotte Stone Crabs.

In 2012, Lara was selected by the Miami Marlins in the Rule 5 draft, but was quickly returned to the Rays organization. He continued to work his way up, reaching Double-A with the Montgomery Biscuits and making a single appearance for the Triple-A Durham Bulls in 2013. He spent 2014 splitting time between Durham and Montgomery, accumulating 57 strikeouts but with a 5.77 ERA.

Lara then signed a minor league contract with the San Francisco Giants in 2014, playing for both the Double-A Richmond Flying Squirrels and Triple-A Sacramento River Cats in 2015. He saw a brief improvement in his performance with Sacramento in 2016, posting a 3.90 ERA, before signing with the SK Wyverns of the Korean Baseball Organization (KBO) League in June of that year. His time in Korea was short-lived, as he struggled with a 6.70 ERA in 17 games.

Returning to the United States, Lara signed with the Washington Nationals in 2016 and spent the 2017 season with their Double-A affiliate, the Harrisburg Senators. Becoming a free agent after the season, he then ventured to the Mexican Baseball League, signing with the Sultanes de Monterrey in 2018. A trade sent him to the Generales de Durango shortly after, but his time there was brief, being released after only two games and a short 1+1⁄3 innings pitched. Throughout his career, Lara pitched at various levels, demonstrating a consistent ability to strike batters out, but often struggled with his earned run average.

title: Cheyenne Brando
text:
Tarita Cheyenne Brando was born in 1970, the daughter of actor Marlon Brando and his third wife, Tarita Teriipaia, whom he met while filming *Mutiny on the Bounty*. She was primarily raised by her mother on the island of Tahiti following her parents’ divorce in 1972. Marlon Brando largely kept Cheyenne and her brother, Tehotu, from visiting the United States, believing the fast-paced American lifestyle would be detrimental to them as Tahitians. 

Initially, Cheyenne admired her father, but this affection soured as she grew older, with her later expressing resentment for his perceived neglect during her childhood. She felt he rarely visited and showed little interest in her well-being. She abandoned her formal education and began experimenting with drugs, including LSD, PCP, marijuana, and tranquilizers, while simultaneously starting a modeling career. This career was abruptly cut short in 1989 when she was seriously injured in a car accident after being denied a visit with her father during a film shoot. The crash necessitated extensive surgery.

In 1987, Cheyenne began a relationship with Dag Drollet, whose father was a politician in French Polynesia. They became pregnant in 1989 and, at Marlon Brando’s urging, moved into his Los Angeles home to prepare for the birth of their child. Tragedy struck in May 1990 when Drollet was shot and killed by Cheyenne’s half-brother, Christian Brando. Christian claimed the shooting was accidental, stating he was acting in defense of Cheyenne after she told him Drollet was abusive. 

Cheyenne refused to testify at Christian’s trial, fleeing to Tahiti and later being declared “mentally disabled” by a French judge, rendering her unable to provide testimony. Without her account, prosecutors offered Christian a plea bargain, and he ultimately pleaded guilty to voluntary manslaughter, serving five years in prison. He later expressed doubt about Cheyenne’s claims of abuse, questioning her mental state.

Following these events, Cheyenne’s mental health sharply declined. She battled drug addiction and repeatedly sought treatment in rehabilitation facilities and psychiatric hospitals. She publicly leveled serious accusations against her father, alleging both sexual abuse and his involvement in Drollet’s death, claims he denied. Eventually, she was diagnosed with schizophrenia, became increasingly isolated, and lost custody of her son, Tuki, to her mother. Tuki was raised in Tahiti and later pursued both medical school and a modeling career.

Cheyenne Brando died by suicide on April 16, 1995, at her mother’s home in Tahiti. Her funeral was held in Tahiti, and she was buried in the Drollet family crypt. Notably, neither Marlon Brando nor Christian Brando attended her funeral.

title: Phife Dawg
text:
Malik Izaak Taylor, professionally known as Phife Dawg, was a Trinidadian-American rapper best known as a member of the influential hip-hop group A Tribe Called Quest. Born on November 20, 1970, in Queens, New York City, to Trinidadian immigrant parents, he tragically passed away on March 22, 2016, at the age of 45 due to complications from diabetes. He earned the nicknames “Five-Foot Assassin” and “Five-Footer” due to his height of 5 feet 3 inches. Phife grew up in the St. Albans neighborhood of Queens, and experienced the early loss of his twin brother, Mikal, shortly after birth. He first met Q-Tip at age two, and the pair began rapping together at age nine after being inspired by the Sugarhill Gang.

Phife Dawg formed A Tribe Called Quest in 1985 with Q-Tip and Ali Shaheed Muhammad, later adding Jarobi White. The group became associated with De La Soul and Jungle Brothers as part of the Native Tongues collective. They initially signed with Jive Records in 1990, releasing their debut album, *People's Instinctive Travels and the Paths of Rhythm*. Phife’s lyrical contributions grew significantly with the critically acclaimed *The Low End Theory* in 1991, where he addressed social and political issues. The group continued to release successful albums throughout the 1990s – *Midnight Marauders*, *Beats, Rhymes and Life*, and *The Love Movement* – before disbanding due to internal conflicts and issues with their record label. Their story was documented in the 2011 film *Beats, Rhymes & Life: The Travels of A Tribe Called Quest*.

Beyond his work with A Tribe Called Quest, Phife collaborated with artists like Fu-Schnickens, Diamond D, and Chi-Ali. He released his debut solo album, *Ventilation: Da LP*, in 2000 and was working on a second, *MUTTYmorPHosis*, at the time of his death. Singles from this posthumous album, “Sole Men” and “Nutshell,” were released shortly after his passing. Remarkably, A Tribe Called Quest reunited in 2015, deciding to record a final album, *We Got It from Here... Thank You 4 Your Service*, which was released in November 2016, just months after Phife’s death. His second solo album, *Forever*, was released on the sixth anniversary of his death, March 22, 2022.

Phife was married to Deisha Head-Taylor and had two children. He was a dedicated fan of the New York Knicks and even appeared as a playable character in the *NBA 2K7* and *NBA 2K9* video games. He was diagnosed with diabetes in 1990, a condition he openly discussed and used as inspiration for his music, even calling himself a "funky diabetic." He received a kidney transplant from his wife in 2008, but it was unsuccessful, requiring another transplant. 

Phife Dawg’s legacy is one of challenging conventions in hip-hop with his self-deprecating style. He influenced artists like Kanye West and Jill Scott. In 2016, a section of Linden Boulevard in Queens was renamed “Malik ‘Phife Dawg’ Taylor Way” in his honor, and in 2024, he was posthumously inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of A Tribe Called Quest.

title: Giorgi Papunashvili
text:
Giorgi Papunashvili, known as Papu, is a Georgian professional footballer born on September 2, 1995, currently playing as a winger for Zira in the Azerbaijan Premier League, having signed a one-year contract with an option for another in August 2024. He has also represented the Georgian national team at both senior and youth levels.

Papunashvili began his club career at Dinamo Tbilisi, progressing through the reserve side before making his debut in the Erovnuli Liga in November 2013. He quickly became a key player for Dinamo, notably scoring 16 goals in all competitions during the 2014-15 season, including a hat-trick against Tskhinvali in October 2014. That season culminated in Dinamo winning the Georgian Cup, with Papunashvili contributing two goals in the final against Samtredia.  He was also part of the team that won the Umaglesi Liga and Georgian Super Cup in 2013-14, and the Georgian Cup again in 2014-15.

In the summer of 2015, he moved to Germany on a season-long loan to Werder Bremen, where he played for the reserve team in the 3. Liga. However, his time in Germany was hampered by injury, limiting him to 20 appearances and two goals. 

He then transferred to Spanish side Real Zaragoza in June 2017, signing a four-year deal and making his debut against Granada CF in August 2017.  After a period with Zaragoza, he joined Racing de Santander on loan in January 2020 for the remainder of the season. 

Following his loan spell, Papunashvili moved to Apollon Limassol FC in Cyprus in December 2020. He returned to Georgia in January 2022, joining Torpedo Kutaisi, but moved again six months later to Serbian club Radnički Niš. His time in Serbia was brief, as he signed with Samtredia in March 2023, followed by a move to Telavi four months later. After a single league appearance for Telavi, he joined Kapaz in Azerbaijan before ultimately signing with Zira.

Internationally, Papunashvili debuted for the Georgian national team in a friendly match against the United Arab Emirates in June 2014. He also represented the Georgia national under-17 team at the 2012 UEFA European Under-17 Championship, scoring a crucial late goal against England during the qualifying stage.

title: Kaoru Kuroki
text:
Kaoru Kuroki, born in 1965, was a Japanese performer who transitioned from adult videos to become a significant media personality known for her candid discussions about sex and society. Often compared to figures like Cicciolina and Dr. Ruth, Kuroki began her career after leaving art college and Yokohama National University, initially viewing adult video (AV) work as a form of artistic expression. She admired filmmakers like Nagisa Oshima and Ingmar Bergman, but found the AV world to be more primal than artistic, likening it to a simple craving satisfied by readily available content.

Kuroki debuted in the AV industry in 1986 with *SM Poi no suki*, working with director Toru Muranishi, who was known for a documentary style in his films. She continued collaborating with Muranishi after he founded Diamond Visual, and their videos typically featured Kuroki delivering spoken-word introductions on topics of sexual liberation, followed by nude or swimsuit modeling, and then explicit performances often involving S&M. Her work was noted for its stark contrast between vulnerability and assertiveness, and she believed it could be liberating for both men and women, forcing them to confront their own desires and expectations.

Kuroki achieved mainstream recognition in 1988 when she publicly stopped shaving her underarm hair as a protest against Japanese censorship of pubic hair depictions. This act gained media attention and led to appearances on talk shows and commercials, appealing to both male fans of her AV work and female viewers who appreciated her feminist perspectives. She even had a role in a television drama. Kuroki felt a social need for someone to openly discuss sex, and saw herself fulfilling that role. 

During her career, Kuroki formed a connection with Cicciolina in Italy, finding common ground but also experiencing differences in their views on S&M. She argued that S&M did not equate to submissiveness and, alongside Kimiko Matsuzaka, helped to establish the topic as a feminist issue in Japan. She collaborated with Matsuzaka on several projects, including instructional sex videos and a pink film.

Kuroki retired from public life in 1994, following allegations of physical violence from Muranishi. Later, she successfully sued a magazine for invasion of privacy after they published details of her personal life without consent, winning a substantial settlement in 2007. At the peak of her career, her videos sold exceptionally well, reaching 17,000 units each, and she is credited with changing the public perception of AV actresses, presenting them as individuals making informed choices rather than being forced into the industry. Her impact was so significant that she is described as "the first high-profile AV actress," and her life story was recently depicted in the Netflix series *The Naked Director*.

title: Chris John (boxer)
text:
Yohannes Christian “Chris” John, born in Banjarnegara, Indonesia in 1979, was a professional boxer who enjoyed a remarkably long and successful career from 1998 to 2013. He became the fourth Indonesian boxer to win a world title, and held the World Boxing Association (WBA) featherweight title from 2004 until his retirement, initially the standard version and then the “Super” version from 2009. His nearly decade-long reign is the second-longest in the division’s history, surpassed only by Johnny Kilbane. Throughout his championship run, John successfully defended his title a total of 16 times, second only to Eusebio Pedroza in featherweight history.

Boxing was ingrained in John’s life from a young age, as his father, Johan Tjahjadi (originally Tjia Foek Sem), was a former amateur boxer of Chinese descent. He began training his sons, Chris and Adrian, at the age of five, sharing stories of his own boxing experiences. Chris excelled, becoming an amateur champion in Banjarnegara before turning professional in 1997, initially fighting under the nickname “Thin Man” before adopting “The Dragon.”

Early in his professional career, John gained recognition after knocking out national featherweight champion Muhammad Afaridzi in a 12-round bout, despite being knocked down twice in the first round. He continued to rise through the ranks, eventually capturing the PABA Featherweight title and earning a shot at the WBA featherweight title against Oscar León in 2003. He won the title by split decision, becoming a world champion. 

John’s reign saw notable victories against fighters like Derrick Gainer, whom he defeated by unanimous decision after a first-round knockdown, and Juan Manuel Márquez, also by unanimous decision, a result Márquez disputed. He also had a technical draw against Jose Rojas due to an accidental head clash. He fought Hiroyuki Enoki, winning by unanimous decision in a sold-out arena in Tokyo, and faced Rocky Juarez twice, with the first fight ending in a controversial draw and the rematch resulting in a unanimous decision win for John. He also secured victories over Daud Yordan, Shoji Kimura, and Chonlatarn Piriyapinyo, defending his title multiple times across Indonesia, Japan, and Singapore. 

John's career ended with a controversial technical draw against Satoshi Hosono, where a headbutt caused severe bleeding, and ultimately a loss to Simpiwe Vetyeka in 2013, marking his first professional defeat. He retired on his stool after six rounds, relinquishing his WBA Super World featherweight title. Following his retirement, John transitioned to business and motivational speaking, also appearing in television commercials.

Throughout his boxing journey, John was trained by his father until 1997, then by Sutan Rambing until 2004, and finally by Craig Christian from 2005 until his retirement. His accomplishments were recognized with the WBA’s Fighter of the Decade award for the 2000s. Before focusing solely on boxing, John was also a successful wushu athlete, earning medals at the Southeast Asian Games and Indonesian national championships.

title: Roman Pavlyuchenko
text:
Roman Pavlyuchenko, born in 1981, is a former Russian footballer who now works as a forwards coach for Rodina-2 Moscow. He began his professional career at Dynamo Stavropol, progressing through youth systems before making his debut in 1999. After a stint at Rotor Volgograd, marked by an early red card for violent conduct, he joined Spartak Moscow in 2003, becoming a key player and the team’s top scorer for several seasons. It was at Spartak where he truly established himself, becoming the league’s top scorer in one season and helping the club qualify for the Champions League. He scored 69 goals in 141 appearances for Spartak, gaining a reputation for loyalty and earning the respect of the club's fans.

In 2008, Pavlyuchenko moved to Tottenham Hotspur in the English Premier League for £13.7 million. While he scored goals for Spurs, including a brace against Birmingham City that relegated them, his time was often marked by inconsistency and being behind other strikers in the pecking order. A notable incident occurred when he stormed down the tunnel after being substituted, drawing criticism from his manager. He did, however, prove a reliable goalscorer in domestic cup competitions and played a part in Tottenham’s Champions League qualification.

Pavlyuchenko also enjoyed a decade-long international career with Russia, earning 51 caps and scoring 21 goals. He debuted in 2003 and became a vital part of the national team, notably playing a key role in Euro 2008 where Russia reached the semi-finals. He scored crucial goals during the qualifying campaign, including both goals in a 2-1 victory over England, and continued to find the net during the tournament itself. He was named to the Team of the Tournament for his performances. He later scored a hat-trick against Armenia in Euro 2012 qualifying.

After leaving Tottenham, Pavlyuchenko returned to Russia with Lokomotiv Moscow and later played for Kuban Krasnodar, Ural Yekaterinburg and Ararat Moscow. He even spent time in the Russian Professional Football League and the Amateur Football League, demonstrating a continued passion for the game. He briefly returned to Ararat and then Znamya Noginsk, where he scored a career-high four goals in a single match. His career ended with a ban for misconduct after an on-field altercation, leading to his retirement. Throughout his career, Pavlyuchenko was known for his goalscoring ability and dedication to the sport.

title: Charley Boorman
text:
Charley Boorman, born in 1966, is a British television presenter, travel writer, and actor with a lifelong passion for motorbikes. He is perhaps best known for his four long-distance motorcycle journeys undertaken with his friend Ewan McGregor, documented in the popular series *Long Way Round* (2004), *Long Way Down* (2007), *Long Way Up* (2020) and the upcoming *Long Way Home* (2025). 

Boorman’s early life was split between Wimbledon, London and County Wicklow, Ireland. He comes from a film industry background; his mother is costume designer Christel Kruse and his father is film director Sir John Boorman. Actor Lee Marvin served as his godfather. He began his acting career as a child, appearing in his father’s films, including *Deliverance* in 1972 and *Excalibur* in 1981, alongside his sister Katrine Boorman. He continued acting into adulthood, with roles in *The Emerald Forest* (1985), *Hope and Glory* (1987), *The Serpent's Kiss* (1997) and *The Bunker* (2001).

Beyond acting, Boorman developed a successful presenting career. Following *Long Way Round*, he participated in the 2006 Dakar Rally, an experience documented in *Race to Dakar*, though he was forced to retire due to injury. He followed this with *Long Way Down*, travelling from Scotland to South Africa. Subsequent travel series included *By Any Means* (2008), travelling from Ireland to Sydney using local transport, and *Right to the Edge* (2009), from Sydney to Tokyo. He also presented *Charley Boorman's Extreme Frontiers* for Channel 5 in 2011, and further series in South Africa and the US. More recently, he began presenting *Motorbike TV* for Motorsport.TV in 2022.

Boorman is also involved in charitable work, having supported UNICEF since 2004 and serving as president of Dyslexia Action from 2009 – he himself is dyslexic and actively raises awareness of the condition. He has also visited troops in Afghanistan and presented Gold Duke of Edinburgh’s Awards. 

In 2016, Boorman suffered serious leg injuries in a motorbike accident in Portugal, requiring surgery and a period of wheelchair use. He continues to ride, although he now walks with a limp. He has written several books detailing his adventures, including *Long Way Round*, *Race to Dakar*, *Long Way Down*, *Extreme Frontiers* and his autobiography *Long Way Back* (2017).

title: Ivan Perišić
text:
Ivan Perišić, born in 1989, is a Croatian professional footballer currently playing as a winger for PSV, though he’s versatile enough to play multiple positions including wing-back and attacking midfielder. He is widely considered one of the greatest Croatian players ever. His youth career was spent with Hajduk Split and Sochaux, ultimately signing with Sochaux in 2006 after interest from several other clubs. Though he impressed in the youth ranks, winning the Coupe Gambardella in 2007, he didn't make a first-team appearance for Sochaux, spending time with the B team and a loan spell at Roeselare.

He truly began to make a name for himself at Club Brugge, joining them in 2009. He quickly became a key player, scoring 9 goals in his first season and then topping the Belgian Pro League scoring charts with 22 goals in the 2010–11 season, earning him the Belgian Footballer of the Year award. This success led to a transfer to Borussia Dortmund in 2011, where he won the Bundesliga title. However, his time there was somewhat disrupted by a perceived lack of support from manager Jürgen Klopp, leading to a transfer to VfL Wolfsburg in 2013 for €8 million.

At Wolfsburg, Perišić continued to excel, winning the DFB-Pokal in 2015 and consistently contributing goals. In 2015, he moved to Inter Milan for €16 million, becoming a consistent performer for the club. A loan spell at Bayern Munich in 2019 proved highly successful, as he won the treble – the Bundesliga, DFB-Pokal, and Champions League. Returning to Inter, he added to his trophy cabinet with a Serie A title in 2020–21, the Supercoppa Italiana, and the Coppa Italia in 2021–22.

Perišić has also been a crucial member of the Croatia national team since his debut in 2011, participating in four European Championships (2012, 2016, 2020, and 2024) and three FIFA World Cups (2014, 2018, and 2022). He famously scored an equalizer in the 2018 World Cup final and earned a bronze medal at the 2022 tournament. He is Croatia’s all-time leading goal contributor in major tournaments, with a total of 18 goal involvements, and is seen as a key figure in the nation’s “golden generation.” Throughout his career he has been recognized for his ambidexterity and adaptability, allowing him to thrive in various roles on the field.

title: Ryan Brasier
text:
Ryan Brasier, born August 26, 1987, is a professional baseball pitcher currently with the Chicago Cubs, having previously played for the Los Angeles Angels, Boston Red Sox, and Los Angeles Dodgers, as well as the Hiroshima Toyo Carp in Japan. He has won two World Series championships, one with the Red Sox in 2018 and another with the Dodgers in 2024. He stands 6 feet tall, weighs 225 pounds, and is a right-handed pitcher and batter.

Brasier initially played catcher at S.H. Rider High School in Texas, but switched to pitching in college at Weatherford College. He was drafted by the Los Angeles Angels in the sixth round of the 2007 MLB draft and spent six years working his way through their minor league system, reaching Triple-A. He made his major league debut with the Angels in 2013, appearing in seven games with a 2.00 ERA. A Tommy John surgery sidelined him for the entire 2014 season, and he was later released by the Angels.
