After a brief stint with the Oakland Athletics organization in 2015-2016, and a period of rehabilitation, Brasier chose to play professionally in Japan with the Hiroshima Toyo Carp in 2017. He credits his time in Japan with helping him refine his pitching mechanics. Returning to the United States, he signed a minor league contract with the Boston Red Sox in 2018. 

Brasier quickly rose through the Red Sox system, earning a spot on the major league roster mid-season and contributing to their 2018 World Series victory. He continued with the Red Sox through 2022, earning a save in 2019 and navigating injury setbacks, including a calf injury and being hit by a line drive in 2021. He experienced varying levels of success with the Red Sox, with some seasons marked by strong performance and others by struggles. 

In May 2023, after a difficult start to the season, the Red Sox designated Brasier for assignment and later released him. He quickly signed a minor league deal with the Los Angeles Dodgers, where he impressed and was called up to the majors, playing a key role in their postseason run and ultimately winning the 2024 World Series. He signed a two-year contract with the Dodgers but was designated for assignment in January 2025 before being traded to the Chicago Cubs a few days later.

title: Rafael Nadal
text:
Rafael Nadal, born in 1986 in Mallorca, Spain, was a highly successful professional tennis player who reached the world No. 1 ranking and held it for 209 weeks, finishing the year as No. 1 five times. Throughout his nearly two-decade career, he amassed 92 ATP Tour singles titles, including a record 14 French Open championships, 36 Masters titles, and an Olympic gold medal. He is one of only three men to achieve the career Golden Slam – winning all four major titles and an Olympic gold. Nadal retired from the sport after playing in the 2024 Davis Cup Finals.

Nadal rose to prominence alongside Roger Federer and Novak Djokovic, forming the “Big Three” who dominated men’s tennis for years. He quickly achieved success as a teenager, winning 16 titles and reaching No. 2 in the world before turning 20, highlighted by his first major title at the 2005 French Open. He first became world No. 1 in 2008 after a historic Wimbledon final victory over Federer, becoming the first to win a Grand Slam outside of clay. He followed this with Olympic gold at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. In 2010, he achieved a career Grand Slam at the young age of 24 by winning the US Open, making him the youngest man in the Open Era to do so, and the first to win majors on three different surfaces in the same year.

Nadal demonstrated remarkable consistency, winning major singles titles in ten consecutive years (2005-2014) and again across a four-year span (2017-2020). He also secured 11 doubles titles, including another Olympic gold at the 2016 Rio Olympics. He surpassed Federer and Djokovic’s shared record for most Grand Slam singles titles at the 2022 Australian Open and became one of only four men to complete the double career Grand Slam.

Known for his powerful left-handed forehand with heavy topspin, Nadal excelled in return games and break points. Clay courts were particularly suited to his game, where he won 63 of his 92 singles titles. Beyond his on-court achievements, Nadal was recognized for his sportsmanship, receiving the Stefan Edberg Sportsmanship Award five times and being named Laureus World Sportsman of the Year in 2011 and 2021. *Time* magazine included him in their list of the 100 most influential people in the world in 2022.

Nadal’s early life was shaped by his family, particularly his father, a businessman, and his uncle, Toni Nadal, a tennis coach who began training him at age three. Initially favoring football, Nadal was encouraged to focus on tennis by his uncle, who implemented rigorous training methods. He excelled in junior competitions, winning multiple Spanish junior championships and reaching the final of the U14 Spanish championship. He turned professional in 2001 at the age of 14 and quickly rose through the ranks, winning his first ATP title in 2004 and leading Spain to a Davis Cup victory that same year. He continued to ascend, winning his first major title at the 2005 French Open and establishing himself as a dominant force in the sport. He also established a tennis academy in Mallorca and actively participates in philanthropic endeavors.

title: Nuh Omar
text:
Nuh Omar, born June 5, 1988, is a Pakistani-born director and screenwriter with a diverse career spanning film, television, and advertising. He comes from a notable family; his grandfather was entrepreneur Safdar Kureishi, and he is related to Hanif and Maki Kureishi. He spent his early years in Karachi, Pakistan, attending Karachi Grammar School alongside Bilawal Bhutto Zardari, and has both an older sister and a younger brother. His mother was a pioneering sports photojournalist in Pakistan.

Omar’s formal education began with the New York Film Academy’s 2nd Year Film Program in 2006, followed by a Bachelor’s degree in The Science of Film from Full Sail University. Post-graduation, he gained experience through an internship at The Institute and freelance assistant directing work on various short films. He also demonstrated early talent with his short film “We're Americans, Eh?”, which won awards at the 24 Hour Film Festival in 2011.

Returning to Pakistan in 2012, Omar directed short films for Engro Corporation Excellence Awards, including “Mojiza-e-Fun (The Miracle of Art),” which became the last documented project featuring sculptor Shahid Sajjad before his death. He then worked in internet-based projects, ghostwriting commercials, and as a director for the entertainment channel DeVida Lifestyle. A period with the advertising agency IAL Saatchi & Saatchi followed, where he contributed to campaigns for major brands like Head & Shoulders and Pampers. He left this role in 2014 to refocus on filmmaking.

Omar has found success with his long-running YouTube series, “The Fortress of Dorkness,” which he both wrote and directed, producing over 100 episodes with collaborator Christian Villarreal between 2015 and 2019. He is currently developing several new projects, including the historical drama “The Alexandrian” with Mark Davis, and the screenplay “The Porter & The Stone,” a modern adaptation of Oscar Wilde’s “The Happy Prince,” which has garnered multiple awards and high rankings on the Coverfly platform. 

He is also working on TV pilot “A Matter of Time,” co-written with Villarreal, which won Filmmatic’s TV Pilot Awards, and the series “I’m Here”, first conceived as a student project in 2007. Current collaborations with Rustic Lightbulb and producer Severn Lang include the short film “The Universe at Midnight” and the feature “Tijuana Bible.” He is also writing two feature films, “The Imaginary Friend Society” and “Ophelia.” 

Currently based between Karachi and Los Angeles, Omar is a vocal advocate for mental health awareness, openly discussing his own experiences with depression.

title: Radhika Apte
text:
Radhika Apte, born on September 7, 1985, in Vellore, Tamil Nadu, is a prominent Indian film and television actress. Her parents, both doctors, were stationed in Vellore at the time of her birth, and her father later became a neurosurgeon in Pune. Apte holds a degree in Economics and Mathematics from Fergusson College, Pune, and initially experienced a liberating homeschooling period with friends. She began her acting journey in theatre, eventually moving to Mumbai before briefly returning to Pune, discouraged by her initial experiences. A year spent studying contemporary dance in London proved transformative, exposing her to a different professional environment and leading to her meeting her future husband, London-based musician Benedict Taylor, whom she married in 2012. 

Apte’s film career began with a small role in the 2005 Hindi film *Vaah! Life Ho Toh Aisi!* and gained momentum with her lead role in the 2009 Bengali drama *Antaheen*, where she was praised for her performance as a TV journalist. Throughout the early 2010s, she appeared in a variety of films across multiple languages, including Marathi, Hindi, Tamil, and Telugu, often tackling challenging roles. She faced a setback when she was deemed “too fat” for a role in a blockbuster production, an experience she later recounted.

A turning point came in 2015 with supporting roles in *Badlapur*, *Hunterrr*, and *Manjhi - The Mountain Man*, earning her wider recognition.  Her leading roles in the independent films *Phobia* and *Parched* in 2016 further cemented her critical acclaim. Apte’s career saw a significant boost with her work on Netflix, starring in the anthology film *Lust Stories*, the thriller series *Sacred Games*, and the horror mini-series *Ghoul* in 2018.  Her performance in *Lust Stories* earned her a historic nomination for an International Emmy Award, making her the first Indian actress to receive such recognition. She continued to work with Netflix on films like *Raat Akeli Hai* (2020) and *Monica, O My Darling* (2022), and appeared in the American film *A Call to Spy* (2019) as Noor Inayat Khan. More recently, her performance in *Sister Midnight* (2024) garnered a British Independent Film Award nomination.

Alongside her independent film work, Apte has also starred in commercially successful mainstream films such as the Tamil action film *Kabali* (2016), the Hindi biographical film *Pad Man* (2018), and the Hindi black comedy *Andhadhun* (2018). She is also involved in theatre, performing with Aasakta Kalamanch and in various other plays, and has participated in several short films.  

Apte is recognized in the media as a versatile and outspoken performer, often described as a “powerhouse performer” and a “poster child of OTT.” She has also been a vocal supporter of the MeToo movement in India and has spoken out against sexual harassment within the film industry.

title: Kevin Anderson (tennis)
text:
Kevin Anderson, born in 1986, is a South African former professional tennis player who reached a career-high ranking of world No. 5 in July 2018, becoming the first South African to achieve this since Kevin Curren in 1985. He began playing tennis at age six and demonstrated athletic ability in running alongside his tennis pursuits. He first competed professionally at 17, quickly gaining a ranking and showing early promise.

Anderson’s collegiate career was spent at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, where he earned All-American honors in both singles and doubles, winning the national doubles championship in 2005-06 with partner Ryan Rowe. He led Illinois to a national runner-up finish in 2007, facing future ATP star John Isner in the championship match.

Turning professional, Anderson steadily climbed the ranks, achieving his first ATP Tour title at the South African Open in Johannesburg in February 2011, defeating Somdev Devvarman in the final. He continued to improve, reaching his first major final at the 2017 US Open, ultimately losing to Rafael Nadal. Interestingly, as a 12-year-old, he regularly competed against Nadal on the junior circuit. 

His most notable achievement came at the 2018 Wimbledon Championships. He reached the final after an epic semi-final victory over John Isner, a match lasting six hours and 36 minutes – the second-longest in major tournament history. He then lost the final to Novak Djokovic. Throughout his career, Anderson consistently demonstrated an ability to defeat top players, including a win over Novak Djokovic in 2008 and Andy Murray at the 2015 US Open.

Anderson experienced periods of injury, notably in 2016 with knee, shoulder and ankle issues, which impacted his performance. He achieved a career milestone in 2015, breaking into the top 10 of the ATP rankings. He enjoyed several strong runs in Masters 1000 events, reaching quarterfinals in Indian Wells, Madrid, Toronto and Cincinnati. 

He retired in May 2022 at the age of 35, but announced a comeback in July 2023. His career included multiple Challenger titles and consistent performances at Grand Slam level, reaching the fourth round or better in all four majors. He was known for his powerful serve and aggressive baseline game, making him a formidable opponent on all surfaces. He faced some of the biggest names in tennis repeatedly, often achieving notable victories against them.

title: Jimmy Weldon
text:
Jimmy Weldon, born Ivy Laverne Shinn on September 23, 1923, in Dale, Texas, was a multifaceted entertainer who worked as an actor, ventriloquist, and television host throughout a long career, passing away on July 6, 2023, at the age of 99. He is most widely recognized for voicing the Hanna-Barbera cartoon character Yakky Doodle.

Weldon’s career began in 1946 at KWCO in Texas, where he was the first announcer hired after the station’s launch following his service in World War II. It was at this radio station that he developed the character of Webster Webfoot, a duck who initially appeared as part of his disc jockey segments. Listeners enjoyed interacting with Webster, often believing him to be a separate individual, leading to the character’s growing popularity. 

He and Webster continued their work at KRHD in Duncan, Oklahoma for two years, before being recruited by WFAA in Dallas, Texas. This led to *The Webster Webfoot Show* premiering on WFAA-TV on April 4, 1950. In 1952, Weldon and Webster moved to California and joined KCOP-TV in Hollywood, continuing their television show. They garnered attention from established stars like Jeff Chandler and Randolph Scott, who playfully acknowledged Webster’s greater appeal to their own children. This notoriety led to an opportunity to co-host *Funny Boners*, a children’s game show on ABC, with Ralph Edwards.

Throughout the 1950s and 60s, Weldon and Webster moved between television stations in California, including a stint at KFRE-TV in Fresno, a brief period replacing Shari Lewis on the *Hi, Mom* show in New York, and a return to Channel 13 in Hollywood. They frequently travelled throughout the San Joaquin Valley, performing shows in cities like Salinas and Bakersfield, utilizing Weldon’s own airplane for transportation.

Beyond his work with Webster, Weldon had a successful voice acting career, most notably as Yakky Doodle. He also provided the voice of Solomon Grundy for Hanna-Barbera’s *Challenge of the Superfriends*. He also made appearances as an actor in live-action television shows including *Dragnet*, *Alfred Hitchcock Presents*, *The Waltons*, *Dallas*, and *Diff'rent Strokes*. Additionally, he contributed to the radio drama *Adventures in Odyssey* and was a member of the Premiere Speakers Bureau. In later life, he maintained a YouTube channel called Jimmy's Lecture where he shared stories from his time serving in WWII.

title: Maya Yoshida
text:
Maya Yoshida, born in Nagasaki, Japan in 1988, is a professional footballer currently captaining and playing as a centre-back for LA Galaxy. He amassed over 120 appearances for the Japan national team, participating in the FIFA World Cups of 2014, 2018, and 2022, as well as the AFC Asian Cup in 2011 (winning the tournament), 2015, and 2019 (where they were runners-up). He also represented Japan’s Olympic team in 2008, 2012, and 2020.

Yoshida’s football journey began with Nanling FC while in elementary school, spurred by his older brother who discovered Nagoya Grampus’s U-15 team. He relocated to Nagoya to join the youth academy and was eventually promoted to the first team in 2007. Initially playing as a defensive midfielder, he was transitioned to centre-back. He debuted for Nagoya Grampus against Oita Trinita, becoming a regular in the team, and scored his first goal against Thespa Kusatsu in the Emperor’s Cup. He earned the "Rookie of the Year" award in 2008 after a successful season where Nagoya Grampus finished third in the league. In 2009, he scored eight goals in all competitions and helped the team reach the Emperor’s Cup final, ultimately losing to Gamba Osaka.

In December 2009, Yoshida transferred to Dutch club VVV-Venlo, fulfilling his ambition to play in Europe. However, his start was hampered by a fractured foot which sidelined him for the remainder of the 2009-10 season. He made his debut in October 2010, quickly becoming a key player. After winning the AFC Asian Cup with Japan in 2011, he helped VVV-Venlo retain their Eredivisie status through the relegation play-offs. He continued to be a prominent figure in the 2011-12 season, scoring five goals and winning the “Goal of the Season” award for a spectacular bicycle kick. He again helped the club avoid relegation via the play-offs.

In August 2012, Yoshida joined Southampton in the Premier League. He became a regular in the starting lineup, forming a strong partnership with José Fonte. He played in various defensive positions, contributing to Southampton’s improvement and their avoidance of relegation in his first season. While his playing time fluctuated in subsequent seasons due to competition and injuries, he remained a valuable squad member, extending his contract in 2015. He helped Southampton qualify for the UEFA Europa League on multiple occasions, experiencing a period of both starting roles and time on the bench. He captained Southampton for the first time in an FA Cup match and reached the EFL Cup final with the team in 2017, though they ultimately lost.

title: Emcee N.I.C.E.
text:
Emcee N.I.C.E., born Aulsondro Hamilton, is a multifaceted American artist with a career spanning music, film, radio, and entrepreneurship. He first gained recognition as the lead vocalist and rapper for the duo KansasCali, contributing to six motion picture soundtracks including those for *Crash*, *Mr. & Mrs. Smith*, and *Haven*. Earlier in his career, from 1994 to 1999, he was a member of A Lighter Shade of Brown. 

Beyond performing, Emcee N.I.C.E. has significant production credits, notably co-producing the acoustic versions of 2Pac’s “Thugz Mansion” and Nas’s “Thugz Mansion (N.Y.).” He transitioned into a solo Christian hip hop career, releasing his debut album *Praise* in 2017, which reached No. 1 on both the Billboard Top Gospel Albums and Billboard Gospel Album Sales charts. *Praise* spawned five No. 1 hit records, including “I Got Angels” which charted twice, and “Glory to God” featuring Fred Hammond.

Emcee N.I.C.E.’s accomplishments have garnered awards and nominations. He won a Stellar Award for Gospel Hip Hop Radio Station of the Year for God’s House of Hip Hop Radio, a station he co-founded and which is powered by Dash Radio. He has received numerous accolades from The Gospel Spin Awards, totaling 17 nominations and 12 wins, including being honored as “Radio Man of the Year” in 2021. He was also nominated for a MTV Video Music Award in 2003 for Best Rap Video for the "Thugz Mansion" music video.

He is also a creative entrepreneur. He co-created the animated music series *Da Jammies* in 2015, voicing the character “Novelist.” He is the president of two non-profit organizations, The iTL Foundation and Urbanomics 101, and serves as the Managing Editor for *RYZE Magazine*, a Christian hip hop lifestyle publication. Furthermore, he is a published author. His book, *Music Release University*, became an Amazon Books New Release Best Seller, achieving No. 1 in the “Music Recording & Sound” category and a Top 10 spot in “Music Business.” He also authored *50 Shades of L.O.V.E.* and *Songwriting Secrets*.  Emcee N.I.C.E. is also described as an American Inventor.

title: Maggie Cogan
text:
Maggie Cogan is a New York City resident best known for being the first female coachman in Central Park, employed by the Plaza Hotel. Her pioneering role garnered media attention, including a 1967 appearance in a Universal newsreel and a 1968 spot on the quiz show *What’s My Line?* where panelists attempted to identify her profession. She famously voiced her opposition to a proposal to install meters on the horse-drawn carriages, believing it would cheapen the experience.

Cogan’s early life included cheerleading and dance in high school in New Hyde Park, Long Island, followed by attendance at several colleges, though she did not earn a degree. She began her career with the Plaza Hotel at the age of 19. However, her life began to experience difficulties in the late 1960s. She endured two unsuccessful marriages and had two sons, whom she ultimately relinquished to her parents after struggling with the aftermath of her failed relationships and being unable to reclaim them upon returning to New York from a four-year stay in Texas.

The 1970s saw a decline in Cogan’s mental health. While living with Lisa Ryan, the daughter of actor Robert Ryan, she developed intense infatuations, first with Robert Ryan, sending him unusual gifts, and later with serial killer David Berkowitz. She also suffered a violent mugging that resulted in facial slashes, and experienced a separate, unspecified sexual assault. These events led to a severe emotional breakdown, culminating in her parents committing her to a mental hospital in 1977.

Following her release and the loss of her job, Cogan became homeless and spent approximately fifteen years living in Central Park. During this time, she created elaborate stories about her life, claiming to be Robert Ryan's daughter and possessing extrasensory perception. Despite her hardships, she maintained friendships and relied on the kindness of others for food and clothing, and found companionship with several dogs she adopted.

Her story came to the attention of filmmaker Michel Negroponte in 1989 while he was working on a different documentary. He shifted his focus to Cogan and created *Jupiter's Wife*, a film documenting her life in the park. The film captured her daily routines and interactions, and ultimately led to public assistance being granted, allowing Cogan to secure an apartment, though this housing was later lost in a 1995 eviction. She briefly lived with a friend at a pet shelter, but returned to Central Park after five weeks. The film received a special jury prize at the Sundance Film Festival.

title: Sayuri Yamauchi
text:
Sayuri Yamauchi, born on May 28, 1956, and passing away on March 6, 2012, was a Japanese voice actress known professionally as Sayuri. Throughout her career, she lent her voice to a wide variety of characters in anime, video games, and dubbed foreign productions. She was associated with Kyu Production at one point and, at the time of her death at the age of 55, was affiliated with Aigumi. 

Yamauchi’s work spanned numerous well-known series. In anime, she voiced Vera Ronstadt in *The Big O*, Hikaru Kosaka in *The Brave Fighter of Legend Da-Garn*, and characters in the *City Hunter* franchise, including a dress store clerk and a performer in the film adaptation. She also contributed to *Crayon Shin-chan* as both Nanako Ohara and Lulu Lu Lulu, and took on the role of 0012 in *Cyborg 009*. Other notable anime roles included Satella in *Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood*, Primada, Ikumi Kaidou, and Ai Amami in *The King of Braves GaoGaiGar*, Astral in *Saint of Braves Baan Gaan*, Lady Une in *Mobile Suit Gundam Wing* and *Gundam Wing: Endless Waltz*, "Twilight" Suzuka in *Outlaw Star*, Osuzu in *Samurai Champloo*, Maya in *Shaman King* and Tiara in *Shamanic Princess*. 

In the realm of video games, Yamauchi’s voice graced titles like *Baten Kaitos Origins* where she played Gena, and *Dragon Force II* as both Bjorn and Medea. She was also involved in the *Super Robot Wars* franchise, lending her voice to characters like Ai Anami and Primada in *Super Robot Wars Alpha 2*, Ikumi Kaidou and Palus Abel in *Super Robot Wars Alpha 3*, and Ikumi Kaidoh in *Super Robot Wars T*. Further video game roles included Tomoe Kawasaki in *Robot Alchemic Drive* and Lorithia in *Xenoblade Chronicles*.

Beyond animation, Yamauchi also performed dubbing work for live-action films and television. She provided the Japanese voice for Monica Swinton (played by Frances O’Connor) in *A.I. Artificial Intelligence*, Donna Jensen (Marg Helgenberger) in *Erin Brockovich*, Trin (Melina Kanakaredes) in *The Long Kiss Goodnight*, Sadie (Sadie Frost) in *Love, Honour and Obey*, and Switch (Belinda McClory) in *The Matrix*. She also voiced characters in *Mission: Impossible*, *Pecker*, *The Sea Inside*, and the 1998 DVD edition of *Suspiria*, as well as Audrey Horne (Sherilyn Fenn) in *Twin Peaks*. 

Perhaps her most recognizable dubbing role was providing the voices for both Itchy and Maude Flanders in the Japanese version of the animated television series, *The Simpsons*.

title: José Hernández Delgadillo
text:
José Hernández Delgadillo was a Mexican painter and muralist born in 1927 in Tepeapulco, Hidalgo, and died in 2000. He is recognized for continuing the traditions of the Mexican muralism movement into the latter half of the 20th century, creating over 160 murals in both Mexico and the United States. A significant portion of his work, particularly after 1970, contained strong political messages, often making him a controversial figure and contributing to a degree of obscurity despite his artistic merit.

Hernández Delgadillo came from humble beginnings, working various manual labor jobs during his youth. He began his artistic training in Mexico City in 1945, studying painting and architectural drawing, and supporting himself by making portraits. He later attended the Escuela Nacional de Pintura, Escultura y Grabado "La Esmeralda" from 1955-1960, where he was inspired by Pablo O’Higgins to continue the ideals of Mexican muralism. 

Beyond his art, Hernández Delgadillo was deeply involved in politics, believing in grassroots organization to influence the government. He wrote a weekly column for the newspaper *Excélsior* from 1980 to 1983, and ran as a candidate for the Partido Mexicano de Trabajadores in 1985. He was also considered as a presidential candidate for the PRD in 1987, ultimately supporting Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas and creating murals for his campaign.

His artistic career began with an exhibition in 1954 and gained international recognition with awards at biennials in Mexico and Paris in 1961, leading to a French government grant that allowed him to exhibit throughout France and Spain. While he achieved success with easel paintings, he became most known for his mural work, beginning with the Escuela Primaria Belisario Dominguez in 1959. He served as director of arte for the Centro Residencial Morelos housing project in 1969, creating a large-scale mural complex there.  He often collaborated with students on these murals, utilizing simple colors and incorporating them as educational and political events. He began creating explicitly political murals in 1973, and later expanded his work to the United States in 1981, with commissions in California.

Despite his prolific output, many of Hernández Delgadillo’s murals have fallen into disrepair or been deliberately destroyed due to their political content. Efforts to restore his work began in 2013 in Pachuca, Hidalgo, his home state, which has increasingly focused on recognizing and preserving his legacy.  He also pursued sculpture and illustrated medical texts. 

Hernández Delgadillo’s artistry aligned with the second state of Mexican muralism, inspired by artists like Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco, and David Alfaro Siqueiros. His work, often expressionistic, frequently denounced violence and championed social justice.  He was a member of the Salón de la Plástica Mexicana, and after his death, the SPM established a prize in his name and held a retrospective of his work in 2009. While his work was often overlooked by the mainstream art world due to its challenging political themes, a biography of his life and work was published in 2008, signaling a growing effort to recognize his contributions to Mexican art.

title: Zhang Yaokun
text:
Zhang Yaokun, born April 17, 1981, was a Chinese footballer who concluded his professional career in November 2018. He began his career with Dalian Shide in 1998, but faced initial setbacks due to an ankle fracture that hampered his progress. After recovering from this injury, he became a vital part of Dalian’s defense, contributing to a period of success for the club. He was a key player in their winning of the Chinese Jia-A League titles in 2001 and 2002, as well as the Chinese FA Cup in 2001. Following a disappointing season for Dalian in 2004, he was loaned to Sichuan Guancheng in 2005, where he quickly became a prominent player. He returned to Dalian the next year and eventually became the team’s captain.

In December 2012, Zhang moved to Guangzhou R&F, making his debut in March 2013 in a match against Liaoning Whowin. He then transferred to Wuhan Zall, a League One side, in February 2017. His time with Wuhan Zall culminated in the team’s promotion to the Chinese Super League, after which he announced his retirement from professional football in November 2018.

Zhang also represented the Chinese national team, receiving a call-up for the 2004 AFC Asian Cup where he appeared as a substitute and played in various defensive positions. He continued to be a regular member of the national squad, contributing to their qualification for the 2007 AFC Asian Cup. During that tournament, he formed the first-choice centre back partnership with Li Weifeng. He also participated in the 2005 East Asian Football Championship, where China won the title.

Throughout his career, Zhang accumulated numerous honors. With Dalian Shide, he won the Chinese Jia-A League four times (1998, 2000, 2001, and 2002), the Chinese FA Cup in 2001, and the Chinese FA Super Cup in 2000 and 2002. More recently, with Wuhan Zall, he secured the China League One title in 2018. Individually, he was recognized for his performance with a place in the Chinese Super League Team of the Year in 2004.

title: Stephen J. Mackwell
text:
Stephen J. Mackwell is a geophysicist whose research focuses on the physical, chemical, and mechanical properties of geological materials. His work investigates fluid transport within rocks, both in Earth's mantle and crust, and how these fluids affect the rocks’ mechanical behavior. He is a prolific author, having published over 80 articles in international scientific journals and also served as an editor of a book concerning the comparative climates of terrestrial planets, published by the University of Arizona Press in 2013.

Mackwell’s academic foundation began with a Bachelor of Science degree in Physics and Mathematics from the University of Canterbury in New Zealand, earned in 1978. He continued at Canterbury, completing a Master of Science in Physics the following year, with a thesis focused on excitation temperatures of late-type stars. He also obtained a Diploma of Education from Christchurch Teachers College in 1979. He then pursued and received a Ph.D. in Geophysics from the Australian National University in 1985, with his dissertation examining the diffusion and weakening effects of water in quartz and olivine.

His early career included a postdoctoral fellowship at Cornell University from 1984 to 1987. He then joined Pennsylvania State University as an assistant professor in 1987, and was promoted to associate professor of geosciences in 1992. A period of public service followed, serving as program director for geophysics at the National Science Foundation from 1993 to 1994, and as an Alexander von Humboldt Fellow at the Bayerisches Geoinstitut in Germany in 1996. In 1998, he became a full professor of experimental geophysics at the Bayerisches Geoinstitut, and subsequently its director from 2000 to 2002.

In late 2002, Mackwell moved back to the United States to become director of the Lunar and Planetary Institute (LPI) in Houston, Texas, a division of the Universities Space Research Association (USRA). Alongside this role, he managed USRA’s Houston facility and oversaw educational programs. He transitioned to the role of USRA Corporate Director of Science Programs in 2016, when Louise Prockter became Director of the LPI. He has remained active in the scientific community through editorial roles with journals like *Geophysical Research Letters* and *Physics and Chemistry of Minerals*, and participation in Planetary Science Decadal Survey activities. He currently holds adjunct professorships at Rice University, the University of Minnesota, and the University of Maryland – College Park. 

From 2019 to 2021, Mackwell served as Deputy Executive Officer of the American Institute of Physics. More recently, from April 2022 to March 2025, he held positions at the National Science Foundation, first as Section Head for Disciplinary Programs and then as Acting Deputy Division Director. Throughout his career, Mackwell has received numerous accolades, including fellowships from the American Association for the Advancement of Science and the American Geophysical Union, and the naming of asteroid 5292 Mackwell in his honor in 2016.

title: Salome Maswime
text:
Salome Maswime is a South African medical doctor specializing in obstetrics and gynaecology, currently serving as the Head of Global Surgery at the University of Cape Town. Her work centers on improving women’s health, advocating for equitable surgical and maternal care, and ensuring healthcare access for underserved communities. She frequently provides advice and consultation to organizations like the World Health Organization. 

Born in Limpopo, Maswime’s path to specializing in maternal health was profoundly influenced by a formative experience during her medical internship in Greytown, KwaZulu-Natal. Witnessing the preventable deaths of two mothers in a maternity ward motivated her to dedicate her career to addressing maternal mortality. She completed her medical degree at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in 2005. 

Following her internship, she spent ten years at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg and the Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital in Soweto. This period led her to pursue further education, culminating in a PhD funded by the Carnegie Corporation of New York and the South African Medical Research Council. Her doctoral research, completed at the University of the Witwatersrand, focused on reducing maternal morbidity related to hemorrhage following caesarean sections across hospitals in Gauteng.

Throughout her career, Maswime has held several key positions, including as a lecturer and Director of the Obstetrics and Gynaecology Clinical Research Division at the University of the Witwatersrand, and as an obstetrician at Chris Hani Baragwanath Hospital. She focuses on high-risk pregnancies and researches maternal near-miss cases and mortality. Her work has highlighted an increase in maternal deaths stemming from bleeding during caesarean sections in South Africa and evaluated hospital preparedness for surgical complications. 

Maswime’s research also reveals the significant global burden of maternal mortality, noting that Africa accounts for approximately two-thirds of all maternal deaths worldwide, totaling around 200,000 deaths annually. She has published articles on this issue, including work concerning the increasing rate of caesarean sections in Africa. 

Recognized for her contributions, Maswime received the Trailblazer and Young Achiever Award in 2017, presented by Jacob Zuma, and was listed among the Mail & Guardian’s Top 200 South Africans the same year. In 2018, she founded the South African Clinician Scientists Society to support emerging specialists and researchers. She was also awarded a Discovery Foundation Harvard University Fellowship, worth R2.1 million, to research the causes of stillbirths in HIV-positive individuals. This fellowship led to her being one of only two representatives from her field at meetings with the World Health Organization and UNICEF, where she also explored the link between maternal and child mental health. She was appointed Professor of Global Surgery at the University of Cape Town in 2019 and named a Young Scientist by the World Economic Forum in 2020. She is a member of both the Academy of Science of South Africa, the South African Perioperative Research Group, and the International Network of Obstetric Survey Systems. She is a mother to two children, Taurai and Farai.

title: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
text:
Muhammad Ali Jinnah, born Mahomedali Jinnahbhai in Karachi in 1876, was a barrister and politician who became the founder of Pakistan, serving as its first governor-general until his death in 1948. He received his legal training at Lincoln's Inn in London and upon his return to India, practiced law at the Bombay High Court, gradually shifting his focus to national politics. Initially, Jinnah was a prominent figure within the Indian National Congress, advocating for Hindu-Muslim unity and playing a key role in the 1916 Lucknow Pact between the Congress and the All-India Muslim League. He proposed a fourteen-point plan for constitutional reform to protect Muslim rights. However, he resigned from the Congress in 1920 due to disagreements over their adoption of satyagraha, which he considered disruptive.

Subsequently, Jinnah dedicated himself to the All-India Muslim League, working to safeguard Muslim interests against potential marginalization in a Hindu-dominated India. He led the League in passing the Lahore Resolution in 1940, outlining the demand for a separate Muslim state. The League’s influence grew during World War II, particularly while Congress leaders were imprisoned, and they achieved significant electoral success in post-war provincial elections. Ultimately, the inability of the Congress and Muslim League to agree on a power-sharing arrangement led to the acceptance of the partition of British India into independent India and Pakistan.

As Pakistan’s first governor-general, Jinnah focused on establishing the new nation’s government and assisting the millions of Muslim migrants who relocated from India to Pakistan. He personally oversaw the establishment of refugee camps to aid this massive displacement. Jinnah died in September 1948, just over a year after Pakistan’s independence, leaving behind a lasting legacy. He is widely revered in Pakistan as “Quaid-e-Azam” (“Great Leader”) and “Baba-e-Qaum” (“Father of the Nation”), with his birthday observed as a national holiday and numerous institutions bearing his name.

Born into a wealthy merchant family, Jinnah's early life included a period of education in Bombay and Karachi. He abandoned an apprenticeship in London to study law, motivated in part by legal issues facing his family. While in England, he was influenced by British liberalism and adopted Western dress and mannerisms. He became the first Muslim barrister to practice in Bombay, quickly gaining a reputation for his legal skills and earning a substantial income. He was also involved in trade union activities, advocating for workers’ rights and contributing to the enactment of the Trade Union Act of 1926.

Jinnah’s political career began with participation in the Indian National Congress, where he initially aligned with moderate leaders promoting Hindu-Muslim cooperation. However, he often clashed with more radical factions and questioned the legitimacy of self-appointed Muslim leaders who sought separate representation. He entered the Imperial Legislative Council in 1909 as a compromise candidate and used this platform to advocate for his community's interests. Throughout his life, Jinnah was known for his self-confidence, sharp intellect, and meticulous attention to detail, earning him respect even from his adversaries.

title: Carlos P. Romulo
text:
Carlos P. Romulo was a remarkably versatile figure in 20th-century Philippine and international affairs, serving as a diplomat, statesman, soldier, journalist, author, and educator. Born in Manila in 1899, his early life was shaped by the transition from Spanish to American colonial rule; his father initially fought against the United States but later served in the U.S. government in the Philippines. Romulo himself rose to prominence quickly, becoming a professor of English at the University of the Philippines and secretary to Senate President Manuel Quezon in the 1920s. He also became involved in publishing, serving as editor of *The Philippines Herald* and co-founding the Boy Scouts of the Philippines.

During World War II, Romulo played a pivotal role, serving as an aide to General Douglas MacArthur and actively participating in propaganda efforts after the fall of the Philippines. He became Secretary of Information in President Quezon’s War Cabinet and achieved the rank of general by the war’s end. A staunch advocate for Philippine independence, Romulo viewed American colonialism more favorably than European imperialism.

Following the war, Romulo embarked on a long and distinguished diplomatic career, serving eight Philippine presidents in various capacities. He was the country’s representative to the United States and the United Nations, and served as resident commissioner to the U.S. House of Representatives from 1944-1946 – uniquely, he was the only member to leave Congress due to his country’s secession.  At the UN, he championed human rights, freedom, and decolonization, famously responding to a belittling remark from a Soviet delegate with a spirited defense of smaller nations’ right to be heard. He served as president of the UN General Assembly from 1949 to 1950, the first Asian to hold the position, and presided over the Security Council multiple times. He was even a nominee for UN Secretary-General in 1953, but was ultimately unsuccessful.

Romulo’s commitment to the Philippines also led him back to domestic politics. He ran for the presidential nomination in 1952 but was sidelined by party politics, and later became a campaign manager for Ramon Magsaysay, who won the presidency in 1953. He held multiple cabinet positions, including Secretary of Foreign Affairs under several presidents, and Secretary of Education. He participated in the Bandung Conference in 1955, though his views on communism differed from other attendees. 

He eventually resigned from the Marcos cabinet in 1983, citing health reasons, but also expressing dismay over the assassination of Benigno Aquino.  A prolific writer, Romulo authored 22 books, including autobiographies and wartime memoirs, and was named a National Artist for Literature in 1982. He received an extraordinary number of honors and awards, including the Pulitzer Prize in 1942, and was widely respected as a leading statesman. Carlos P. Romulo died in 1985 and is remembered as a key figure in Philippine history and a significant voice on the world stage.

title: Joseph Michael Linsner
text:
Joseph Michael Linsner, born December 13, 1968, is an American comic book writer and artist, best known for creating the character Dawn, a mature-audiences, supernatural figure, and for his depictions of female characters. He’s established himself as a prominent cover artist within the comics industry. Growing up in Queens, New York, Linsner was influenced early on by titles like Batman and X-Men, as well as the work of Alberto Vargas, and later by creators such as Alan Moore, Pat Mills, and David Cronenberg. His father’s death when he was 14 had a significant impact on his life.

Linsner began his career by self-publishing *Cry for Dawn* in 1989 through Cry for Dawn Productions, co-founded with Joseph M. Monks, which ran for nine issues. After the production company dissolved in 1993, he continued to publish Dawn through Sirius Entertainment with various limited series and one-shots until 2000. He entered mainstream comics by providing a cover for *Justice League Quarterly* #13 in 1993. He subsequently worked with Marvel Comics on projects like *Killraven* #1, covers for *Mystique*, and the *Wolverine-Black Cat* limited series, *Claws*, and its sequel in 2011. 

Beyond his character-driven work, Linsner is also known for his benefit work. In 2002, he self-published *I Love New York*, a comic intended as a fundraiser for the American Red Cross following the September 11th attacks, reflecting his personal experience as a New Yorker.  He has also provided illustrations for the book *Our Gods Wear Spandex* and contributed cover art to titles from Topps Comics, Dark Horse Comics, and Dynamite Entertainment, becoming a prolific cover artist for the latter, particularly for licensed characters like Red Sonja and Vampirella starting in 2012. Linsner is a long-time supporter of The Hero Initiative, an organization providing assistance to comic book creators.

Linsner’s career has been marked by some controversy. In 2013, he publicly accused his former assistant, Eva Hopkins, of selling his original artwork without his permission, leading to a public dispute. He is married to Kristina Deak-Linsner.

Throughout his career, Linsner has received recognition for his work. He was nominated for an Eisner Award for Best Painter/Digital Artist in 1997 and was awarded an Inkpot Award at the 2007 San Diego Comic-Con. He was also a guest of honor at the 2008 Toronto Comic Con alongside Herb Trimpe and Greg Land. He has an extensive bibliography including numerous *Dawn* series, *Dark Ivory*, and contributions to titles like *Harley Quinn*.

title: Djimon Hounsou
text:
Djimon Gaston Hounsou, born in Cotonou, Benin in 1964, is an actor who has achieved recognition in both American and international cinema. He immigrated to France with his brother at age 12, experiencing homelessness before beginning a successful modeling career in Paris after being discovered by a photographer and encouraged by designer Thierry Mugler. He moved to the United States in 1990, initially appearing in music videos for artists like Paula Abdul, Tina Turner, Janet Jackson, and Madonna.

Hounsou’s film career began in 1990 with *Without You I'm Nothing*. He gained wider attention with roles in *Stargate* (1994) and *Gladiator* (2000), but his breakthrough came with his critically acclaimed performance as Cinqué in Steven Spielberg’s *Amistad* (1997), earning him a Golden Globe nomination. He has since received two Academy Award nominations for Best Supporting Actor, for *In America* (2002) and *Blood Diamond* (2006), winning a National Board of Review Award for the latter.

He has become a recognizable face in major franchises, notably portraying Korath the Pursuer in the Marvel Cinematic Universe films *Guardians of the Galaxy* (2014) and *Captain Marvel* (2019), as well as the animated series *What If...?* (2021). He also joined the DC Extended Universe, playing the Fisherman King in *Aquaman* (2018) and taking over the role of the Wizard Shazam in *Shazam!* (2019), *Black Adam* (2022), and *Shazam! Fury of the Gods* (2023). Other significant film roles include appearances in *The Island* (2005), *Furious 7* (2015), *The Legend of Tarzan* (2016), *A Quiet Place Part II* (2021) and *Rebel Moon* (2023 & 2024) among many others.

Beyond acting, Hounsou has explored other creative avenues. He directed the documentary *In Search of Voodoo: Roots to Heaven* (2018), focusing on the history and religious practices of West African Vodun. He has also lent his voice to animated projects like *How to Train Your Dragon 2* (2014) and been involved in advertising, serving as a Calvin Klein underwear model in 2007, and narrating ESPN’s commercials for the 2010 FIFA World Cup.  He's also contributed to discussions on global issues, speaking at the United Nations on climate change. 

In his personal life, Hounsou had a long-term relationship with model Kimora Lee Simmons, with whom he has a son. They participated in a traditional commitment ceremony in Benin but were never legally married. He has expressed frustration with challenges faced by Black actors in Hollywood, including typecasting and unfair compensation, attributing these issues to systemic racism.

title: Abdul Halik Hudu
text:
Abdul Halik Hudu, nicknamed Rooney, is a Ghanaian professional footballer born on March 19, 2000, who currently plays as a midfielder for Al-Wehdat SC in the Jordanian Pro League. He began his career with Inter Allies in the Ghana Premier League, having progressed from their youth system at Accra Youth FC. He quickly became a regular starter, appearing in 19 games during his debut season in 2016, and was recognized for his talent by winning both the “Most Promising Player of the Year” award and the “Fans' Player of the Season” award for Inter Allies that same year. 

In 2017, Hudu had a trial period with Swedish club Hammarby IF, participating in friendly matches. He returned to Inter Allies before the season began, and continued to impress, earning “Man of the Match” honors in three league games throughout the year. Over two seasons with Inter Allies, he made a total of 37 competitive appearances and scored two goals.

Hudu eventually secured a permanent move to Hammarby IF in early January 2018, signing a three-and-a-half-year contract shortly after turning 18. He scored on his competitive debut for the club on August 23rd in a 3–0 win against Carlstad United in the Svenska Cupen. Following a season with Hammarby, he was loaned to IK Frej in the Superettan in 2019, playing 26 games and scoring twice, though the club was relegated during his time there. He then spent the latter part of 2020 on loan at GIF Sundsvall, simultaneously extending his contract with Hammarby for another year. 

A significant achievement in his career came on May 30, 2021, when he won the Svenska Cupen with Hammarby IF, defeating BK Häcken in a penalty shootout after a 0–0 draw. Later in 2021, on July 16th, Hudu moved to Lyngby in Denmark, signing a two-year contract and making his debut as a substitute in a 2–1 win over Jammerbugt. In March 2022, he returned to Sweden, joining AFC Eskilstuna on another two-year deal. Most recently, in December 2023, he signed a three-season contract with GIF Sundsvall before moving to Al-Wehdat SC in January 2025.

Internationally, Hudu has represented Ghana at the under-17 level, even captaining the team to an 8–0 victory over Namibia in March 2016. He also received a call-up to the Ghana under-20 team in 2018 for a match against Algeria. He has received individual recognition for his play, earning the "Most Promising Player of the Year" award in the Ghanaian Premier League in 2016.

title: Robert Jennings (rugby league)
text:
Robert Jennings, born in Blacktown, New South Wales in 1996, is a rugby league footballer of Tongan international calibre. He comes from a strong sporting family, with his brother Michael playing for the Sydney Roosters and another brother, George, for the Melbourne Storm. He is also the nephew of former All Black Arthur Jennings. His early football development took place with the Western City Tigers and Minchinbury Jets before he was signed by the Penrith Panthers.

Jennings began his National Rugby League (NRL) career with the Penrith Panthers, making his debut in round 7 of the 2015 season against the Gold Coast Titans. He also represented the Junior Kangaroos and the New South Wales Under-20s that year. Despite being contracted with Penrith until the end of 2016, he saw limited game time in 2016 and subsequently signed a one-year deal with the South Sydney Rabbitohs.

His time with the Rabbitohs proved more fruitful. He debuted in 2017 and in 2018 enjoyed a breakout season, scoring a hat-trick against Manly and later a remarkable four tries in a game against Parramatta. He finished the 2018 season with an impressive 19 tries. 

In 2019, Jennings moved to the Wests Tigers on a two-year contract, making 18 appearances in his first season, although the team missed out on finals contention. He was released from the Tigers in September 2020. He then returned to the Penrith Panthers for the 2021 and 2022 seasons, primarily as cover during State of Origin periods, and was part of their NSW Cup Grand Final winning team in 2022, also featuring in their NRL State Championship victory.

Most recently, Jennings signed a two-year contract with the newly established Dolphins in May 2022, debuting for the club in 2023. After his contract expired at the end of the 2023 NRL season, he transitioned away from the NRL, and in 2025 joined the Stanley River Wolves, a local Queensland rugby league club, where he now plays in the second row, continuing his rugby league career at a community level. As of round 11, 2025, he has scored six tries for the Wolves.

title: James Theodore Bent
text:
James Theodore Bent, born in 1852 in Liverpool, was a British explorer, archaeologist, and author who dedicated much of his life to investigating ancient civilizations and documenting his findings. He came from a wealthy background; his grandfather founded Bent’s Breweries, a successful business that provided the family fortune. He was educated at Malvern Wells, Repton School, and Wadham College, Oxford, graduating from the latter in 1875. 

Bent’s travels and research began after marrying Mabel Hall-Dare in 1877, who became a crucial partner in his work, acting as his photographer and keeping a detailed diary of their expeditions. They frequently travelled abroad, initially exploring Italy and Greece, and Bent published several books early in his career, including works on San Marino, Genoa, and Giuseppe Garibaldi.  He focused increasingly on archaeological and ethnographic research, publishing “The Cyclades” based on extensive research in the Aegean islands.

Much of Bent’s work centered on the Eastern Mediterranean and Anatolia between 1883 and 1888, with findings shared through publications in journals like the *Journal of Hellenic Studies*. He undertook significant excavations in the Bahrein Islands in 1889, seeking evidence of Phoenician origins, and travelled through Persia, meeting Shah Naser al-Din Shah Qajar. In 1890, he moved on to South Africa, specifically Mashonaland, where he conducted the first detailed examination of the Great Zimbabwe ruins, believing them to be built by ancestors of the Shona people – a view contested at the time but now largely accepted by modern archaeologists.

Bent continued his explorations in Ethiopia in 1893, documenting the ruins of Axum in his book “The Sacred City of the Ethiopians.” He then ventured into the remote Hadramut region of Southern Arabia, undertaking risky journeys between 1893 and 1894 to study the region’s ancient history and physical features. Further explorations along the Dhofar coast in 1894-1895 led him to identify ruins he believed to be related to the frankincense trade. 

Tragically, Bent contracted malarial fever during a journey to South Arabia and Socotra in 1896-1897 and died in London in May 1897, shortly after his return. His wife, Mabel, continued their work by publishing “Southern Arabia, Soudan and Sakotra” in 1900, detailing their final expedition. 

Bent’s extensive collections of artefacts, numbering in the hundreds, are largely held in the British Museum, with smaller collections distributed amongst various museums in the UK, Greece, Turkey, South Africa, and Zimbabwe. His legacy extends beyond his written works and collections; several species of shells, plants, and a lizard have been named in his honour. Digitized versions of his original notebooks are now accessible through the Hellenic Society’s archive.

title: Brianna Keilar
text:
Brianna Keilar is an American journalist born on September 21, 1980, in Canberra, Australia. Her father, Glenn, is Australian, while her mother, Miriam, is American. The family relocated to Orange County, California in 1982. She graduated from Mission Viejo High School in 1998, having been voted homecoming queen, and then went on to earn dual bachelor's degrees in mass communications and psychology from the University of California, Berkeley in 2001.

Keilar began her broadcasting career in Yakima, Washington, working at the CBS affiliate KIMA and co-hosting a morning radio show on KFFM. She then moved to CBS News, where she worked as an anchor, reporter, and producer for a newscast on MTVU, MTV's college network. She also filled in as an anchor for the CBS News overnight program, *Up to the Minute*, and contributed reporting to the weekend edition of *CBS Evening News*.

She joined CNN as a correspondent for CNN Newsource, covering breaking news for its partner stations.  She later became a general assignment correspondent for CNN, reporting on stories such as the 2007 Virginia Tech massacre, where she was the first CNN correspondent to arrive on the scene. While covering Congress, Keilar received the 2009 National Press Foundation Everett McKinley Dirksen Award for her reporting on the $700 billion bank bailout.  Later, while reporting on the Obama White House, she was awarded the 2014 Aldo Beckman Memorial Award from the White House Correspondents’ Association for her coverage of the rollout of the Affordable Care Act, often referred to as Obamacare.

In 2019, Keilar began writing a column called “Home Front,” focusing on the experiences of military families and aiming to connect civilian and military communities. She hosted the CNN program *CNN Right Now with Brianna Keilar* before joining *New Day* in 2021, co-anchoring the show with John Berman until September 2022. Following the cancellation of *New Day*, she continued to co-anchor until it was replaced by *CNN This Morning* in November 2022. 

As of April 2023, Keilar is a co-anchor of *CNN News Central*, alongside Boris Sanchez and Jim Sciutto, specifically hosting the afternoon edition of the program, which airs from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m. 

In her personal life, Keilar was first married to Dave French, but they later divorced. She married Fernando Lujan, an active-duty Green Beret and National Security Council director, in Las Vegas on December 30, 2016, after becoming engaged in July 2016. They have a son, born on June 8, 2018.

title: Paul Anka
text:
Paul Anka, born in Ottawa, Ontario in 1941, is a Canadian and American singer, songwriter, and actor with a career spanning decades. He achieved early fame with the 1957 hit “Diana,” which topped charts in both Canada and the United States and remains one of the best-selling singles by a Canadian artist. He followed this success with a string of Top 20 hits in 1958, including “It’s Time to Cry” and “(All of a Sudden) My Heart Sings”, quickly becoming a teen idol. He also wrote “It Doesn’t Matter Anymore”, which Buddy Holly recorded shortly before his death, with Anka dedicating royalties from the song to Holly’s family.

Beyond performing, Anka demonstrated songwriting talent, composing the theme for *The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson* and the English lyrics to “My Way,” originally a French song that became a signature piece for Frank Sinatra and has been covered extensively by artists like Elvis Presley. He also penned “She’s a Lady” for Tom Jones and contributed to the soundtrack of *The Longest Day*, even appearing in a cameo role in the film.

While enjoying continued success, Anka experienced a chart comeback in the 1970s with the 1974 hit "(You're) Having My Baby," a duet with Odia Coates that broadened his appeal. This led to further collaborations with Coates, producing three more Top 20 duets. He also recorded the popular jingle for Kodak, “Times of Your Life,” which was later released as a full song and reached the Top 10. 

Anka’s career saw further peaks in the 1990s with the album *A Body of Work*, featuring collaborations with artists such as Celine Dion and Kenny G. In 2005, his album *Rock Swings*, featuring big-band arrangements of contemporary rock songs, earned him renewed recognition, including a star on Canada’s Walk of Fame. He also became involved in later collaborations with Michael Jackson, receiving co-writing credit and royalties for songs like "This Is It," "Love Never Felt So Good," and "Don't Matter to Me," released posthumously.

Anka’s international appeal is notable, particularly in Italy where “Ogni giorno” reached number one in 1962, and in Finland, where he has performed multiple times. He also attempted to gain traction in France and Japan, with some success. He has also performed in Israel and refused to participate in boycott attempts against the country.

Alongside his musical career, Anka has acted in numerous films and television shows, including *The Longest Day*, *Girls Town*, and guest appearances on *That '70s Show* and *Gilmore Girls*. He was also the subject of a National Film Board of Canada documentary, *Lonely Boy*. He even appeared as himself on *The Simpsons* and *American Idol*, and competed on *The Masked Singer* as “Broccoli”. 

Throughout his life, Anka has been recognized for his contributions, including being named an Officer of the Order of Canada. He has also explored business ventures, co-founding the holographic tech startup ARHT Media. He has been married four times and has children, including a daughter who is married to actor Jason Bateman.

title: Elizabeth Inglis
text:
Elizabeth Inglis, born Desiree Mary Lucy Hawkins on July 10, 1913, was a British actress who achieved recognition for her work in film and theatre, and is also known as the mother of actress Sigourney Weaver. She passed away on August 25, 2007, in Santa Barbara, California, at the age of 94. Her parents were Margaret Inglis, born Hunt, and Alan George Hawkins.

Inglis began her film career with a role in *Borrowed Clothes* in 1934. A year later, she appeared in a small part as Hilary Jordan in Alfred Hitchcock’s renowned film, *The 39 Steps* (1935). A significant early role came with the original British production of Patrick Hamilton’s play *Gas Light*, where she portrayed the young maid Nancy. The play ran successfully for 141 performances, opening on December 5, 1938, and closing on June 10, 1939. The success of the stage production led to a live television adaptation for BBC Television in 1939, in which Inglis reprised her role alongside the original cast. 

Following her work in British productions, Inglis moved to Hollywood and took on the stage name Elizabeth Earl. There, she played Adele Ainsworth in William Wyler’s 1940 film *The Letter*, a role for which she became well known. This film marked a high point in her career.

In 1942, she married Pat Weaver, an American television executive. Shortly after their marriage, she chose to retire from acting. The couple remained together until Weaver’s death in 2002. They had two children together, one of whom was the acclaimed actress Sigourney Weaver. 

Interestingly, a connection to her daughter’s most famous role occurred in 1986 with the film *Aliens*. A photograph of Inglis herself was utilized in a deleted scene to depict Amanda Ripley, the elderly mother of Sigourney Weaver’s character, Ellen Ripley. This served as a visual representation of the family history woven into the narrative of the *Alien* franchise.

title: Chris Woakes
text:
Chris Woakes, born in Birmingham in 1989, is a prominent English cricketer who represents England in all international formats and plays domestic cricket for Warwickshire. Initially a promising footballer, playing as a winger for Walsall F.C. until the age of 14, he transitioned to cricket, beginning with Aston Manor Cricket Club at age seven and later Walmley Cricket Club. He progressed through Warwickshire’s youth system, playing for their under-15, under-17, academy, and Second XI teams before making his first appearance for the Warwickshire First XI in 2008, where he quickly became a key bowler, taking 42 wickets that season.

Woakes debuted for England in Twenty20 Internationals in 2011 against Australia, notably scoring the winning runs, and followed this with a successful ODI debut, claiming 6 wickets. He gradually established himself in the England ODI side, and made his Test debut in 2013 during the Ashes series. He became a reliable member of the ODI team, particularly during a 2014 tour of Sri Lanka where he stepped up in the absence of senior bowlers. A standout performance during that tour was a spell of 6/47, considered among the best ODI bowling performances of the year.

Woakes experienced a career highlight in 2018, scoring his maiden Test century (137 not out) against India at Lord’s, and achieving his best match figures with the ball (11/102) against Pakistan at the same venue. This led to his name being added to the Lord’s honours board, an achievement only accomplished by ten players, and him becoming one of five to be honoured for both bowling and batting achievements at the ground. 

He was a crucial part of England’s victories in both the 2019 Cricket World Cup and the 2022 T20 World Cup, earning the Player of the Match award in the 2019 semi-final against Australia for taking three vital wickets. He also contributed significantly to the 2022 T20 World Cup win, playing in every match. He is one of only six players to have been part of both of England’s World Cup winning squads. 

Beyond his international career, Woakes has participated in the Indian Premier League (IPL), representing Kolkata Knight Riders, Royal Challengers Bangalore, and Delhi Capitals, although he opted out of the 2020 season to focus on England’s Test schedule. He also played for the Birmingham Phoenix in The Hundred in 2022. He reached significant milestones in his career, including taking his 100th Test wicket and 150th ODI wicket in 2021 and was recalled for the 2023 Ashes, where he was named England’s Player of the Series following a strong bowling performance and hitting the winning runs in the 3rd Test.

title: Avraham Eilam-Amzallag
text:
Avraham Eilam-Amzallag, born on September 28, 1941, is an Israeli musician and composer with a distinct style rooted in his background and musical training. He began his life in Casablanca, Morocco, before immigrating to Israel during his childhood. This early experience appears to have profoundly influenced his later artistic pursuits.

Eilam-Amzallag pursued formal musical education in Israel, initially focusing on the flute as his instrument of study. He later expanded his musical skillset through compositional studies at the Buchman-Mehta Music Academy in Tel Aviv, suggesting a dedication to both performance and the creation of original works. 

His career has centered around the exploration and presentation of oriental music, a genre he actively champions through the ensemble he founded. This ensemble is specifically dedicated to performing music within this tradition. However, his work isn’t simply a preservation of traditional forms; instead, Eilam-Amzallag's compositions are characterized by a unique fusion. He blends the sounds and structures of oriental Jewish music with contemporary compositional techniques, creating a sound that is both deeply connected to its cultural origins and innovative in its approach.

Although the article doesn’t detail the scope of his wider output, it does list several specific compositions. These include “Desolation,” a piece lasting three minutes and thirty-three seconds, and “(composition for flute)” which is identified as a “Mawal” and runs for five minutes and thirteen seconds. Further evidence of his work is given by “Music for flute and percussion,” a piece composed in 1975. 

Beyond the performance aspect of his musical life, Eilam-Amzallag has also engaged in the publication of his work, with “Music for flute and percussion” (1975) being a formally published composition. This indicates a desire to share his musical ideas beyond the realm of live performance and establish a lasting record of his artistry.

Within the broader context of Israeli musical culture, Eilam-Amzallag’s work is relevant to the field of Music of Israel, as noted in the "See also" section of the article, showcasing his contribution to the country's musical landscape. The article itself provides a concise overview of his life and career, establishing him as a figure who bridges tradition and innovation in Israeli music.

title: Fernando da Costa Novaes
text:
Fernando da Costa Novaes was a Brazilian ornithologist born on April 6, 1927, and who died on March 24, 2004. He dedicated his career to the study of birdlife in the Amazon region. He earned his doctorate in 1971 from the State University of São Paulo at Rio Claro, with his thesis focusing on the ecology of birds in a secondary growth area of the lower Amazon River, in the state of Pará.

Novaes spent much of his professional life at the Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi in Belém, where he built up the second largest bird skin and skeleton collection in Brazil. This collection was later named in his honor, recognizing his significant contribution to the museum. His research primarily focused on defining the geographical boundaries of the Amazon’s bird fauna and clarifying complex taxonomic relationships within the region’s avian species.

In 1954, Novaes received a fellowship from the Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation, allowing him to conduct research at the Museum of Vertebrate Zoology at the University of California, Berkeley, under the guidance of prominent ornithologist Alden H. Miller. 

Throughout his career, Novaes was a prolific publisher, with his work detailed in obituaries written by Oren and Silva. He authored and co-authored numerous articles across a variety of scientific journals including *Acta Amazonica*, *Anais da Academia Brasileira de Ciencias*, *Ararajuba*, *Arquivos de Zoologia*, *The Auk*, *Biological Conservation*, *Boletim do Museu Nacional Zoologia*, *Boletim do Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi*, *Bulletin of the British Ornithologists' Club*, *The Condor*, *Goeldiana zoologia*, *Papéis Avulsos de Zoologia*, *Revista Brasileira de Biologia*, *Revista Brasileira de Zoologia*, *Revista Científica*, and *Summa Brasiliensis Biologiae*. These publications covered a wide range of topics, including species descriptions, geographic variation, ecological studies, and behavioral observations of various Amazonian birds.

Novaes is also commemorated in the scientific name of the Alagoas foliage-gleaner, *Philydor novaesi*, a testament to his lasting impact on the field of ornithology. His extensive body of work continues to be a valuable resource for researchers studying the birds of the Amazon and Brazil.

title: Mukesh (actor)
text:
Mukesh, born Mukesh Babu on March 5, 1957, is a prominent Indian actor, producer, television personality, and politician primarily known for his work in Malayalam cinema. Over a four-decade career, he has appeared in over 275 films, alongside occasional roles in Tamil productions. He comes from a family steeped in acting; his parents, O. Madhavan and Vijayakumari, were both actors, and his sister Sandhya Rajendran, along with her husband, are also performers.

Mukesh’s education includes a Bachelor of Science degree from Sree Narayana College, Kollam, and a law degree from The Kerala Law Academy Law College, Thiruvananthapuram. Before entering films, he was involved in stage dramas. He debuted on screen in 1982 with *Balloon*, quickly following with a leading role in *Ithu Njangalude Katha*, a remake of a Tamil film. He gained recognition through comedic roles in films directed by Priyadarshan during the mid-1980s, often in supporting capacities. *Mutharamkunnu P.O.* (1985) gained cult status over time, while *Boeing Boeing* (1985) marked his first major commercial success and his initial collaboration with Mohanlal, leading to numerous joint projects. He also worked alongside Mammootty in several popular films of the late 1980s, including *Snehamulla Simham* and *Oru CBI Diary Kurippu*, reprising his role in subsequent installments of the CBI series. *Ramji Rao Speaking* (1989) proved to be a breakthrough role, becoming a major box office hit and cementing his position in the industry.

The 1990s saw Mukesh taking on more leading roles. He starred in *In Harihar Nagar*, a defining film of Malayalam cinema's golden age of comedy, and formed a successful pairing with Jayaram in films like *Thoovalsparsham* and *Malayogom*. He also achieved solo success with films like *Gajakesariyogam* and *Champion Thomas*.  He was part of the hugely successful *Godfather* (1991) which ran for a record-breaking 417 days in theatres. He continued to deliver hits such as *Mannar Mathai Speaking* and *Kanakkinavu*, which won the Nargis Dutt Award for Best Feature Film on National Integration at the IFFI.

In more recent years, Mukesh ventured into film production, co-producing *Kadha Parayumbol* (2007) which won the Kerala State Film Award, and *Thattathin Marayathu* (2012), considered a key film in the Malayalam New Wave. He has also hosted television shows, including a Malayalam version of *Deal or No Deal* and the comedy talk show *Badai bungalow*. 

Beyond acting and production, Mukesh is actively involved in politics as a member of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) (CPI-M). He was first elected to the Kerala Legislative Assembly in 2016, representing the Kollam constituency, and was re-elected in 2021, though with a reduced margin. He unsuccessfully contested for a Lok Sabha seat in 2024. His public life has also faced controversy, including allegations of inappropriate phone calls and, more seriously, accusations of sexual harassment, leading to his arrest in September 2024. He authored two books, *Mukesh Kathakal* and *Mukesh Babu and Party in Dubai*. He served as chairman of the Kerala Sangeetha Nataka Academy.

title: Jan-Michael Gambill
text:
Jan-Michael Gambill, born June 3, 1977, is a former American professional tennis player who reached a career-high ranking of world No. 14 in 2001. He is particularly remembered for his distinctive double-handed forehand. He began his professional career in 1996 and achieved significant results, including reaching the quarterfinals of Wimbledon in 2000 and the final of the Miami Masters in 2001. Over the course of his career, he secured three singles titles.

Growing up in the countryside of Spokane, Washington, Gambill currently splits his time between Los Angeles and Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, where he lives with his partner, Malek Alqadi, an architect and developer. He has had sponsorship deals with both Jaguar cars and Prince sporting goods. Beyond tennis, Gambill is dedicated to wildlife conservation, supporting Cat Tales Zoological Park and fundraising for Sir Elton John’s AIDS Foundation.

Gambill was inspired by tennis greats Jimmy Connors and John McEnroe as a young player, starting tennis at the age of five. He distinguished himself by defeating several highly ranked players throughout his career, including former World No. 1s like Roger Federer, Carlos Moyá, Lleyton Hewitt, Gustavo Kuerten, Marcelo Ríos, Pete Sampras, and Andre Agassi, alongside Grand Slam champions such as Michael Chang and Thomas Johansson. His most notable Grand Slam run was at Wimbledon in 2000, where he defeated Hewitt, Santoro, Goldstein and Enqvist before being stopped by Pete Sampras in the quarterfinals. He also reached the fourth round of the US Open in 2002.

A significant portion of Gambill’s career was affected by injuries. He struggled with a recurring shin condition while ranked in the top 40, which limited his play after 2004. Attempting to compensate for reduced mobility, he increased his serve speed, which ultimately led to a shoulder injury. 

After officially retiring from consistent tour play, Gambill remained involved in tennis, playing for the Boston Lobsters in World Team Tennis starting in 2008, alongside players like Agassi, Isner, and Ginepri. He briefly returned to competition in 2009 and 2010, reaching the semifinals of a Futures tournament and the quarterfinals of another. However, he has not competed on the pro tour since October 2010. He transitioned into coaching, working with CoCo Vandeweghe, a former Lobsters teammate, starting in 2011. Later, in 2017, he coached Jared Donaldson. Currently, as of 2020, he works as a sports analyst for the Tennis Channel. Gambill is openly gay and maintains a relationship with Malek Alqadi.

title: Lina Marulanda
text:
Lina Marulanda, born Lina María Marulanda Cuartas on May 15, 1980, was a Colombian television personality and model who tragically died on April 22, 2010. She was originally from Medellín, Colombia, and began her career in modeling at the young age of twelve. Her early life involved balancing her education with the demands of a burgeoning modeling career, a situation she later expressed regret about in a 2004 interview. 

Marulanda initially attended Santa María del Rosario de Medellín High School, but transferred to Parra Paris High School after experiencing difficulties with the school's administration and nuns. Following her graduation from high school, she pursued higher education at Jorge Tadeo Lozano University in Bogotá, studying advertising. 

Her career in television began in 2002 when she started presenting for CM& News. She then became a prominent figure at Caracol News, working there for six years. During her time at Caracol News, she presented the 0700 edition and covered international news. She also co-hosted the entertainment segment of the evening news, first with actress Margarita Ortega and later with model Adriana Arboleda, starting in 2003. In December 2005, she took the lead role in presenting the entertainment portion of Caracol News at 12:30, alongside journalist Ivan Lalinde. 

Beyond news presentation, Marulanda expanded her television work to include hosting the reality show *Challenge 20-07* on Canal Caracol in early 2007. That same year, she returned to CM& News to provide special coverage of Colombiamoda 2007, and also reported on the event for W Radio.  She then joined the W Radio team for *La hora del Regreso* on July 24, 2007, replacing Marcela Sarmiento. 

In addition to her work in television, Marulanda was a successful spokesmodel for several major clothing brands and graced the pages of popular magazines such as *SoHo*, *Don Juan*, *Cromos*, and *G*.

Marulanda’s life was cut short when she died after falling from the balcony of her sixth-floor apartment. Authorities determined her death to be a suicide. At the time of her death, she was undergoing divorce proceedings from her second husband, Carlos Oñate, after a marriage of only three months. She was surrounded by family and a doctor when the incident occurred, with her parents, ex-husband, and a physician present.

title: Imbolo Mbue
text:
Imbolo Mbue, born in 1981, is a Cameroonian-American novelist and short story writer currently residing in New York City. She is best known for her acclaimed debut novel, *Behold the Dreamers*, published in 2016, which brought her significant recognition including the PEN/Faulkner Award for Fiction and the Blue Metropolis Words to Change Award. Her writing frequently explores the experiences of immigrants, drawing heavily from her own life and the stories of others.

Mbue was raised in Limbé, Cameroon, in the English-speaking region, until her family supported her pursuit of higher education in the United States. She arrived in the U.S. in 1998 and earned an undergraduate degree in business management from Rutgers University in 2002, followed by a Master’s degree from Columbia University in 2006. She initially worked in the corporate sector in New York City, but lost her job during the economic downturn of the Great Recession. This experience, coupled with her observations of the economic disparities in the city – specifically witnessing the contrast between cab drivers and the executives they drove – provided the inspiration for *Behold the Dreamers*.
