She had previously competed at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, where the team finished fourth.

Pisani’s involvement with hockey began at the club level with Burnside Hockey Club in 1976, where she was part of eight premiership-winning teams over fifteen years. She was recognised as their Best and Fairest player in 1985 and 1987 and later awarded Life Membership in 2002. She also achieved individual accolades, winning the Association Medal as South Australia’s Best and Fairest Player in both 1985 and 1992. She later played and coached at Port Adelaide for six years, leading them to a premiership in 1993 and earning Hockey SA’s Coach of the Year award. She also coached Woodville Hockey Club’s Premier League team for two years and was jointly named Hockey SA Coach of the Year again in 2012.

Beyond club hockey, Pisani dedicated significant time to state level hockey, serving as a State Selector, State Coach and State Team Manager for South Australia. She represented South Australia’s Southern Suns for twelve years, captaining the team for five of those. Internationally, she debuted for Australia at the 1981 World Cup and participated in numerous tournaments, including the 1983 World Cup where Australia won bronze and the 1987 Champions Trophy where they took silver. 

Following her playing career, Pisani transitioned into a highly successful role as a selector and manager. She was a National Women’s Senior Selector for the Hockeyroos from 1993 to 2000, serving as Head Selector during a period of unprecedented national success. Under her leadership, and with coach Ric Charlesworth, the Hockeyroos secured gold medals at both the 1996 and 2000 Summer Olympics. She continued to contribute to the sport as a National Youth Selector from 2012, and as Team Manager for a development tour in 2014.

Pisani received numerous accolades for her contributions to hockey. She was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia (OAM) in 1989, inducted into the South Australian Sport Hall of Fame in 2015, and recognised on the South Australian Sports Institute Hockey Honour Roll. She also received the Australian Sports Medal in 2000 and a Team Sport Australia Award in 2003, acknowledging the significance of the 1988 Olympic gold medal. She was twice a finalist for the Caltex SA Sports Star of the Year Award.

title: Timothy Evans
text:
Timothy John Evans was a Welsh lorry driver executed in 1950 for the murder of his infant daughter, Geraldine. The case became notorious as a major miscarriage of justice, as evidence later revealed his neighbour, John Christie, was a serial killer responsible for the deaths of Beryl Evans, Geraldine, and several other women. Evans, born in 1924 in Merthyr Tydfil, Wales, had a difficult childhood marked by his father’s abandonment, learning difficulties, and a chronic foot condition that disrupted his education. He worked various jobs, including painting and decorating, and coal mining, before moving to London with his mother in 1939.

In 1947, Evans married Beryl Thorley, and in 1948 they moved into a flat at 10 Rillington Place in Notting Hill, sharing the property with John and Ethel Christie. Their marriage was troubled by frequent arguments stemming from financial difficulties and Evans’s drinking. When Beryl became pregnant with their second child, she decided to have an abortion, and Evans initially agreed. Following this, Evans reported his wife’s death to police, initially claiming it was accidental during an attempted abortion facilitated by an unknown man. He later changed his story, implicating Christie as the one who offered to perform the abortion.

The subsequent police investigation was flawed. Despite finding inconsistencies in Evans's statements and overlooking crucial evidence, such as skeletal remains in the garden, he confessed to strangling both his wife and daughter, influenced by lengthy and emotionally draining interrogations and a fear of police violence. He was convicted of Geraldine’s murder in a swift trial, with Christie providing key testimony against him. 

Three years after Evans’s execution, Christie was exposed as a serial killer following the discovery of multiple bodies hidden within 10 Rillington Place. He confessed to murdering Beryl Evans while awaiting his own execution. A 1966 inquiry confirmed Christie’s responsibility for Geraldine’s death, leading to a posthumous pardon for Evans. Despite acknowledging Evans’s innocence, the High Court refused to formally quash his conviction in 2004 due to cost concerns. 

The Evans case sparked significant public outcry and contributed to reforms in the British legal system, including restrictions on capital punishment, the introduction of diminished responsibility as a defense, and the eventual abolition of hanging for murder. The case highlighted the dangers of relying on questionable confessions obtained through coercive interrogation tactics and the importance of thorough forensic investigation. Crucially, evidence later emerged – including testimony from workmen – that directly contradicted the prosecution’s case and supported Evans’s claim of Christie’s involvement, but this evidence was ignored or suppressed during the original investigation and trial.

title: Mamunul Islam
text:
Mamunul Islam, born December 12, 1988, is a Bangladeshi footballer who primarily plays as a midfielder. He had a lengthy career with both club and national team, representing Bangladesh from 2009 to 2020, and serving as captain of the national team from 2013 until his international retirement in 2020. Throughout his career, he has secured five league titles playing for multiple clubs.

Mamunul began his professional journey with Brothers Union in 2005, winning both the Dhaka Premier Division League and the Federation Cup that year. He then moved to Abahani Limited Dhaka in the 2008-09 season, promptly winning the Bangladesh Premier League. A subsequent transfer took him to Mohammedan SC, where he achieved success by winning the Federation Cup and Super Cup. 

He then joined Sheikh Jamal Dhanmondi Club in 2010-11, adding another league title to his collection. After a season with Muktijoddha Sangsad KC, he moved to Sheikh Russel KC in 2012-13, where he won the league, the Federation Cup and the Independence Cup. A return to Sheikh Jamal Dhanmondi Club in 2013-14 yielded two more league titles, with Mamunul captaining the team to victory in the 2013-14 season. 

In a notable period, he was loaned to Indian Super League side Atlético de Kolkata for the inaugural season, becoming the only South Asian player outside of India to participate. He also impressed in the IFA Shield with Sheikh Jamal Dhanmondi Club, leading them to the final.  He later joined Chittagong Abahani Limited for a record transfer fee of 65 lakh taka, captaining the team in his first season before returning to Abahani Limited Dhaka in 2018, contributing his experience to the team. He rejoined Mohammedan SC in 2021 and later played for Rahmatganj MFS in 2022.

Beyond club success, Mamunul also achieved international recognition, winning a gold medal with the Bangladesh U-23 team at the 2010 South Asian Games. His career has been marked by consistent performance and leadership, making him a prominent figure in Bangladeshi football.

title: Generoso Rossi
text:
Generoso Rossi, born on January 3, 1979, is an Italian former professional footballer who played as a goalkeeper throughout his career. He began his professional journey with A.S. Bari, experiencing loan spells with Serie C1 teams before returning to Bari in 2000, where he eventually made his Serie A debut against Verona on September 30th of the same year.

His career took a turn in January 2001 with a transfer to Venezia, which was quickly followed by a move to Palermo as a result of a change in ownership, with Maurizio Zamparini acquiring both clubs. Rossi then spent time on loan with U.S. Lecce and ultimately signed with A.C. Siena in the summer of 2003.

A significant setback occurred when Rossi was banned from football due to involvement in a betting scandal. After serving the ban, he resumed his career in January 2005, signing an 18-month contract with Queens Park Rangers. He then moved to Triestina in the summer of 2005. 

In January 2008, Rossi joined Calcio Catania on loan in a swap deal involving Babu. At Catania, he served as the third-choice goalkeeper, positioned behind Ciro Polito and Albano Bizarri, and ahead of Raffaele Ioime. The following season, in 2008/2009, he transferred to Gallipoli in Lega Pro Prima Divisione – B. Although Gallipoli achieved promotion to Serie B, financial difficulties within the club led to Rossi’s departure.

Rossi found a relatively stable period with Sorrento, joining them in February 2010 and remaining for two and a half seasons. He became a key player for the team, which narrowly missed promotion to Serie B on two occasions. Following the resignation of Sorrento’s president and uncertainty surrounding the club's future in the summer of 2012, Rossi left to pursue other opportunities. However, after a period without a club, he was re-signed by Sorrento on a free contract in November 2012.

Beyond his club career, Rossi also represented Italy at the youth level. He participated in the Toulon Tournament for Italy in 2000 and was selected for the under-21 squad during the 2002 UEFA European Under-21 Football Championship. 

He achieved one notable honour during his time with Sorrento, winning the Lega Pro Prima Divisione title in 2009.

title: Frank Middlemass
text:
Francis George Middlemass was an English actor born in 1919 and passing away in 2006, known for frequently portraying older characters even early in his career. He achieved significant recognition for a number of television roles, most notably as Rocky Hardcastle in the long-running sitcom *As Time Goes By*, Algy Herries in *To Serve Them All My Days*, and Dr. Alex Ferrenby in *Heartbeat*. 

Middlemass’s acting journey began after serving in the army, where he rose to the rank of lieutenant colonel and was wounded during the Dunkirk retreat. He started his stage career in repertory theatre in Penzance before joining the Old Vic Company, with whom he toured extensively across the globe, including performances in *Twelfth Night* alongside Vivien Leigh. He later worked with Ian McKellen’s Actors’ Company and performed alongside Peter O’Toole in *Waiting for Godot*. 

His television career started in 1958 with a role in *Dixon of Dock Green*, and he became a familiar face throughout the 60s, 70s, and 80s with appearances in shows like *Z-Cars*, *The Avengers*, *Doctor at Large*, *War and Peace* (as Kutuzov), *Upstairs, Downstairs*, and *The Sweeney*. He also took on film roles, including a part in Stanley Kubrick’s *Barry Lyndon*. He played a range of characters in numerous television dramas and comedies, including roles in *Juliet Bravo*, *Yes Minister*, and *Miss Marple*.

Beyond television and film, Middlemass had a substantial radio career, most famously as the fourth actor to portray Dan Archer in the radio soap opera *The Archers* – a role he held for four years until the character's death. He also lent his voice to several radio plays and albums, including *The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy*. A committed advocate, he made a BBC Radio appeal for Headway, the National Head Injuries Association, successfully raising considerable funds. 

He was involved with the Royal Shakespeare Company from 1984, performing in productions of *Romeo and Juliet* and *A Midsummer Night's Dream*, among others. Throughout his career, he continued to work on stage, even into his eighties, with roles in *The Importance of Being Earnest* and a one-man show called *Frankly Speaking*. His final television appearances were in the 2005 reunion specials of *As Time Goes By*.  Middlemass never married and lived with his close friend, fellow actor Geoffrey Toone, for forty years until Toone’s death in 2005. He died in 2006 at the age of 87.

title: Ahsee Tuala
text:
Ahsee Tuala, born on August 23, 1989, is a rugby union player currently playing as a fullback for Northampton Saints in the Aviva Premiership. Though originally from Samoa, his family moved to New Zealand when he was two years old, and he was raised in South Auckland. He began his professional rugby career with the Counties Manukau Steelers in New Zealand, making his debut during the 2009 Air New Zealand Cup season at the age of 20. He quickly became a valuable player for the Steelers, accumulating over 50 ITM Cup appearances due to his versatility across the backline. He also participated in development squads for the Chiefs in both 2010 and 2011.

Tuala transitioned to English rugby in February 2015, initially signing with Northampton Saints for the remainder of the 2014-15 season. He subsequently agreed to a permanent contract with the club, establishing himself at Franklin's Gardens. While he had been with the Saints for a couple of seasons, the 2016/17 season marked a significant step forward in his career. He consistently secured a starting position, initially while George North was fulfilling international commitments, and continued to do so even upon North’s return. During that season, he scored five tries for the Saints, becoming a key component of their attacking backline. 

His contributions were recognized with the Saints’ Supporter’s Breakthrough Player of the Year award at the end of the 2016/17 season, surpassing fellow nominees Nic Groom and Juan Pablo Estelles. More recently, Tuala played a crucial role in securing Northampton Saints’ qualification for the European Rugby Champions Cup, scoring the decisive try in a narrow one-point victory against Stade Francais.

Tuala’s international representation began with New Zealand. He was initially involved with the New Zealand Under-20 wider squad in 2009, and later included in the New Zealand sevens wider training group in 2012. However, he chose to pursue international opportunities with Samoa, withdrawing from the New Zealand sevens squad in January 2012 to focus on achieving recognition with his birth nation. This ambition was fulfilled in 2014 when he was selected for the Samoan squad for the end-of-year rugby union tests. He made his debut for Samoa on November 14, 2014, in a match against Canada, which Samoa won 23-13, played in Vannes, France. He was again called up to represent Samoa, alongside teammate Ken Pisi from Northampton Saints, for the 2017 internationals.

title: Vasily Chuikov
text:
Vasily Ivanovich Chuikov was a prominent Soviet military commander who rose to fame for his tenacious defense of Stalingrad during World War II and for accepting the surrender of German forces in Berlin. Born in 1900 to a peasant family near Tula, he began working in a factory at the age of twelve. Following the 1917 Russian Revolution, he joined the Red Army and distinguished himself in the ensuing Civil War, earning awards for bravery. He continued his military education at the Frunze Military Academy, after which he served as a military attaché and intelligence officer, notably in China and the Russian Far East.

Prior to the German invasion of the Soviet Union, Chuikov commanded armies during the Soviet invasion of Poland in 1939 and the Winter War against Finland in 1940. In 1940, he was assigned as a military attaché to China, tasked with supporting Chiang Kai-shek and the Nationalist forces against Japan, a mission directed by Stalin to keep Japan occupied and prevent them from threatening the Soviet Union. He provided substantial military aid to the Nationalists, despite criticism from Communist leaders like Mao Zedong.

In 1942, Chuikov was recalled to the Soviet Union to confront the German advance. He was appointed commander of the 62nd Army and tasked with defending Stalingrad at all costs. Recognizing the Wehrmacht’s superior firepower, he implemented a tactic of keeping Soviet positions as close as possible to the German lines, minimizing the effectiveness of German air support and enabling close-quarters combat. Despite the immense destruction and heavy losses, Chuikov’s army held on, contributing significantly to the eventual Soviet counter-offensive in November 1942, which encircled and ultimately led to the surrender of the German 6th Army in early 1943.

Following Stalingrad, Chuikov’s 8th Guards Army participated in Operation Bagration and the Vistula–Oder Offensive, pushing through Poland. He culminated his wartime service by personally accepting the unconditional surrender of German forces in Berlin on May 2, 1945. 

After the war, Chuikov held several high-ranking positions, including Chief of the Group of Soviet Forces in Germany, commander of the Kiev Military District, Chief of the Soviet Armed Forces, and head of the Soviet Civil Defense Forces. He received the title Hero of the Soviet Union twice, and was also awarded the Distinguished Service Cross by the United States. In 1955, he was promoted to Marshal of the Soviet Union. He died in 1982 and, at his request, was buried at the Stalingrad memorial at Mamayev Kurgan, a poignant testament to the battle that defined his military career. His death was ultimately caused by complications from a war wound sustained in Poland in 1920.

title: Karni Liddell
text:
Karni Liddell, born on March 1st, 1979, in Rockhampton, Queensland, is an Australian Paralympic swimmer who also works as a radio presenter for 4BC. Her life has been significantly shaped by a long and difficult journey to receive an accurate medical diagnosis. Initially diagnosed with Spinal Muscular Atrophy as an infant, at twelve months old, she recently discovered in 2019, through whole genome sequencing conducted in Europe, that she actually has Congenital Titinopathy, another neuromuscular wasting disease. This followed a twelve-year search for a definitive explanation for her condition, a process described as lengthy, traumatic, and financially burdensome for her family. 

From a young age, medical professionals predicted a limited future for Liddell, informing her parents she would likely never walk and would not survive into adulthood. Despite these initial prognoses, she achieved remarkable success as an athlete. By the age of fourteen, she had already broken a world record in swimming, demonstrating significant athletic talent and resilience. 

Liddell represented Australia at the Paralympic Games on two occasions: in 1996 and again in 2000. She was successful at both Games, winning medals and establishing herself as a prominent figure in Paralympic sport. Her accomplishments culminated in being named Captain of the Australian Swimming Team for the 2000 Sydney Paralympic Games, a testament to her leadership and standing within the team.

Beyond her athletic achievements, Liddell has also engaged in public awareness campaigns and artistic projects. She was one of eighteen Australian Paralympians who participated in a nude calendar project photographed by Emma Hack, aimed at challenging perceptions of disability. Liddell’s contribution to the calendar involved body paint designed to resemble a polka-dotted bikini, and she wore sunglasses as part of the image. Furthermore, in 2008, she was featured in artwork by Ludmila Clark, with her image displayed at the Customs House in her hometown of Rockhampton, alongside other Queenslanders. This demonstrates her willingness to participate in projects that celebrate diversity and challenge conventional representations.

title: Vladimir Lenin
text:
Vladimir Lenin, born Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov in 1870, was a pivotal figure in 20th-century history, leading the Bolsheviks and establishing the first socialist state. He served as the first head of government of Soviet Russia from 1917 until his death in 1924, and subsequently of the Soviet Union until 1924. His adaptation of Marxist theory, known as Leninism, became a dominant force in the communist movement internationally. 

Lenin’s path to revolution began with personal tragedy. After his father, a dedicated educator who rose to middle-class status from a lower-class background, died in 1886, his older brother, Alexander, became involved in a plot to assassinate the Tsar and was executed in 1887. This profoundly impacted Lenin, leading him to embrace revolutionary socialist politics. He was expelled from Kazan University for protesting and later earned a law degree before becoming a Marxist activist in Saint Petersburg.  His early activism led to arrest and a three-year exile to Siberia in 1897, after which he moved to Western Europe, becoming a leading figure within the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party.

A key moment came in 1903 when the party split between Lenin’s Bolshevik faction and the Mensheviks. Lenin advocated for a tightly organized “vanguard party” to lead the proletariat in overthrowing capitalism, a concept central to Leninism. He briefly returned to Russia during the unrest of 1905. During World War I, he campaigned for the war’s transformation into a Europe-wide proletarian revolution. Following the February Revolution of 1917, which overthrew Tsar Nicholas II, Lenin returned to Russia and spearheaded the October Revolution, successfully overthrowing the Provisional Government and establishing Bolshevik rule.

Lenin’s government implemented radical changes, abolishing private land ownership, nationalizing major industries and banks, and withdrawing Russia from World War I through the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk. He also sought to promote global revolution through the Communist International. The Bolsheviks, initially in a coalition, eventually consolidated power during the Russian Civil War, employing a brutal policy known as the Red Terror to suppress opposition. Facing famine and unrest, Lenin introduced the New Economic Policy in 1921, a temporary retreat from strict communism designed to stabilize the economy. The Red Army ultimately prevailed in the Civil War, leading to the formation of the Soviet Union in 1922, though some nations, like Poland, gained independence.

Lenin suffered a series of strokes beginning in 1922, which incapacitated him before his death in 1924. His death triggered a power struggle within the Communist Party, ultimately resulting in Joseph Stalin’s ascent to power.  After his death, Lenin became the subject of a widespread personality cult within the Soviet Union, becoming an ideological figurehead under Stalin. He remains a controversial figure, praised by some for establishing a revolutionary government and criticized by others for establishing a repressive dictatorship responsible for mass killings. Despite the debate, he is widely considered one of the most influential figures of the 20th century.

title: Kerwin Bell
text:
Kerwin Bell is an American football coach and former player, currently the head coach of Western Carolina University’s football team, a position he’s held since 2021. Born in Live Oak, Florida in 1965, Bell enjoyed a 14-year professional career spanning the Canadian Football League (CFL), World League of American Football (WLAF), and the National Football League (NFL) before transitioning to coaching. He grew up on a tobacco farm in Mayo, Florida and excelled in multiple sports at Lafayette County High School, leading the football team to their only state championship.

Despite his high school success, Bell was lightly recruited and walked on at the University of Florida in 1983. He quickly rose to prominence, becoming the starting quarterback in 1984 after injuries to other players. In his first collegiate start against defending national champion Miami, he demonstrated poise, throwing a late touchdown pass despite ultimately losing a close game. He led the Gators to a 9-1-1 record that season, earning SEC Player of the Year honors, although the team was later penalized for NCAA violations. Bell continued to excel at Florida for three more seasons, solidifying his place as a standout quarterback and graduating in 1987.

Bell’s professional career was marked by success in the CFL and WLAF, though he never became a consistent starter in the NFL. He played for several teams, including the Miami Dolphins, Atlanta Falcons, Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Orlando Thunder, Sacramento Gold Miners, Edmonton Eskimos, Indianapolis Colts, Toronto Argonauts, and Winnipeg Blue Bombers. Remarkably, he holds the highest career passer rating in NFL history, completing all five of his attempted passes for 75 yards and a touchdown during a brief stint with the Colts, albeit in a very limited sample.

Following his playing career, Bell moved into coaching, starting at the high school level with Trinity Catholic High School in Ocala, Florida, where he led the team to their first state championship in 2005. He then transitioned to collegiate coaching, becoming the head coach at Jacksonville University in 2007. During nine seasons there, he led the Dolphins to three conference championships. He continued his success at Valdosta State University, leading the Blazers to an undefeated season and the NCAA Division II national championship in 2018 with a high-powered offense. A brief stint as offensive coordinator at the University of South Florida under Charlie Strong ended with both being dismissed after one season. 

In 2021, Bell accepted the head coaching position at Western Carolina, where he has begun to turn around a struggling program, leading them to their first winning season in six years in 2022. He is known for his offensive philosophies, which were heavily influenced by his time working under Steve Spurrier at the University of Florida.
